docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A teaching book on how randomness is tested: p-values and entropy, the NIST SP 800-22 and SP 800-90B batteries, Diehard, FIPS 140-2, AIS 31, TestU01 and PractRand, and what a pass can and cannot prove.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Additional Tests (I): Bias, Entropy, Correlation and Compression
docs.text: The next five chapters describe twenty-one further tests, grouped by what they look for. They come from a reference implementation written by the author, and they are included for two reasons: each is a compact lesson in how to design a test with an exact or well-understood null distribution, and the suite as a whole shows how to calibrate tests on known-good data and combine their results into an honest verdict. This first chapter covers the core statistical tests: bias, multi-scale entropy, correlation, entropy stability across windows, periodicity and predictability, the Shannon entropy test and compression.

docs.title: 10.1 The additional tests and how to read their results
docs.text:
The tests of Chapters 10 to 14 are 21 numbered tests: 18 statistical tests that each give a p-value, 2 generator tests that either find a matching rule or do not, and test 8, which reads all the others and gives a verdict. They come from a reference implementation written by the author, and they were built so that every result can be explained and defended. In these chapters "we" and "our" mean that implementation and its measurements.

Group Tests What the group asks Core statistical tests 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10 Is the data even, independent and incompressible? TRNG/QRNG source tests 11, 12, 13 Does it behave like raw physical noise, or stall? Advanced mathematical tests U1, U2, U3, U4, U5, U6 Is there structure that needs heavier mathematics to see? Research-grade tests H1, H2 Can a trained predictor win? Do Hamming weights depend on each other? Generator proofs 6, 7 Does the data follow a simple generator's rule? Source classification 8 Given all of the above, what can we honestly say?

Each statistical test passes when \(p \ge 0.01\). Where a test combines several sub-tests, it reports a Bonferroni or Sidak value, so its single p-value already accounts for the combining.

How to read the measured results. Each test below reports two measurements.

False alarms come from calibration: 120 samples of good data, each 1 MiB, half from os.urandom and half from SHA-256 counter mode. We count how many fail at \(p < 0.01\). With only 120 samples the count is rough. Even "0 of 120" is consistent with a true rate of up to 3.0% (95% interval), so read it as "no sign of trouble", not as "never". The counts are from the full rerun on the final code, and they move with chance: test 5 went from 4 of 120 in an earlier run to 1 of 120 here.

Detections come from a power run: 59 samples, 58 of them with an expected verdict (parity has none). Most are 2 MiB, and 50 of them come from two runs of the author's own corpus (a different seed each time, with the jitter sources re-measured), so counts are samples, not distinct generators. In these chapters:

  • "Raw physical" means the 10 unconditioned physical samples. Four are real CPU timing jitter, and six are simulations of physics, driven by a PRNG.
  • "Weak generators" means the 30 samples labelled as weak PRNGs.
  • "Defective" means one sample: SHA-256 used as a stateless conditioner with repeating input.
  • "Parity" means one public Zenodo dataset: real quantum data from entangled photons, but its authors repeated an 8,000-byte string to fill the file. So it is not a fair test of a QRNG, and most of its flags below come from the repetition.
  • "Flagged" means \(p < 0.01\). The count at the stricter verdict line is added only where it differs.

Two more samples are real-world PRNG files from Zenodo (GFSR4 and MT19937), and the other 15 are the clean samples listed at the end of Chapter 2. A sample can be flagged by a test without changing its verdict.

docs.title: 10.2 Bias (test 1)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Imagine a slightly bent coin. A few tosses will not show it, but thousands will. We also treat a byte as eight separate seats, each with its own coin, because one bent coin in seat 3 can be hidden when you only look at the overall total.

Example 10.2: Bias

Take 100 bits with 62 ones. The exact two-sided binomial p-value is 0.0210. (The normal shortcut gives 0.0164, a fair approximation.) On its own that would pass at 0.01 anyway, and because the test checks 9 things, it would be reported as \(9 \times 0.0210 = 0.189\) if it were the smallest. For the side measurement, suppose the most common byte appears 12 times in 1000 bytes. Then \(\hat{p} = 0.012\), the upper bound is \(p_u = 0.0209\), and the min-entropy estimate is 5.58 bits per byte.

The mathematics. The whole-file test counts ones among \(n\) bits, and each position test counts ones in one seat across \(N\) bytes:

\[ S \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, \tfrac{1}{2}), \qquad p_{\text{all}} = \min\bigl(1,\ 2\, P(X \ge \max(S, n-S))\bigr) \] \[ z_b = \frac{S_b - N/2}{\sqrt{N/4}}, \qquad p_b = \mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{|z_b|}{\sqrt{2}}\right), \quad b = 0, \dots, 7 \] \[ p = \min\bigl(1,\ 9 \min(p_{\text{all}}, p_0, \dots, p_7)\bigr) \]
  • \(n\): the number of bits, equal to \(8N\).
  • \(S\): the number of 1 bits in the whole sample.
  • \(X\): a binomial variable with the same \(n\) and probability one half.
  • \(S_b\): the number of 1 bits at position \(b\) of each byte.
  • \(z_b\): how many standard deviations \(S_b\) sits from \(N/2\).

The factor 9 is Bonferroni over the 9 sub-tests. The binomial test is exact below \(10^7\) bits. Above that the code uses the normal approximation, \(\mathrm{erfc}\) of the z-score, which at this size is accurate.

The test also reports, without using it for pass or fail, the SP 800-90B most-common-value min-entropy: \(H = -\log_2 p_u\), with \(p_u = \min(1,\ \hat{p} + 2.576 \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/(N-1)})\), where \(\hat{p}\) is the share of the most common byte. This reproduces the standard's worked example (\(p_u = 0.6895\) gives 0.5363 bits).

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 1 of 120. It flagged 15 of 59: all 10 raw physical, 4 weak generators (MINSTD and RANDU) and parity. At the verdict line that falls to 13, because the sim-drifting-bits sample only reached \(p = 0.0035\) and \(p = 0.0094\). At 1 MiB, the overall ones fraction has to reach about 0.50056 to fail. It sees balance and nothing else. A file running 0, 1, 2, ..., 255 over and over passes with \(p = 1\), because every seat is balanced, although it is totally predictable. MT19937 and java.util.Random passed too. (A repeating 0101 pattern does fail, because each seat is constant.)

docs.title: 10.3 Multi-scale entropy (test 2)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Read a sentence one letter at a time and it may look fine. Read it in pairs and you notice that "qu" always travels together. This test looks at the bit stream with sixteen different lenses: 1 bit at a time, 2 bits at a time, and so on up to 16.

Example 10.3: Multi-scale entropy

Take 80 bits of 01010101... (ten bytes of value 0x55). At 1 bit, there are 40 zeros and 40 ones, so \(X^2 = 0\) and \(p = 1\). It looks perfect. At 2 bits, there are 40 symbols and each of the 4 cells expects 10, but every symbol is "01". The counts are 0, 40, 0, 0, so \(X^2 = (100 + 900 + 100 + 100)/10 = 120\) with 3 degrees of freedom, and \(p = 7.7 \times 10^{-26}\). At 3 bits only 3.25 symbols per cell would be expected, below our minimum of 5, so we stop. Bonferroni over the 2 scales gives \(p = 1.5 \times 10^{-25}\).

The mathematics. Cut the \(n\) bits into \(m_k = \lfloor n/k \rfloor\) non-overlapping \(k\)-bit symbols, and compare the counts with their expected value:

\[ X_k^2 = \sum_{j=0}^{2^k - 1} \frac{(O_{k,j} - m_k/2^k)^2}{m_k/2^k} \sim \chi^2(2^k - 1) \] \[ p = \min\bigl(1,\ L \min_k p_k\bigr) \]
  • \(k\): the symbol size in bits, from 1 to 16, while at least 5 symbols per cell are expected.
  • \(O_{k,j}\): the number of times the \(k\)-bit symbol \(j\) occurred.
  • \(p_k\): the chi-square tail probability of \(X_k^2\).
  • \(L\): the number of scales used, which is 16 at 1 MiB.

The test also reports an entropy per bit at each scale, with the Miller-Madow correction (a small top-up, because counting from a finite sample underestimates entropy), but the pass or fail decision uses only the p-value above.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120. It flagged 15 of 59 (14 at the verdict line): 9 raw physical, 4 weak generators (MINSTD and RANDU), the defective conditioner and parity. It misses order that shows up only beyond 16 bits, and since symbols do not overlap, it looks at only one alignment of the stream at each size.

We found and fixed a defect here. Our first version used the G-statistic, and it failed 89% of good samples. At \(k = 16\), with about 8 expected counts per cell, G overshoots its chi-square reference by a factor of about 1.02, which is a lot at that scale. Pearson's \(X^2\) has a mean of exactly \(2^k - 1\) under the null, and false alarms dropped to 0 of 120.

docs.title: 10.4 Correlation analysis (test 3)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. If today's weather tells you something about tomorrow's, the days are not independent. We ask the same of bytes and bits: does a value say anything about the one that came 1, 2 or 32 steps before it? We also check whether two seats inside a byte tend to move together, like two friends who always vote the same way.

Example 10.4: Correlation analysis

Take the ten values 10, 20, 30, ..., 100, a plain upward trend. The sample autocorrelations are \(r_1 = 0.700\) and \(r_2 = 0.412\). With \(n = 10\) and \(h = 2\) lags:

\[ Q = 10 \times 12 \times \left(\frac{0.700^2}{9} + \frac{0.412^2}{8}\right) = 9.08 \]

Against \(\chi^2(2)\) this gives \(p = 0.0107\). Ten values is far too few for the chi-square reference to be reliable, so treat this as a picture of the arithmetic only.

The mathematics. The serial part is the Ljung-Box statistic, and the cross-bit part is Pearson correlation:

\[ r_k = \frac{\sum_{i} (x_i - \bar{x})(x_{i+k} - \bar{x})}{\sum_{i} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad Q = n(n+2) \sum_{k=1}^{h} \frac{r_k^2}{n-k} \sim \chi^2(h) \] \[ z_{ab} = r_{ab} \sqrt{N}, \qquad p_{ab} = \mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{|z_{ab}|}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \]
  • \(x_i\): the series, either bytes (first \(2^{21}\) bytes, \(h = 32\)) or bits (from the first \(2^{18}\) bytes, \(h = 64\)).
  • \(r_k\): the correlation between the series and itself shifted by \(k\).
  • \(n\): the length of that series.
  • \(r_{ab}\): the correlation between bit positions \(a\) and \(b\) of each byte.
  • \(N\): the number of bytes used for this, up to \(2^{20}\).

Bonferroni runs over the 28 position pairs to give \(p_{\text{cross}}\), then the final value is

\[p = \min(1,\ 3\min(p_{\text{byte}}, p_{\text{bit}}, p_{\text{cross}})).\]

This is conservative.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 1 of 120. It flagged 18 of 59 (17 at the verdict line): all 10 raw physical, 7 weak generators and parity. Six of the weak flags are LCG word streams (the Numerical Recipes LCG, MINSTD and RANDU). The seventh is xorshift128+ at \(p = 0.0072\) on one seed only, and it did not repeat on the other seed, so we would not read much into it. The test sees only straight-line dependence at short lags. Relationships that do not show as a straight line in byte values, such as those in MT19937 or java.util.Random, pass untouched.

docs.title: 10.5 Entropy stability across windows (test 4)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. A school's yearly average can look fine while one class had a terrible week. So we mark each 4 KiB page of the data separately, then ask two questions. Do the page marks spread the way chance says they should? And are too many pages terrible?

Example 10.5: Entropy stability across windows

A 1 MiB file has 256 windows. Suppose one window gives \(X^2 = 340\). Against \(\chi^2(255)\), \(p = 0.00029\), so it counts as a bad window. By chance we expect \(256 \times 0.001 = 0.256\) bad windows. Seeing 2 bad windows has tail probability 0.0276, which after doubling (for the 2 parts of the test) is 0.0552, a pass. Seeing 3 has tail probability 0.00229, or 0.00458 after doubling, a fail.

The mathematics. For each window \(w\) of 4096 bytes, with 16 expected per byte value:

\[ X_w^2 = \sum_{v=0}^{255} \frac{(c_{w,v} - 16)^2}{16}, \qquad p_w = P\bigl(\chi^2(255) \ge X_w^2\bigr) \] \[ B = \#\{w : p_w < 10^{-3}\} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(W, 10^{-3}), \qquad p_{\text{tail}} = P(B' \ge B) \] \[ p = \min\bigl(1,\ 2\min(p_{\text{KS}}, p_{\text{tail}})\bigr) \]
  • \(c_{w,v}\): how many times byte value \(v\) occurs in window \(w\).
  • \(p_w\): the window's p-value. Under the null these are independent and uniform between 0 and 1.
  • \(p_{\text{KS}}\): the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test that the \(p_w\) really are uniform.
  • \(W\): the number of windows.
  • \(B\): the number of bad windows, and \(B'\) a fresh binomial variable with the same law.

Despite the test's name, its p-value uses only these chi-square results. The code also reports each window's entropy as side information, and that plays no part in pass or fail.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 1 of 120. It flagged 17 of 59: all 10 raw physical, 6 weak generators (the Numerical Recipes LCG words, MINSTD and RANDU) and parity. It suits local faults, such as a stuck run, a dropout or a burst, and the code tells a local fault from a whole-sample problem by checking whether most windows fail. It checks only byte counts inside each window, so it is blind to the order of bytes. Generators with even byte counts, such as MT19937, pass.

docs.title: 10.6 Periodicity and predictability (test 5)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This test has two parts. The first listens for a hum: if a single note in the data is far louder than all the others, something periodic is going on. The second is a fortune teller who has to write down each guess before seeing the answer, and we simply keep score. Fair bytes give her 1 chance in 256, however clever she is.

Example 10.6: Periodicity and predictability

Take 16 values that repeat a period-4 shape with small wobbles: 200, 128, 50, 128, 205, 131, 47, 126, 198, 125, 52, 130, 203, 127, 49, 129. A transform splits the values into frequencies, and each frequency's entry is called an ordinate. With \(m = 7\) ordinates, one holds almost everything: \(g = 0.9985\), and the bound is \(7(1-g)^6 = 8.0 \times 10^{-17}\). A jumbled 16 values we tried gave \(g = 0.493\) and a bound of 0.118. For the fortune teller, take 7, 42, 99 repeated to 60 bytes. The lag predictor gets 56 of 59 guesses right, where chance would give about 0.23, and \(p = 4.4 \times 10^{-131}\).

The mathematics. The hum part is Fisher's g over the periodogram (the table of how much power each frequency holds) of the mean-removed bytes:

\[ I_j = \left| \sum_{t=0}^{L-1} (x_t - \bar{x})\, e^{-2\pi i j t / L} \right|^2, \qquad g = \frac{\max_j I_j}{\sum_j I_j}, \qquad P(g > x) \le m (1-x)^{m-1} \]

The predictor part compares hits with a binomial law:

\[ H \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, 1/256), \qquad p_{\text{pred}} = P(B \ge H) \] \[ p = \min\bigl(1,\ 3\min(p_{\text{Fisher}}, p_{\text{lag}}, p_{\text{Markov}})\bigr) \]
  • \(L\): the number of bytes in the transform, up to \(2^{20}\).
  • \(x_t\), \(\bar{x}\): the byte at position \(t\) and the mean of those bytes.
  • \(i\): the imaginary unit, the square root of minus one.
  • \(I_j\): the power at frequency index \(j\), leaving out both zero frequency and the very top one.
  • \(m\): the number of ordinates, \(L/2 - 1\). Under the null they are asymptotically i.i.d. exponential.
  • \(g\): the share of all the power in the loudest ordinate. The bound is the first term of Fisher's exact series.
  • \(H\): the hits over \(n\) guesses, using up to \(2^{19}\) bytes.
  • \(B\): a binomial variable with the same law as \(H\).

The lag predictor copies the byte from whichever of 32 lags has scored best so far (SP 800-90B section 6.3.8). The Markov predictor guesses the most common successor seen so far of the previous byte. Each guess uses only the past, so if the bytes are fair, every guess is right with probability \(1/256\) regardless. That is a martingale argument (a fair-game argument: whatever has happened so far, the next step is fair on average), and it is why the binomial law holds. Steps with no prediction yet count as misses, which can only make the test more cautious.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 1 of 120, at \(p = 0.0082\), well above the verdict line. An earlier run of the same size gave 4 of 120, the most of any test then, and 500 further samples gave 4 failures, 0.8%, so that high count looks like chance. It flagged 16 of 59: 8 raw physical, 6 weak generators (the Numerical Recipes LCG words, MINSTD and RANDU), the defective conditioner and parity. It missed the simulated photon time-bin source on both seeds. A plain period of 2 falls on the very top frequency, which \(g\) leaves out, so that case relies on the predictors. Strong non-linear generators beat both parts.

docs.title: 10.7 Shannon entropy test (test 9)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Think of a lottery with 256 numbers. Your average surprise is highest when all numbers are equally likely, and any favouritism lowers it. So a small entropy shortfall means uneven byte counts. This is the point people often miss: an entropy test and an evenness test are the same test in different clothes.

Example 10.7: Shannon entropy test

Use a toy alphabet of 4 symbols, where the maximum entropy is 2 bits, with counts 30, 20, 25, 25 out of \(n = 100\). The entropy is \(\hat{H} = 1.98548\) bits. Then \(2n \ln 2\, (2 - \hat{H}) = 2.0136\), and computing \(G\) directly from the counts gives the same 2.0136, as the identity promises. With 3 degrees of freedom, \(p = 0.570\).

Now at full size. Good data of 1 MiB does not reach 8.0 bits. It averages about 7.999825, and that is normal. A value of \(\hat{H} = 7.99982\) gives \(G = 261.7\) and \(p = 0.374\). A value of \(\hat{H} = 7.9997\) sounds equally perfect, but gives \(G = 436.1\) and \(p = 1.2 \times 10^{-11}\).

The mathematics. For byte counts \(c_v\) adding up to \(n\):

\[ \hat{H} = -\sum_v \frac{c_v}{n} \log_2 \frac{c_v}{n}, \qquad G = 2n \ln 2\, (8 - \hat{H}) = 2 \sum_v c_v \ln \frac{c_v}{n/256} \sim \chi^2(255) \]
  • \(c_v\): the number of times byte value \(v\) occurs.
  • \(n\): the number of bytes.
  • \(\hat{H}\): the measured Shannon entropy, in bits per byte.
  • \(G\): the likelihood-ratio statistic against the uniform distribution (Wilks' theorem, which says such statistics follow chi-square in large samples, gives its reference).

The p-value is the upper tail of \(\chi^2(255)\). With 4096 expected per cell, the Williams correction, a multiplier that adjusts \(G\) when counts are small, is 1.00004, which is negligible.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120, and the p-values look uniform. It flagged 13 of 59: 8 raw physical, 4 weak generators (MINSTD and RANDU) and parity. It looks at byte counts only. A file running 0, 1, 2, ..., 255 over and over has perfect counts, so \(G = 0\) and \(p = 1\), despite being totally predictable. So reading "7.9999 bits per byte" on a datasheet tells you very little on its own.

docs.title: 10.8 Compression (test 10)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Try to give everyone in a big town a short nickname. There simply are not enough short names to go round, so most people must keep long ones. Compression works the same way: very few strings can have a short description. So if a real compressor shrinks a file noticeably, the file was almost certainly not random. We do not need any statistics to say this, only counting.

Example 10.8: Compression

Counting first. Take strings of \(N = 4\) bits (16 of them), and a compressor whose output tells the decoder where to stop. Then no description is the start of another, a property called prefix-free. Compressing by \(s = 2\) bits means a description of at most 2 bits, and a prefix-free set can hold at most 4 of those (for example 00, 01, 10, 11). So at most 4 of the 16 strings can compress that far, which is exactly the bound of \(2^{-2} = 1/4\). Drop the prefix-free rule and there are 7 descriptions of at most 2 bits, counting the empty one, so the rule matters.

Now real compressors, on 1000 bytes. "ABCD" repeated 250 times compresses to 20 bytes with zlib. Then \(s = 8(1000 - 20 - 64) = 7328\) bits, and the bound is so small it rounds to 0. For 1000 random bytes, zlib gives 1011 bytes and lzma 1060, so no saving, and \(p = 1\). A saving of just 1 byte beyond the allowance gives \(s = 8\) and \(p = 0.0078\), which fails at 0.01.

The mathematics. Fix a decompressor whose files are self-delimiting, so that its descriptions are prefix-free. Both of ours qualify: we checked that the zlib and lzma decoders stop at their own end marker and leave any trailing bytes unread. Kraft's inequality says the lengths of a prefix-free set satisfy \(\sum_d 2^{-|d|} \le 1\), so at most \(2^{N-s}\) descriptions can have \(N - s\) bits or fewer. There are \(2^N\) strings of \(N\) bits, so:

\[ P(\text{random data compresses by at least } s \text{ bits}) \le 2^{-s} \] \[ s = 8(n - c - 64), \qquad p = \begin{cases} 1 & s \le 0 \\ \min(1,\ 2 \cdot 2^{-s}) & s > 0 \end{cases} \]
  • \(n\): the bytes tested, up to the first \(2^{21}\).
  • \(c\): the smallest compressed size, from lzma (preset 6) and zlib (level 9).
  • 64: the bytes we allow for container overhead before counting any saving.
  • \(s\): the saving in bits.
  • The factor 2: Bonferroni, because we tried two compressors.

This is an exact counting argument, not an approximation.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120 (every good sample gets \(p = 1\)). It flagged 12 of 59: 6 raw physical, 4 weak generators (the Numerical Recipes LCG words and RANDU), the defective conditioner and parity. Its strength is that a failure is close to unarguable. Its weakness is that general compressors are not looking for arithmetic structure. MT19937, java.util.Random and most weak generators pass, as do several raw physical samples, such as the simulated photon source.

During verification we found the bound was being applied once, although two compressors were tried. It never caused a false alarm, but it was unjustified, so we added the Bonferroni factor of 2.

docs.title: 10.9 Summary
docs.text:
• The bias test checks the whole-file balance and each of the eight bit positions; multi-scale entropy applies a chi-square at 1 to 16 bits at a time; correlation combines Ljung-Box on bytes and bits with cross-bit correlations.
  • Entropy stability checks each 4 KiB window; periodicity combines Fisher's \(g\) with predictors whose hits are exactly binomial.
  • The Shannon entropy test is the same test as the evenness test in different clothes: \(G=2n\ln2\,(8-\hat H)\sim\chi^2(255)\). A reading of "7.9999 bits per byte" on a datasheet tells you very little on its own.
  • Compression is a counting argument: at most \(2^{N-s}\) of the \(2^N\) strings can be compressed by \(s\) bits, so a real compressor that shrinks a file noticeably proves it is not random.
  • Three defects were found and fixed in this suite (the G statistic at 16-bit symbols, the handling of ties in the runs formula, and a missing Bonferroni factor for two compressors). Each is a lesson in why calibration on known-good data is essential.

docs.title: 10.10 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Take 100 bits with 62 ones. Find the exact two-sided binomial p-value, and say whether it fails at \(\alpha=0.01\). What would the bias test report if this were the smallest of its 9 sub-tests?

    Answer

    The exact two-sided value is \(2P(X\ge62)=0.0210\), which does not fail at 0.01. Because the bias test checks 9 things (the whole file and eight positions), a smallest sub-test p-value of 0.0210 is reported as \(9\times0.0210=0.189\).

  2. A source has byte counts 30, 20, 25, 25 over a toy alphabet of four symbols (\(n=100\)). Compute \(\hat H\), then \(G=2n\ln2(2-\hat H)\) and the p-value on 3 degrees of freedom.

    Answer

    \(\hat H=1.9855\) bits. Then \(G=2\times100\times0.6931\times(2-1.9855)=2.0136\), which equals \(2\sum c_v\ln(c_v/25)\), as the identity promises. On \(\chi^2(3)\), \(p=0.570\).

  3. A 1000-byte file compresses to 930 bytes with its best compressor. Using \(s=8(n-c-64)\) and \(p=\min(1,2\cdot2^{-s})\) for \(s>0\), find \(s\) and \(p\). What if it compresses to 20 bytes?

    Answer

    For \(c=930\): \(s=8(1000-930-64)=48\) bits, so \(p=2\times2^{-48}=7.1\times10^{-15}\), a clear failure. For \(c=20\): \(s=8(1000-20-64)=7328\), and the bound is so small that it rounds to 0. If \(c\ge936\) then \(s\le0\) and \(p=1\).

  4. Why does a datasheet figure of "7.9999 bits per byte of entropy" tell you very little about a generator?

    Answer

    It is a Shannon entropy computed from byte counts only. A file running 0, 1, 2, ..., 255 over and over has perfect counts and scores 8.0, yet is totally predictable. Also, good 1 MiB data does not reach 8.0 (it averages about 7.999825), and 7.9997 gives \(p=1.2\times10^{-11}\) even though it sounds equally perfect.

  5. What was wrong with the first version of the multi-scale entropy test, and what did the fix teach?

    Answer

    It used the G-statistic, which failed 89% of good samples at 16-bit symbols, where only about 8 counts per cell are expected and G overshoots its chi-square reference by about 2%. Pearson's \(X^2\) has mean exactly \(2^k-1\) under the null, and using it brought false alarms to 0 of 120. The lesson is to measure false alarms on known-good data before trusting a test.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Additional Tests (II): Source Behaviour and Health
docs.text: Physical sources misbehave in ways that algorithms do not: they drift as temperature or voltage change, their histograms are smooth because the analog signal is continuous, and they can stall. The three tests of this chapter are aimed at raw data from a physical source. Stationarity and runs up and down look for drift, the analog fingerprint looks for a smooth histogram, and the SP 800-90B health tests act as smoke alarms. A conditioner erases most of these signs, so these tests are mainly for raw data.

docs.title: 11.1 Stationarity and runs up and down (test 11)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Watch a runner across 64 legs of a race: is she slowing down? Physical sources drift as temperature or voltage changes, so we check whether the average byte and the share of ones stay put along the file. Then we look at a stock chart and count its streaks of ups and downs. Trending or sticky data has too few streaks, and jittery data has too many.

Example 11.1: Stationarity and runs up and down

For the values 3, 7, 5, 6, 8, 2, the moves are up, down, up, up, down, which makes \(R = 4\) runs. For \(n = 6\), the expected number is \((2 \times 6 - 1)/3 = 3.667\), with variance \((96 - 29)/90 = 0.744\). So \(z = 0.386\) and \(p = 0.699\). For the drift part, take 4 blocks of 1000 bits holding 470, 490, 510 and 530 ones. The overall share is 0.5, each block's variance is 250, and \(\chi^2 = (900 + 100 + 100 + 900)/250 = 8\). With 3 degrees of freedom, \(p = 0.046\).

The mathematics. The first part is one-way ANOVA (analysis of variance, which asks whether group averages differ by more than the scatter inside the groups) of byte values over 64 blocks, and the second is a chi-square test of the share of ones across 64 blocks:

\[ F = \frac{\sum_b n_b (\bar{x}_b - \bar{x})^2 / 63}{\sum_b \sum_i (x_{b,i} - \bar{x}_b)^2 / (n - 64)} \sim F(63,\ n-64) \] \[ \chi^2 = \sum_{b=1}^{64} \frac{(S_b - t_b \hat{q})^2}{t_b \hat{q} (1 - \hat{q})} \sim \chi^2(63) \]

The third counts runs up and down in \(u_i = x_i + U_i\), on up to \(2^{20}\) bytes:

\[ E[R] = \frac{2n-1}{3}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}[R] = \frac{16n-29}{90}, \qquad p_{\text{runs}} = \mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{|R - E[R]|}{\sqrt{2\,\mathrm{Var}[R]}}\right) \]
  • \(n\): the number of bytes used, and \(\bar{x}\) their mean.
  • \(x_{b,i}\), \(\bar{x}_b\), \(n_b\): the bytes of block \(b\), their mean and their count.
  • \(S_b\), \(t_b\): the ones and total bits in block \(b\).
  • \(\hat{q}\): the share of ones over the whole sample.
  • \(U_i\): independent uniform noise between 0 and 1.
  • \(R\): the number of runs in the \(u_i\) series.

The final value is \(p = \min(1,\ 3\min(p_{\text{mean}}, p_{\text{bits}}, p_{\text{runs}}))\). The block means are averages of about 16,000 values at 1 MiB, so the normal assumption behind ANOVA is sound.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 1 of 120. It flagged 10 of 59: 8 raw physical, RANDU on one seed only (\(p = 8.5 \times 10^{-5}\), while the other seed gave 0.17) and parity. Failing this test also feeds the analog condition in the verdict. It misses drift that is short compared with a block, and a conditioner will erase drift completely, so it mainly tests raw data.

We found and fixed a defect here too. The formulas for \(R\) hold for continuous data, but bytes tie about 1 time in 256. Our first version dropped ties, which shifted the expected run count by about 0.2%. That sounds tiny, but it is about 3 standard deviations at \(n = 2^{20}\), and it failed 52% of good samples. Adding \(U_i\) fixes this cleanly: if the bytes are i.i.d., then \(x_i + U_i\) is exactly continuous i.i.d., so the formulas hold exactly.

docs.title: 11.2 Analog fingerprint (test 12)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Draw a bar for each byte value and look at the skyline. Random data gives a jagged comb, because each bar's height has nothing to do with its neighbours'. An analog sensor read through a converter gives rolling hills, because value 100 and value 101 are nearly the same voltage. So we ask one narrow question: do neighbouring bars have similar heights?

Example 11.2: Analog fingerprint

A toy with 8 bars. The smooth hill 2, 5, 9, 12, 12, 9, 5, 2 has neighbour correlation \(r = 0.611\). For this toy, \(z = r\sqrt{6} = 1.50\) and \(p = 0.067\). The same bars scrambled as 12, 2, 9, 5, 12, 2, 5, 9 give \(r = -0.703\), \(z = -1.72\) and \(p = 0.958\). Eight bars are too few for a firm answer. At the full 256 bars, \(r = 0.05\) gives \(p = 0.21\), \(r = 0.2\) gives \(p = 0.00072\), and \(r = 0.4\) gives \(p = 9.2 \times 10^{-11}\).

The mathematics. Count each byte value, then correlate the counts of neighbouring values:

\[ r = \mathrm{corr}\bigl((c_0, \dots, c_{254}),\ (c_1, \dots, c_{255})\bigr), \qquad z = r\sqrt{254} \approx N(0, 1) \] \[ p = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \]
  • \(c_v\): the number of times byte value \(v\) occurs.
  • \(r\): the Pearson correlation over the 255 neighbouring pairs.
  • \(z\): its standardised value. Under the uniform multinomial null, the counts are exchangeable (reordering them does not change their joint law) with only a tiny negative correlation.

The p-value is one-sided, because only "smoother than chance" counts as a fingerprint. If all counts are identical, the code sets \(r = 1\).

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120, with p-values that look uniform. It flagged 11 of 59 (10 at the verdict line): 8 raw physical, 2 weak generators (MINSTD on both seeds) and one os.urandom sample at \(p = 0.0048\), which is simply the expected occasional chance result. It missed the simulated drifting source, since drift does not shape a histogram. A spiky or lopsided histogram without smoothness passes too: RANDU fails test 1 at \(p = 0\), yet got \(p = 0.51\) here. And MINSTD shows that a smooth histogram is not proof of hardware. On its own this test cannot change a verdict; it only explains other failures as analog.

docs.title: 11.3 SP 800-90B health tests (test 13)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. These are the two smoke alarms that NIST approves for real entropy sources. A developer may replace them with their own tests that meet the standard. One goes off if the same value repeats too many times in a row, as if the source got stuck. The other goes off if one value turns up too often in a short window. Both are set by how much entropy the source claims, so that a healthy source trips them only about once per million samples.

Example 11.3: SP 800-90B health tests

If \(H = 2\) bits per sample, the repetition cutoff is \(C = 1 + \lceil 20/2 \rceil = 11\) and the proportion cutoff is 177 out of 512. Those match the standard's examples, and our code reproduces its whole table: 410, 311, 177, 62 and 13 for \(H\) of 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8.

Now typical good data. The most common byte appears about 4275 times in 1 MiB. Then \(p_u = 0.00424\) and \(H = 7.88\), so the cutoffs are 4 repeats and 13 of 512. A run of 4 equal bytes is expected only \(2^{20} \times 2^{-24} = 0.0625\) times. If we see 1 such alarm, its p-value is 0.632, which means nothing. If we see 10, it is \(1.1 \times 10^{-7}\).

The mathematics. With \(\alpha = 2^{-20}\) per sample, and \(H\) from the most-common-value upper bound as in test 1:

\[ C_{\text{RCT}} = 1 + \left\lceil \frac{20}{H} \right\rceil, \qquad C_{\text{APT}} = 1 + \mathrm{CRITBINOM}(512,\ 2^{-H},\ 1 - 2^{-20}) \] \[ A_{\text{RCT}} \le_{\text{st}} \mathrm{Binomial}(N, \alpha), \qquad A_{\text{APT}} \le_{\text{st}} \mathrm{Binomial}(W, \alpha) \] \[ p = \min\bigl(1,\ 2\min(p_{\text{RCT}}, p_{\text{APT}})\bigr) \]
  • \(H\): the assessed min-entropy per byte.
  • \(C_{\text{RCT}}\): the run length that raises a repetition count alarm.
  • \(C_{\text{APT}}\): the count in a 512-byte window (of that window's first value) that raises an adaptive proportion alarm.
  • CRITBINOM: the smallest count whose binomial cumulative probability reaches the third argument.
  • \(A_{\text{RCT}}, A_{\text{APT}}\): the alarm counts. The symbol \(\le_{\text{st}}\) means "no larger than, in distribution".
  • \(N\), \(W\): the number of bytes and of non-overlapping 512-byte windows.
  • \(p_{\text{RCT}}, p_{\text{APT}}\): the upper tail probabilities of those binomials at the observed alarm counts, or 1 if there were no alarms.

\(H\) comes from the same sample's upper bound. If \(H\) is so low that no window could reach the cutoff, as on constant data, the source has no usable entropy and the test returns \(p = 0\). At 1 MiB the true APT window rate is slightly above nominal, though the Bonferroni factor 2 keeps \(p\) valid at 0.01 and at the verdict line.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120 (every good sample gets \(p = 1\)). It flagged 4 of 59: only the real CPU jitter samples (raw bytes and low bit, on both measurements). That is by design. These alarms are for a source that stalls or sticks, not for mild imperfection, and the other raw physical samples did not trip them. Note one difference from a real deployment. There, \(H\) comes from the design claim, while here it is measured from the sample itself, so a source that is evenly bad raises its own cutoffs. Treat this as a check on the sample, not as a replacement for health tests running in the device.

docs.title: 11.4 Summary
docs.text:
• Stationarity combines one-way ANOVA of block means, a chi-square on the share of ones across 64 blocks, and runs up and down on \(x_i+U_i\) with \(U_i\) uniform noise, which removes the effect of ties exactly.
  • Ignoring ties in the runs formula shifted the expected run count by about 0.2%, about 3 standard deviations at \(n=2^{20}\), and failed 52% of good samples. Adding \(U_i\) fixes it.
  • The analog fingerprint correlates the counts of neighbouring byte values: a smooth histogram gives a positive \(r\). It is one-sided and cannot change a verdict on its own.
  • The health tests (RCT and APT) are set by the claimed entropy so that a healthy source trips them about once per million samples; they catch a source that stalls, not mild imperfection.

docs.title: 11.5 Exercises
docs.text:
1. For the values 3, 7, 5, 6, 8, 2, count the runs up and down and give the expected number and variance of \(R\) for \(n=6\).

    Answer

    The moves are up, down, up, up, down, so \(R=4\) runs. \(E[R]=(2n-1)/3=11/3=3.667\) and \(\mathrm{Var}[R]=(16n-29)/90=67/90=0.744\). Then \(z=(4-3.667)/\sqrt{0.744}=0.386\) and \(p=0.699\).

  2. Four blocks of 1000 bits contain 480, 495, 505 and 520 ones. Test whether the share of ones is stable across blocks.

    Answer

    The overall share is \(\hat q=0.5\) and each block has variance \(1000\times0.25=250\). So \(\chi^2=(400+25+25+400)/250=3.4\) on 3 degrees of freedom, giving \(p=0.334\). There is no sign of drift.

  3. Why must the runs-up-and-down test add independent uniform noise \(U_i\) to the bytes?

    Answer

    The formulas for the number of runs assume continuous data, but bytes tie about 1 time in 256. Dropping ties shifted the expected run count by about 0.2%, which is about 3 standard deviations at \(n=2^{20}\) and failed 52% of good samples. With \(U_i\) uniform on \((0,1)\) and independent, \(x_i+U_i\) is exactly continuous i.i.d. when the bytes are i.i.d., so the formulas hold exactly.

  4. Find the repetition count cutoff for a source assessed at \(H=2\) bits per sample and say when an alarm is raised.

    Answer

    \(C_{RCT}=1+\lceil20/2\rceil=11\). An alarm is raised when a sample repeats 11 or more times in a row.

  5. A smooth histogram of byte counts is observed. Does it prove the data came from hardware? Use the example of MINSTD.

    Answer

    No. The analog fingerprint detects only "smoother than chance". MINSTD, a pseudo-random generator, also produced a smooth histogram, so smoothness is evidence about the data, not proof of a physical origin. That is also why the test cannot change a verdict on its own.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Additional Tests (III): Spectral, Ordinal, Matrix and Betting Tests
docs.text: These four tests need heavier mathematics to see structure that simple counts miss. The Weyl-sum test searches for the angles at which pairs of bytes line up like trees in an orchard; the ordinal-pattern test keeps only the order of five words; the random-matrix test uses the Tracy-Widom law to bound the strongest accidental correlation among 200 variables; and the universal betting test hires a clever gambler whose winnings are a valid statistical bound. Each has an exact or well-understood null distribution, which is what makes it worth studying.

docs.title: 12.1 Weyl-sum spectral test (test U1)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Plot each pair of bytes as a point on a 256 by 256 grid. Some generators' points fall in neat rows, like trees in an orchard: walk at the right angle and every tree lines up. A wild forest has no such angle. To find those angles, we turn each point into a small arrow whose direction depends on the point and the angle tested. In a wild forest the arrows roughly cancel, but at the orchard's angle they all point the same way and add up.

Example 12.1: Weyl-sum spectral test

Take 4 pairs on a line: (0, 0), (64, 64), (128, 128), (192, 192). At frequency \((u, v) = (1, 255)\), each arrow's angle depends on \(x - y\), which is 0 every time. So all four arrows align, \(F = 4\), and the normalised power is \(|F|^2/4 = 4\), for a single-frequency tail of \(e^{-4} = 0.018\). Four scattered pairs, (10, 200), (77, 3), (130, 91), (250, 45), give power 0.93 at the same frequency.

At full size, there are 32,769 frequencies to check, so the largest power from chance alone is expected to be about 11. A power of 15.0 is needed to fail at 0.01, and 17.9 to reach the verdict line. On one os.urandom sample the peak was 11.66, giving \(p = 0.246\).

The mathematics. Take \(m\) non-overlapping byte pairs \((x_j, y_j)\):

\[ F(u, v) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} e^{-2\pi i (u x_j + v y_j)/256}, \qquad E(u, v) = \frac{|F(u, v)|^2}{m} \sim \mathrm{Exp}(1) \] \[ p = 1 - (1 - p_{\min})^{K} \]
  • \(x_j, y_j\): the two bytes of pair \(j\).
  • \(i\): the imaginary unit, the square root of minus one. (It is not an index here.)
  • \(u, v\): the frequency, with \((u, v) \ne (0, 0)\).
  • \(F\): the sum of \(m\) independent unit arrows, each with mean 0 under the null.
  • \(E\): the normalised power. On the 3 frequencies where \(F\) is purely real, namely \((128, 0)\), \((0, 128)\) and \((128, 128)\), its reference is \(\chi^2(1)\) instead.
  • \(p_{\min}\): the smallest single-frequency tail, which is \(e^{-E}\) on all the other frequencies.
  • \(K = 32{,}769\): the frequencies tested, taking one from each conjugate pair.

The final value is Sidak over \(K\). A peak on an axis (\(u = 0\) or \(v = 0\)) means uneven single-byte frequencies. A peak off the axes means joint structure, such as points lying in rows.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 1 of 120, with p-values that look uniform. It flagged 16 of 59 (15 at the verdict line): 8 raw physical, 6 weak generators (MINSTD, MSVC rand() low byte, RANDU), the defective conditioner at \(p = 0.0011\), and parity. The peak location helps diagnosis. In our corpus only the MSVC rand() low byte has an off-axis peak, at \((5, 87)\) with power 933. MINSTD and RANDU peak on the axis at \((0, 1)\), showing uneven bytes, and the Numerical Recipes LCG is not significant here (\(p = 1\) for its words, \(p = 0.71\) for its top byte). It looks only at adjacent byte pairs, so structure that appears only among three or more values, or between bytes further apart, can pass. Generators with good 2-byte behaviour pass, such as MT19937.

Figure 12.1. Pairs of bytes plotted as points. Independent bytes fill the square; consecutive outputs of a small linear congruential generator fall on a few lines, which is the kind of structure a Weyl sum detects at the right frequency.

docs.title: 12.2 Ordinal-pattern test (test U2)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Line up five people picked at random and note who is tallest, second tallest, and so on. Forget their actual heights; keep only the order. There are 120 possible orders, and for truly unrelated people all 120 are equally likely. A deterministic system can make some orders common and others impossible. Because we use only rank, a smooth bias in the values does not confuse the test.

Example 12.2: Ordinal-pattern test

Take the words 40, 10, 30, 50, 20. Sorting gives the positions 1, 4, 2, 0, 3, and the code turns these into a single class number between 0 and 119, here 44. For a toy version with 3 words per window (6 orderings) and 12 windows, suppose the counts are 5, 3, 2, 1, 1, 0. Each cell expects 2, so \(X^2 = (9 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 4)/2 = 8\) with 5 degrees of freedom, and \(p = 0.156\). The full test uses 5 words per window. At 1 MiB this gives 52,428 windows and about 437 per class.

The mathematics. Split the 32-bit words into non-overlapping windows of 5:

\[ X^2 = \sum_{\pi=1}^{120} \frac{(O_\pi - w/120)^2}{w/120} \sim \chi^2(119) \]
  • \(\pi\): one of the \(5! = 120\) orderings, numbered with a Lehmer code (a standard way to give each ordering one whole number).
  • \(O_\pi\): the number of windows with that ordering.
  • \(w\): the number of windows.

For i.i.d. continuous data, every ordering has probability exactly \(1/120\), because the values are exchangeable. With 32-bit values, ties have a probability of about \(10^{-9}\) and are broken in a fixed way, which is negligible. The p-value is the upper tail of \(\chi^2(119)\).

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 1 of 120, with p-values that look uniform. It flagged 5 of 59, only the real CPU jitter samples (4) and parity. So it is narrow, but it adds an angle: it asks about dynamics, not values. Even strongly biased sources pass: RANDU got \(p = 0.13\) while failing many other tests, because rank alone does not reveal its faults. It looks only at the 32-bit word view, aligned to the start of the file, and at 5 words at a time. It says nothing about structure in the low bits of a word, since the order of two words is almost always decided by their top bits.

docs.title: 12.3 Random-matrix test (test U3)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Imagine 200 musicians, each playing their own random part for 2000 beats. Even with no coordination, there is a predictable limit to how loud the strongest accidental "shared tune" can be, and random-matrix theory gives that limit to high accuracy. If some musicians secretly follow the same score, a shared tune escapes above the limit. This test is sensitive to weak correlation spread across many variables at once.

Example 12.3: Random-matrix test

A tiny matrix is pointless here, because the theory is about large sizes. So we ran a toy with the real dimensions but plain simulated Gaussian numbers (not bytes). An eigenvalue measures how strong one shared pattern across the rows is, and the top eigenvalue is the strongest. For \(N = 200\), \(T = 2000\), the theory says the top eigenvalue centres on \(\mu = 1.7318\) with scale \(\sigma = 0.01334\). Our clean run gave \(\lambda_{\max} = 1.7471\), a score of 1.15 and a one-sided tail of 0.039. The bottom eigenvalue also sat in place (0.4714, against a centre of 0.4672). Bonferroni over the 2 edges gives \(p = 0.078\), a pass.

Then we made just 20 of the 200 rows share a hidden factor, with a correlation of 0.2 between them. Now \(\lambda_{\max} = 5.06\), a score of about 250, and \(p = 0\).

The mathematics. Each 16-bit word \(w\) becomes a Gaussian value \(z = \Phi^{-1}((w + \tfrac{1}{2})/65536)\). Stack them into a matrix \(Z\) that is \(N \times T\):

\[ S = \frac{1}{T} Z Z^{\top}, \qquad s_{\text{hi}} = \frac{\lambda_{\max} - \mu_{\text{hi}}}{\sigma_{\text{hi}}}, \qquad s_{\text{lo}} = \frac{\mu_{\text{lo}} - \lambda_{\min}}{\sigma_{\text{lo}}} \] \[ \mu_{\text{hi}} = \frac{(\sqrt{T-1} + \sqrt{N})^2}{T}, \qquad \sigma_{\text{hi}} = \frac{\sqrt{T-1} + \sqrt{N}}{T} \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T-1}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right)^{1/3} \] \[ \mu_{\text{lo}} = \frac{(\sqrt{T-1} - \sqrt{N})^2}{T}, \qquad \sigma_{\text{lo}} = \frac{\sqrt{T-1} - \sqrt{N}}{T} \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{T-1}}\right)^{1/3} \] \[ s \to \mathrm{TW}_1, \qquad \mathrm{TW}_1 \approx \Gamma(46.446,\ 0.186054) - 9.84801, \qquad p = \min\bigl(1,\ 2\min(p_{\text{hi}}, p_{\text{lo}})\bigr) \]
  • \(N = 200\), \(T = 2000\): the rows and columns of \(Z\), using 800,000 bytes.
  • \(\Phi^{-1}\): the inverse of the standard normal distribution function.
  • \(Z^{\top}\): \(Z\) with rows and columns swapped (its transpose).
  • \(S\): the sample covariance matrix, with eigenvalues from \(\lambda_{\min}\) to \(\lambda_{\max}\).
  • \(\mu, \sigma\): the centring and scaling (Johnstone 2001), at the two Marchenko-Pastur edges (the theoretical top and bottom of the eigenvalue spread for pure noise).
  • \(\mathrm{TW}_1\): the Tracy-Widom law for real matrices, using Chiani's gamma approximation, which is good to about \(10^{-3}\). Here \(\Gamma\) has a shape and a scale.
  • \(p_{\text{hi}}, p_{\text{lo}}\): the upper Tracy-Widom tails at \(s_{\text{hi}}\) and \(s_{\text{lo}}\).

There are three approximations: the 16-bit rounding of the Gaussian, finite sizes, and Chiani's fit. Calibration is what confirms they do no harm.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120. It flagged 13 of 59: 8 raw physical, 4 weak generators (MINSTD and RANDU) and parity. It reads the data only as 16-bit words, and it finds correlation among the 200 rows of 2000 values, so structure at other lags or in other widths can be missed. Linear generators like MT19937 pass. One practical trap: below 800,000 bytes, the test is skipped and reported as \(p = 1\). That happened with our random.org sample (115,000 bytes), so its clean verdict does not include this test.

docs.title: 12.4 Universal betting test (test U4)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. A gambler starts with 1 unit and bets on each bit at fair odds. If the coin really is fair, then no strategy has any edge. Her expected wealth stays at 1 forever, and the chance she ever reaches 100 units is at most 1%. So we hire a clever gambler who keeps track of what followed each recent pattern of bits. If she gets rich, the bits were not fair. Her winnings are the evidence, and the mathematics holds without any approximation.

Example 12.4: Universal betting test

Bits: 0101010101010101 (16 bits). A gambler who ignores history (order 0) sees equal counts, and her wealth ends at 0.196. She paid for learning and found nothing. A gambler who remembers one bit (order 1) bets on the first bit evenly, and then her wealth runs: 1, 1, 1, 1.5, 2.25, 3.75, 6.25, 10.94, 19.14, 34.45, 62.02, 113.70, 208.44, 387.11, 718.91, 1347.96.

In this toy we hire 3 gamblers (orders 0 to 2) and split the stake, so the wealth we credit is \(1347.96/3 = 449.3\). That gives \(p = 1/449.3 = 0.0022\). The real test splits among 23 gamblers, so it would credit only about 58.6 here, and on 16 bits it would not fail. It needs real length. To fail at 0.01 the credited wealth must reach 100, and to reach the verdict line, 1800.

The mathematics. For each order \(k\) from 0 to 22, use the Krichevsky-Trofimov estimator in each context:

\[ P_k(x_1 \dots x_n) = 2^{-k} \prod_{\text{contexts}} \frac{\Gamma(a + \tfrac{1}{2})\, \Gamma(b + \tfrac{1}{2})}{\pi\, \Gamma(a + b + 1)} \] \[ W_n = 2^n \cdot \frac{1}{23} \sum_{k=0}^{22} P_k \ \ge\ 2^n \cdot \frac{\max_k P_k}{23} = W' \] \[ P(W_n \ge 1/\alpha) \le \alpha, \qquad p = \min\left(1,\ \frac{1}{W'}\right) \]
  • \(n\): the bits used, up to \(2^{23}\).
  • context: the previous \(k\) bits. For order 0 there is one context.
  • \(a, b\): the number of zeros and ones that followed that context.
  • \(\Gamma\): the gamma function. This product is what betting \((b + \tfrac{1}{2})/(a + b + 1)\) on a 1 at each step comes to.
  • \(2^{-k}\): the first \(k\) bits, each priced at one half.
  • \(W_n\): the wealth of the mixture, a non-negative martingale with mean 1 under fair flips.
  • \(W'\): the wealth the code actually computes, the best single order divided by 23.

The tail bound is Markov's inequality (and Ville's inequality, which extends the same bound to every moment along the way, not just the end). Because \(W'\) never exceeds \(W_n\), using \(W'\) is valid and slightly more cautious.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120 (every good sample gets \(p = 1\), which is expected for a bound this cautious). It flagged 13 of 59: 8 raw physical, 4 weak generators (MINSTD and RANDU), and parity. RANDU reached wealth of about \(2^{11544}\) at order 2. The gambler only knows about patterns of consecutive bits up to 22 long, so it misses relationships at longer distances. MT19937, for instance, passes.

We found and fixed a defect here while re-deriving the formula for the Java port. Our rolling context shifted the previous order's context, so the "order \(k\)" context was really one past bit repeated \(k\) times. The test stayed valid but was far weaker than described. After the fix, our records show an order-3 Markov source going from undetected to a wealth of \(2^{30079}\).

docs.title: 12.5 Summary
docs.text:
• Weyl sums turn each byte pair into a unit arrow; in a random stream the arrows cancel, and the normalised power of one frequency is approximately Exp(1). A peak on an axis means uneven single-byte frequencies; a peak off the axes means joint structure.
  • With \(K=32{,}769\) frequencies the Sidak step is needed: a power of 15.0 is needed to fail at 0.01, and 17.9 to reach the verdict line.
  • Ordinal patterns use only the order of 5 words, giving 120 equally likely orderings; the test is blind to size and to low bits.
  • Random-matrix theory gives the Tracy-Widom distribution of the extreme eigenvalues of \(S=\frac1T ZZ^\top\); it needs at least 800,000 bytes and is sensitive to weak correlation spread over many variables.
  • Universal betting: the wealth of a gambler betting at fair odds is a non-negative martingale with mean 1, so \(P(W_n\ge1/\alpha)\le\alpha\) holds exactly; to fail at 0.01 the credited wealth must reach 100.

docs.title: 12.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Four byte pairs (0,0), (64,64), (128,128), (192,192) lie on a line. At the frequency \((u,v)=(1,255)\), find \(F\), the normalised power \(E\) and the single-frequency tail probability.

    Answer

    Each arrow has angle proportional to \(x-y\), which is 0 for every pair, so all four arrows align and \(|F|=4\). The normalised power is \(|F|^2/4=4\) and the single-frequency tail is \(e^{-4}=0.018\). Four scattered pairs would give a power near 1 at the same frequency.

  2. How many 5-word windows does a 1 MiB sample provide for the ordinal-pattern test, and how many windows are expected for each of the 120 orderings?

    Answer

    1 MiB is \(2^{20}\) bytes \(=262{,}144\) 32-bit words, giving \(\lfloor262144/5\rfloor=52{,}428\) windows. Each ordering is expected about \(52{,}428/120\approx437\) times.

  3. For the random-matrix test with \(N=200\) and \(T=2000\), verify the centring \(\mu_{hi}=(\sqrt{T-1}+\sqrt N)^2/T\) and say why the test is skipped for samples below 800,000 bytes.

    Answer

    \(\sqrt{1999}=44.71\) and \(\sqrt{200}=14.14\), so \(\mu_{hi}=(58.85)^2/2000=1.7318\). The matrix needs \(N\times T=400{,}000\) 16-bit words, which is 800,000 bytes. Below that size the test cannot be built, so it is skipped and reported as \(p=1\).

  4. In the universal betting test, why does a gambler who starts with 1 unit and bets at fair odds reach 100 units with probability at most 1%?

    Answer

    If the coin is fair, her wealth is a non-negative martingale with mean 1. By Markov's inequality (and Ville's inequality for the whole path), the probability that it ever reaches \(1/\alpha=100\) is at most \(\alpha=0.01\). The bound is exact mathematics, not an approximation.

  5. Why does the Weyl-sum test need a Sidak correction over \(K=32{,}769\) frequencies?

    Answer

    It tests thousands of frequencies and keeps the largest power. Even for good data the largest of 32,769 powers is expected to be about 11, so a power that would be remarkable at one frequency is ordinary as a maximum. The Sidak step, \(1-(1-p_{\min})^K\), corrects for looking at all of them.

docs.title: Chapter 13: Additional Tests (IV): Collisions, Memory and Learning
docs.text: The last four statistical tests ask: do exact repeats occur at the rate of the birthday paradox, does the data show long memory under detrended fluctuation analysis, can a model trained on the first half of the sample predict the second half, and do the Hamming weights of successive words depend on each other. The first two have exact or Poisson reference laws; the last two are sequential or held-out designs in which each prediction depends only on the past, so the null law is exact and no correction for the number of patterns tried is needed.

docs.title: 13.1 Birthday-collision test (test U5)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Put 23 people in a room and two probably share a birthday. That is the famous surprise. So random words should repeat a predictable number of times. Too many repeats suggests a small hidden state or bias. Too few is just as suspicious: some generators never repeat a word until they run through their whole cycle, like a room where somehow nobody ever shares a birthday.

Example 13.1: Birthday-collision test

The classic case: \(m = 23\), 365 days, so \(\lambda = 23 \times 22/(2 \times 365) = 0.693\). The chance of at least one shared birthday is about \(1 - e^{-0.693} = 0.5000\). The exact figure is 0.5073, so the approximation is good.

Now the real thing, on a 2 MiB sample: \(m = 2^{19}\) 32-bit words, so \(\lambda \approx 32\). With 32 repeats, \(p = 1\) (one os.urandom sample showed exactly that). With 50 repeats, the 32-bit p-value is 0.0039, or 0.0077 after Bonferroni. With 0 repeats, it is \(2.5 \times 10^{-14}\), or \(5.1 \times 10^{-14}\) after Bonferroni, and we measured that exact value on RANDU, LFSR32 and xorshift32.

The mathematics. For \(m\) uniform \(w\)-bit words:

\[ C = m - \#\{\text{distinct words}\} \approx \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda), \qquad \lambda = \frac{m(m-1)}{2^{w+1}} \] \[ p_w = \min\bigl(1,\ 2\min(P(C' \le C),\ P(C' \ge C))\bigr), \qquad p = \min\bigl(1,\ 2\min(p_{32}, p_{64})\bigr) \]
  • \(w\): the word size, 32 or 64 bits.
  • \(m\): the words used, capped at \(2^{19}\) for 32 bits and \(2^{18}\) for 64 bits.
  • \(C\): the number of repeated values.
  • \(C'\): a Poisson variable with mean \(\lambda\).
  • \(\lambda\): the expected number of repeats (the Arratia-Goldstein-Gordon approximation).

At those caps, which need 2 MiB, \(\lambda \approx 32\) for 32 bits and about \(2 \times 10^{-9}\) for 64 bits, so a single 64-bit repeat is damning. On a 1 MiB sample, as in our calibration, \(m\) halves and \(\lambda \approx 8\) for 32 bits.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120. It flagged 21 of 59, the most of any statistical test (20 at the verdict line): 6 raw physical, 13 weak generators, the defective conditioner and parity. Because the stateless conditioner produces repeated hash blocks, this test gave it \(p = 0\). One of the 13 was MT19937 words at \(p = 0.0056\), on one seed only. It looks only at exact repeats at the 4-byte and 8-byte alignments. On 1 MiB, zero repeats gives only \(p = 0.0013\), which fails at 0.01 but stays above the verdict line, so give this test at least 2 MiB. Generators with long periods and no repeat quirks, such as PCG and xoshiro, pass.

Figure 13.1. The number of repeated 32-bit words among 2^19 words is approximately Poisson with mean 32. Observing no repeats at all is astronomically unlikely for good data.

docs.title: 13.2 Detrended fluctuation analysis (test U6)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Turn the data into a walk: take a step up or down for each value, based on how far it is from the average. Now look at windows of different sizes, and measure how far the walk strays from a straight line. For memoryless data, that wobble grows like the square root of the window size, an exponent of one half. Memory changes the exponent. Rather than trust a formula, we keep shuffling the same data, which destroys any order, and see if the original exponent stands out. We stop as soon as the answer is clear: ordinary data is usually settled after a few dozen shuffles, and only a suspicious sample earns the full 1999.

Example 13.2: Detrended fluctuation analysis

Take the values 3, 9, 1, 7, 5, 6, 2, 8, with mean 5.125. The walk is \(-2.125\), 1.75, \(-2.375\), \(-0.5\), \(-0.625\), 0.25, \(-2.875\), 0. After fitting and removing a straight line in each window, the wobble is \(F(4) = 1.449\) and \(F(8) = 1.454\). Eight points only show the steps; you need a longer series to see a slope.

So we ran the shuffling rule on 4096 simulated values, with window sizes 16 to 256. One stream of white noise gave an exponent of 0.511. The tenth shuffle at least as far from one half arrived after just 13 shuffles, so we stopped with \(p = 10/13 = 0.77\). A second stream gave 0.431. It is not exactly 0.5, because short series scatter, and that is the reason we shuffle instead of comparing with 0.5 directly. It took 668 shuffles to reach ten, so \(p = 10/668 = 0.015\), still a pass at 0.01. The running sum of that second stream gave an exponent of 1.524. None of the 1999 shuffles came close, so \(p = 1/2000 = 0.0005\).

The mathematics. Build the walk, detrend it in windows of size \(s\), and fit a slope:

\[ Y_t = \sum_{i \le t} (x_i - \bar{x}), \qquad F(s) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{|\text{windows}|\, s} \sum_{\text{windows}} \sum_{t} \bigl(Y_t - \hat{Y}_t\bigr)^2} \] \[ \log F(s) \approx \hat{\alpha} \log s + \text{constant} \] \[ G_\ell = \#\{b \le \ell : |\hat{\alpha}_b - \tfrac{1}{2}| \ge |\hat{\alpha} - \tfrac{1}{2}|\} \] \[ p = \begin{cases} h / L & \text{if } G_\ell \text{ first reaches } h = 10 \text{ at } \ell = L \le B \\ (1 + G_B) / (B + 1) & \text{otherwise, with } B = 1999 \end{cases} \]
  • \(x_i\): the first \(2^{18}\) bytes, and \(\bar{x}\) their mean.
  • \(Y_t\): the walk, a running total of how far each byte sits from the mean.
  • \(s\): one of 16 window sizes, spaced evenly in log scale from 16 to 16,384.
  • \(\hat{Y}_t\): the straight line fitted to \(Y\) in that window.
  • \(F(s)\): the typical size of the wobble around those lines.
  • \(\hat{\alpha}\): the fitted exponent, about one half for memoryless data.
  • \(\hat{\alpha}_b\): the same exponent after shuffle number \(b\).
  • \(G_\ell\): how many of the first \(\ell\) shuffles were at least as far from one half as the real data.
  • \(h = 10\): the count at which we stop early.
  • \(L\): the number of shuffles used when that happens.
  • \(B = 1999\): the most shuffles we will ever run.

Under i.i.d. data the sample is exchangeable, so the real exponent is equally likely to rank anywhere among the shuffles. This makes it an exact permutation test, with no distribution assumed. The stopping rule is the sequential Monte Carlo test of Besag and Clifford (Biometrika, 1991), which keeps the p-value valid while saving most of the work on good data. On a clean simulated 1 MiB sample, our routine stopped after 58 shuffles with \(p = 0.17\).

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120, with p-values that look uniform. It flagged 6 of 59, all at \(p = 0.0005\) and so below the verdict line: two raw jitter forms and one LCG, each on two seeds, 6 samples in all. The smallest p-value this test can give is \(1/2000 = 0.0005\), which sits only just below the verdict line of 0.000556. So test U6 can reach the verdict line only when none of the 1999 shuffles is as extreme as the data, and even one such shuffle gives \(p = 0.001\), which is above the line. It looks only at memory, so bias alone does not trigger it, because shuffling keeps the byte values and only changes their order. A slow linear drift we added to the 4096-value toy did not stand out either (exponent 0.437, stopped after 303 shuffles at \(p = 0.033\)).

docs.title: 13.3 Held-out learned predictor (test H1)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Give a student the first half of the exam with the answers. Let them study as long as they like, then freeze what they have learned and test them on the second half, which they have never seen. If they beat a coin toss there, they really did learn something. Because the marking is on unseen data, we do not need to correct for how many patterns the student tried, and they cannot cheat by memorising.

Example 13.3: Held-out learned predictor

Say the frozen model makes 1000 predictions of the top bit and gets 540 right. Then \(P(\text{at least 540 of 1000}) = 0.0062\), or 0.0124 after Bonferroni for the 2 targets, a narrow pass. With 550 right, it is 0.00087, or 0.0017 after Bonferroni, a fail. Note how little edge it takes at scale: at 1 MiB, a hit rate of just 0.5018 on one target reaches the 0.01 line.

For a live toy, we built 131,072 bytes in which each byte's top bit copies the previous byte's top bit 60% of the time and is otherwise a fresh coin, so it matches about 80% of the time. The test got 52,340 of 65,536 top bits right, a hit rate of 0.7986, and \(p = 0\). On the low bit, which we left alone, it got 0.4984 and \(p = 0.80\). On clean bytes of the same size, it got 0.5006 and 0.5029, with an overall \(p = 0.145\).

The mathematics. Predict the top bit and the low bit of byte \(i\) from a 55-feature row \(f_i\). The features are a constant, the 16 previous byte values (scaled), their top bits, their low bits (each as plus or minus 1), and the 6 pairwise products of lags 1 to 4.

\[ w = (F^{\top} F + \lambda I)^{-1} F^{\top} y, \qquad \hat{y}_i = \mathrm{sign}(f_i^{\top} w) \] \[ H \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(N, \tfrac{1}{2}), \qquad p_{\text{target}} = P(B \ge H), \qquad p = \min\bigl(1,\ 2\min(p_{\text{MSB}}, p_{\text{LSB}})\bigr) \]
  • \(F, y\): the features and the target bit (as plus or minus 1), over the first half of the sample (up to \(2^{20}\) rows).
  • \(\top\): the transpose, which swaps rows and columns.
  • \(\lambda = 10^{-6}\): a small ridge term for stability, and \(I\) the identity matrix.
  • \(\hat{y}_i\): the predicted bit for byte \(i\), from the sign of the score.
  • \(w\): the fitted weights, frozen before scoring.
  • \(H\): the correct predictions in the second half, out of \(N\) (up to \(2^{20}\)).
  • \(B\): a binomial variable with the same law.

Each prediction uses only earlier bytes and frozen weights. If the bytes are i.i.d., the target bit is a fair coin, independent of all of that, so \(H\) is exactly binomial, with no approximation. The framework comes from Kelsey, McKay and Sonmez Turan (CHES 2015) and Truong et al. (IEEE TIFS 2019). The test also reports a predictor-based min-entropy estimate, \(-\log_2 \max(P_u, \tfrac{1}{2})\) bits per predicted bit, with \(P_u\) the 99% upper bound on the hit rate.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 1 of 120 (95% interval 0.02% to 4.6%), consistent with 1%. It flagged 16 of 59 (15 at the verdict line): 8 raw physical, 6 weak generators (the Numerical Recipes LCG words, MINSTD and RANDU), parity, and one os.urandom sample at \(p = 0.0016\), which we read as an ordinary chance result since it stayed above the verdict line. The model is small and mostly linear, and it looks back only 16 bytes. It cannot learn java.util.Random or MT19937, and those passed. A failure is strong evidence, but a pass only says this student could not learn it.

docs.title: 13.4 Hamming-weight dependency (test H2)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Think of each word as a bag of coins, and its Hamming weight as the number of heads in it. Note whether each of the last few bags came out light, middling or heavy. Then ask: does that pattern tell you anything about the next bag's weight? Some generators pass many tests, yet leave exactly this kind of faint trace. Blackman and Vigna designed this test to find it.

Example 13.4: Hamming-weight dependency

Say that for one signature pattern, 4 bytes landed in the cell, with weights 6, 5, 4, 7. Centred on 4, they add up to \(S = 6\). With variance \(8/4 = 2\) per byte, \(Z = 6/\sqrt{4 imes 2} = 2.12\).

Next the rotation, in a toy with \(k = 1\) and so 3 cells, \(Z = (2.12, -0.40, -1.60)\). Multiplying by the orthogonal matrix gives \((0.069, 2.630, 0.539)\). We drop the first (constant) coefficient. The other two have tails 0.0085 and 0.590, so Sidak over 2 gives \(p = 0.017\). The real test does this over 6560 and 728 coefficients.

The mathematics. Each word goes into one of 3 classes by its weight \( u\): below, inside or above a centre band. A block of \(k + 1\) words gives a signature (the classes of the first \(k\) words) and a target (the weight of the last word):

\[ S_c = \sum_{ ext{blocks in cell } c} igl( u_{ ext{target}} - frac{w}{2} igr), \qquad Z_c = rac{S_c}{\sqrt{n_c\, w/4}} \approx N(0, 1) \] \[ M = egin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{3} & 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{6} \ 1/\sqrt{3} & 0 & -2/\sqrt{6} \ 1/\sqrt{3} & -1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{6} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad C = (M^{ op})^{\otimes k}\, Z \] \[ p_{w} = 1 - (1 - p_{\min})^{3^k - 1}, \qquad p_{\min} = \min_{j e 0} \mathrm{erfc}\!\left( rac{|C_j|}{\sqrt{2}} ight), \qquad p = \min igl(1,\ 2\min(p_8, p_{32}) igr) \]
  • \(w\): the word size in bits, 8 (with \(k = 8\), band: weight 4) or 32 (with \(k = 6\), band: weights 15 to 17).
  • \(c\): a cell, one of the \(3^k\) signatures.
  • \(n_c\): the number of blocks in cell \(c\).
  • \(S_c\): the total centred weight of the target words in cell \(c\).
  • \(Z_c\): that total, scaled to have variance 1 under the null.
  • \(M\): an orthogonal matrix, which only rotates, and \(M^{ op}\) its transpose.
  • \((M^{ op})^{\otimes k}\): the \(k\)-th Kronecker power of \(M^{ op}\), which applies \(M^{ op}\) once along each of the \(k\) signature positions.
  • \(C_j\): the rotated coefficients, and \(j = 0\) is the constant one that we drop.

Signature and target words never overlap, so under i.i.d. data the \(Z_c\) are independent and close to standard normal. An orthogonal rotation of independent standard normals is again independent standard normal. Blackman and Vigna's paper (ACM TOMACS 2022) slides its window over overlapping runs of consecutive words, which is more powerful. Our block variant gives up some power to get an exact independence argument.

What it catches and misses. False alarms: 0 of 120 (95% interval 0 to 3.0%), consistent with 1%. It flagged 13 of 59: 4 raw CPU jitter samples, 8 weak generators (the Numerical Recipes LCG words, MINSTD, RANDU and xorshift32) and parity, the last at \(p = 8.4 imes 10^{-155}\). The honest limit is sample size. The paper's own table (arXiv 2108.13061v3) gives the data its overlapping test needed to reach \(p < 10^{-20}\): \(1 imes 10^{10}\) bytes for xoroshiro128, \(5 imes 10^{12}\) for xoroshiro128+, and \(4 imes 10^{10}\) for a 521-bit Mersenne Twister. MT19937 is not in that table. At our sizes, of a few MiB, this test mainly catches gross weight dependence: MT19937 and xoroshiro128+ both passed here. For those linear generators, test 7 does the job at this sample size.

docs.title: 13.5 Summary
docs.text:
• Birthday collisions: the number of repeated \(w\)-bit words among \(m\) uniform words is approximately Poisson with \(\lambda=m(m-1)/2^{w+1}\). Too many repeats and too few are both suspicious.
  • Detrended fluctuation analysis uses a sequential permutation test (Besag and Clifford) so that ordinary data stops after a few dozen shuffles while a suspicious sample earns the full 1999.
  • Held-out predictor: train on the first half, freeze the weights, score on the second half; under the null every hit is an independent fair coin, so the law is exactly binomial.
  • Hamming-weight dependency (Blackman and Vigna) checks whether the weight classes of the last few words predict the next word's weight; an orthogonal rotation keeps the coefficients independent and standard normal.
  • The honest limit of H2 is sample size: the published tests needed \(10^{10}\) bytes or more to expose some generators.

docs.title: 13.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Check the birthday approximation for 23 people in a 365-day year: compute \(\lambda\) and the chance of at least one shared birthday.

    Answer

    \(\lambda=23\times22/(2\times365)=0.693\). The chance of at least one shared birthday is about \(1-e^{-0.693}=0.5000\); the exact figure is 0.5073, so the approximation is good.

  2. For \(m=2^{19}\) 32-bit words, find \(\lambda\). What is \(\lambda\) for a 1 MiB sample, which supplies \(m=2^{18}\) words? What p-value results from zero repeats at the larger size?

    Answer

    At \(m=2^{19}\): \(\lambda=2^{19}(2^{19}-1)/2^{33}\approx32\). At \(m=2^{18}\): \(\lambda\approx8\). With \(\lambda=32\) and no repeats, \(P(C=0)=e^{-32}=1.3\times10^{-14}\), so the two-sided value is \(2.5\times10^{-14}\) (and \(5.1\times10^{-14}\) after the Bonferroni factor 2).

  3. A frozen model predicts the top bit of 1000 bytes and is right 540 times. Find the one-sided tail probability, and the value after Bonferroni for the 2 targets.

    Answer

    \(P(\text{at least 540 of 1000})=0.0062\), and after the factor 2 it is 0.0124. That is a narrow pass at \(\alpha=0.01\). With 550 right, the tail is 0.00087, or 0.0017 after Bonferroni, which fails.

  4. Why does the held-out predictor not need a correction for the number of patterns the model tried?

    Answer

    The model is trained on the first half and then frozen, and each prediction on the second half depends only on earlier bytes and the frozen weights. Under the null each hit is an independent fair coin, so the number of hits is exactly binomial whatever the model tried during training. The student cannot cheat by memorising, because the marking is on unseen data.

  5. What do both too many and too few repeats suggest in the birthday-collision test?

    Answer

    Too many repeats suggest a small hidden state or bias. Too few are just as suspicious: some generators never repeat a word until they have run through their whole cycle, so zero repeats where about 32 are expected (as for RANDU, LFSR32 and xorshift32) is a failure.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Comparing the Batteries
docs.text: Having met every battery, the natural question is which to use. The answer depends on what you are testing and what you need to conclude. This chapter compares the batteries by the data they need, whether they estimate entropy, whether they can catch a specific generator such as MT19937, and whether they play a role in certification. It then draws the practical conclusion of the whole book: tests of output can show that a source is defective, but they cannot show that it is good.

docs.title: 9.1 What the batteries are for
docs.text:
Each battery was built for a purpose, and the purposes differ. SP 800-22, Diehard, Dieharder, TestU01, PractRand and ENT all look at output and ask whether it looks random. SP 800-90B and AIS 31 are different: they ask how much entropy the source actually produces, and AIS 31 demands a physical model of the noise. The research batteries (TestU01 and PractRand) are the strongest statistical tools for finding flaws in pseudo-random generators, but they get their power from enormous amounts of data. They find flaws in algorithms and say nothing about how much entropy a physical source produces.

SP 800-22 is a weak discriminator for a physical or quantum source: a weak but statistically clean generator passes it. SP 800-90B is the right framework for a noise source, although its estimators have known biases in both directions. AIS 31 is the most serious scheme, and also the most demanding, because it asks the vendor to justify the entropy claim from the physics of the device.

docs.title: 9.2 The batteries side by side
docs.text:
No single row of the table tells the whole story. The cells for catching MT19937 are stated only where a source reports them, or where the test's limits decide the matter. Cells that say "not reported" mean that no primary source was found saying either way.

Capability SP 800-22 SP 800-90B Diehard TestU01 BigCrush PractRand AIS 31 (2011) Data needed about \(10^6\) bits per sequence, on the order of \(1/\alpha\) sequences \(10^6\) samples, plus \(1000 \times 1000\) restart matrix 10 to 12 million bytes close to \(2^{38}\) numbers no fixed amount; grows until you stop 8,285,728 bits for A; about 7 million bits or more for B Estimates min-entropy No Yes, this is its purpose No No No Not in version 2.0: T8 estimates Shannon-style entropy; version 3.0 allows min-entropy claims Can prove a specific PRNG No No No No No No Catches MT19937, and at what size Not with blocks of at most 5000 bits Not reported; no estimator models long linear recurrences Not reported; rank grids are at most 32x32 Yes, two linear complexity tests, in a run of about \(2^{38}\) numbers Yes, by its binary rank test, listed as failing at 256 GB Not reported; not designed for this Recognises raw physical noise No Assesses it, but does not identify it No No No Through the stochastic model, not the tests alone Used for certification No role that we confirmed in the document Yes, NIST CAVP and CMVP validation No No No Yes, in the German Common Criteria scheme

docs.title: 9.3 What a pass can and cannot mean
docs.text:
Chapter 2 gave the central limit of all this: a CSPRNG is, by definition, a generator whose output no practical test can tell apart from true coin flips, and a conditioned physical source is, if its conditioner works, also very close to true coin flips. So both should pass every test, and if a test could reliably separate them, that test would be a break of the CSPRNG. The difference is real, but it lies in where the bits came from, and the bits carry no label.

What a pass means

Passing means "no defect found", never "quantum" and never "secure". Treat a clean result as the absence of one kind of evidence against the source. To judge a source you also need its design, its raw data before conditioning, and the health data from the device.

The practical rule that follows is to match the tool to the question. To find a weak generator, use the research batteries on as much data as you can generate. To assess a physical noise source, use SP 800-90B on raw samples, with restart data, and the health tests inside the device, and read the design rationale alongside. To meet a certification scheme, follow the scheme: NIST validation for SP 800-90B, or the Common Criteria scheme with AIS 31.

docs.title: 9.4 Summary
docs.text:
• The batteries answer different questions. SP 800-22, Diehard, Dieharder, TestU01, PractRand and ENT look at output and ask whether it looks random; SP 800-90B and AIS 31 ask how much entropy the source produces, and AIS 31 demands a physical model.
  • Only SP 800-90B is built to estimate min-entropy; only SP 800-90B and AIS 31 play a role in certification schemes (NIST CAVP and CMVP validation, and the German Common Criteria scheme respectively).
  • The amount of data needed ranges from about \(10^6\) bits per sequence (SP 800-22) to a stream that grows until you stop (PractRand) and about \(2^{38}\) numbers (BigCrush).
  • Catching one generator, MT19937, needs the right test: linear-complexity tests in a very long run (TestU01), the binary rank test at 256 GB (PractRand), and not SP 800-22 with short blocks.
  • A pass never proves quality. A clean result is not evidence of a quantum origin.

docs.title: 9.5 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Which battery or standard in the comparison table (a) is built to estimate min-entropy, (b) needs no fixed amount of data, (c) is used in the German Common Criteria scheme?

    Answer

    (a) NIST SP 800-90B. (b) PractRand. (c) BSI AIS 31.

  2. You are asked to evaluate a physical noise source for a certification. Which battery would you consider first, and why is SP 800-22 on its own a poor choice?

    Answer

    SP 800-90B (and, under the German scheme, AIS 31 with its stochastic model) addresses the entropy of the source, which is what certification needs. SP 800-22 is a poor discriminator: it looks only at output, and a weak but statistically clean generator, or a well-conditioned weak source, passes it.

  3. A colleague has run SP 800-22 on 100 sequences of one million bits and everything passed. List three things this does not tell you.

    Answer

    It does not tell you where the bits came from (a CSPRNG and a conditioned quantum source both pass), how much min-entropy the raw source has, or whether a generator with structure larger than the tests' blocks, such as MT19937 with its linear complexity of 19,937, is present. It also says nothing about behaviour at start-up or over a long run.

  4. Explain why the cells of the comparison table for "catches MT19937" are filled in only where a source reports it.

    Answer

    The table states a capability only where a primary source reports it or where the test's own limits decide the matter (for example blocks of at most 5000 bits cannot expose a generator of linear complexity 19,937). Elsewhere it says "not reported", because a claim without a source would be a guess.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Diehard and Dieharder
docs.text: Diehard was written in 1995 as a deliberately varied stress test. Its idea is to simulate situations whose answer is known: if the numbers are uniform, the count of parked cars or the closest pair of points follows a known law. Dieharder, its open and extensible successor, reads from a generator directly, draws far more p-values and rates its own tests. This chapter describes the Diehard tests and the four RGB tests added by Dieharder, with the same four-part presentation as before, and explains how to read hundreds of p-values without being fooled.

docs.title: 6.1 About Diehard
