docs.text: George Marsaglia of Florida State University released Diehard in 1995 with a CD-ROM of random numbers, as a tough, varied stress test for generators. It reads a binary file of about 10 to 12 million bytes as 32-bit integers. Most tests return a p-value that should be uniform on \([0, 1)\), and many combine repeated runs with a Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test (see Chapter 2). Marsaglia's own advice on reading the output is worth remembering. Hundreds of p-values come out, so a value below 0.025 or above 0.975 is not a failure by itself. The normal approximations behind many of them are weakest in the tails. A stream that truly fails big gives p-values of 0 or 1 to six or more places.

docs.title: 6.2 Birthday spacings
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Pick random birthdays in a very long year and sort them. The gaps between neighbouring birthdays should rarely match each other. It is a twist on the classic birthday puzzle, and generators whose values fall on a regular lattice give far too many matching gaps.

Example 6.2: Birthday spacings

Take 6 birthdays in a 32-day year: 3, 9, 14, 20, 27, 31. The gaps are 6, 5, 6, 7, 4, and only the value 6 occurs more than once, so \(j = 1\). Here \(\lambda = 6^3/(4 \cdot 32) = 1.6875\), although a year this short is far from the real conditions.

The mathematics.

\[\lambda = \frac{m^3}{4n}, \qquad j \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda) \text{ approximately}, \qquad \chi^2 = \sum_k \frac{(\mathrm{obs}_k - \mathrm{exp}_k)^2}{\mathrm{exp}_k}\]
  • \(m\) is the number of birthdays, \(n\) the length of the year, and \(j\) the number of gap values that occur more than once.
  • The written description uses \(m = 512\) and \(n = 2^{24}\), so \(\lambda = 2\), with 500 values of \(j\).
  • The Diehard report printed by the program uses \(m = 1024\), so \(\lambda = 16\), with 17 degrees of freedom.

The chi-square test runs on nine bit windows, bits 1 to 24 through 9 to 32, and a KS test combines the nine p-values.

What it catches and misses. It catches lattice structure, including linear congruential and some lagged-Fibonacci generators. Bit windows outside its nine positions are not examined, and it says nothing about order in time, because the data is sorted.

docs.title: 6.3 Overlapping 5-permutations (OPERM5)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Look at five numbers in a row and rank them from smallest to largest. There are 120 possible orderings, and each should be equally common. Then move along by one number and do it again. Because the windows overlap, neighbouring results are linked, and the test has to allow for that.

Example 6.3: Overlapping 5-permutations (OPERM5)

The five values 0.3, 0.7, 0.1, 0.9, 0.5 have rank pattern 2, 4, 1, 5, 3, one of \(5! = 120\) orderings, each with probability \(1/120 = 0.00833\). In a million windows, you expect about 8333 of each.

The mathematics.

\[Q = (c - \mu)^{T} \Sigma^{+} (c - \mu)\]
  • \(c\) holds the 120 ordering counts, and \(\mu\) their expected values.
  • \(\Sigma^{+}\) is the weak inverse of the \(120 \times 120\) covariance matrix of the counts. A weak inverse is the nearest thing to an inverse when, as here, the matrix cannot be inverted outright.
  • Diehard states rank 99 and compares \(Q\) with a chi-square on 99 degrees of freedom, on two samples of 1,000,000 integers.

Robert Brown's dieharder notes that the true rank is \(5! - 4! = 96\), says the original test almost certainly had errors, and uses 96.

What it catches and misses. It catches ordering preferences among close neighbours. It is blind to the actual sizes of values, only their order. Treat Diehard's own version with care: dieharder rates the original test Suspect, for failing even good generators.

docs.title: 6.4 Binary rank 31x31
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Build square grids of bits from the generator's numbers and ask how many rows are truly independent, with arithmetic where 1 + 1 = 0. This is the same idea as the rank test in SP 800-22. Random grids nearly always have rank within a few of full.

Example 6.4: Binary rank 31x31

If 40,000 grids produced counts 220, 5130, 23050, 11600 for ranks at most 28, then 29, 30, 31, then against the expected counts below, \(\chi^2 = 0.678\). With 3 degrees of freedom, that gives \(p = 0.878\).

The mathematics.

\[p_r = 2^{r(2M-r)-M^2} \prod_{i=0}^{r-1} \frac{(1-2^{i-M})^2}{1-2^{i-r}}, \qquad \chi^2 = \sum_{\text{classes}} \frac{(\mathrm{obs} - \mathrm{exp})^2}{\mathrm{exp}}\]
  • \(M = 31\), and each row is the leftmost 31 bits of one 32-bit integer.
  • With 40,000 grids, the expected counts are 211.4 for rank at most 28, 5134.0 for rank 29, 23103.0 for rank 30 and 11551.5 for rank 31. The formula reproduces all four.

What it catches and misses. It catches linear dependence between successive words in the upper bits. Bit 32 of each integer is never used here. Also, generators with a linear recurrence longer than the grid can look fine.

docs.title: 6.5 Binary rank 32x32
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This is the same experiment with a slightly larger grid, and this time each row is a whole 32-bit integer. Any bit position that is stuck or tied to other bits will start to pull ranks down. Think of a jury in which some members just copy others.

Example 6.5: Binary rank 32x32

Counts of 230, 5100, 23200, 11470 for ranks at most 29, then 30, 31, 32 give \(\chi^2 = 2.844\) and, on 3 degrees of freedom, \(p = 0.416\). If a generator could never reach full rank, the count for rank 32 would be 0, and that term alone would add 11551.5 to \(\chi^2\).

The mathematics.

\[\chi^2 = \sum_{\text{classes}} \frac{(\mathrm{obs} - \mathrm{exp})^2}{\mathrm{exp}}, \qquad p = P\!\left(\chi^2_3 \ge \chi^2\right)\]
  • \(\chi^2_3\) is a chi-square variable with 3 degrees of freedom, from 4 classes.
  • The expected counts for 40,000 grids are 211.4 for rank at most 29, 5134.0 for rank 30, 23103.0 for rank 31 and 11551.5 for rank 32.
  • The rank formula is the same as for the 31x31 test, with \(M = 32\).

What it catches and misses. It catches dependence across all 32 bits, including poor low-order bits. As with its smaller sibling, 1024 bits per grid is far too few to expose a long recurrence.

docs.title: 6.6 Binary rank 6x8
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Now the grid is small and not square: pick one byte from each of six integers and stack them into a 6 by 8 grid. Because only one byte of each integer is used, this test can look at each byte position in turn, like inspecting each lane of a road separately.

Example 6.6: Binary rank 6x8

Against 100,000 grids, counts of 950, 21650, 77400 for ranks at most 4, then 5, 6 give \(\chi^2 = 0.541\). On 2 degrees of freedom, that gives \(p = 0.763\).

The mathematics.

\[p_r = 2^{r(R+C-r)-RC} \prod_{i=0}^{r-1} \frac{(1-2^{i-R})(1-2^{i-C})}{1-2^{i-r}}, \qquad \chi^2 = \sum_{r \in \{\le 4,\, 5,\, 6\}} \frac{(\mathrm{obs}_r - \mathrm{exp}_r)^2}{\mathrm{exp}_r}\]
  • \(R = 6\) rows and \(C = 8\) columns.
  • For 100,000 grids, the expected counts are 944.3, 21743.9 and 77311.8.
  • The chosen byte moves through 25 windows, bits 1 to 8 through 25 to 32, and a KS test combines the 25 p-values.

What it catches and misses. It catches a weak byte position, which a test on whole words might dilute. It looks at only 48 bits at a time, so it is sensitive only to very local linear structure.

docs.title: 6.7 Bitstream
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Picture a monkey typing on a two-key keyboard and write out every overlapping 20-bit word. There are \(2^{20}\) possible words, and we produce \(2^{21}\) of them, so on average each is typed twice. Yet by pure chance, some are never typed. The number of missing words is the test.

Example 6.7: Bitstream

Each word is missing with probability about \(e^{-2}\), so the expected number missing is \(2^{20} e^{-2} = 141{,}909.3\), in line with the published 141,909. A run with 141,000 missing words gives \(z = (141000 - 141909)/428 = -2.12\).

The mathematics.

\[z = \frac{j - 141909}{428}, \qquad p = \Phi(z)\]
  • \(j\) is the number of the \(2^{20}\) possible 20-bit words that never appear.
  • The stream holds \(2^{21} + 19\) bits, giving \(2^{21}\) overlapping words.
  • The 428 is specific to the overlapping version. Dieharder's notes give 290 for independent samples.
  • The test is repeated 20 times, giving 20 p-values.

What it catches and misses. It catches any bias towards some 20-bit patterns, without needing to know which ones. It is not sensitive to dependence beyond 20 bits apart.

docs.title: 6.8 OPSO
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. OPSO stands for overlapping pairs sparse occupancy. Our monkey now has a keyboard of 1024 letters, each made from 10 chosen bits of a 32-bit integer, and it types overlapping two-letter words. We count the words it never typed. It gives a sharp view of how pairs of numbers fit together.

Example 6.8: OPSO

With 2 letters of 10 bits, there are \(2^{20}\) possible words and \(2^{21}\) are typed, so the expected number missing is again 141,909. A count of 142,000 gives \(z = (142000 - 141909)/290 = 0.314\) and \(p = 0.623\).

The mathematics.

\[z = \frac{j - 141909}{290}, \qquad p = \Phi(z)\]
  • \(j\) is the number of missing two-letter words, from \(2^{21} + 1\) keystrokes.
  • The 10-bit window moves through 23 positions, bits 1 to 10 through 23 to 32.
  • Dieharder's notes describe the \(\sigma = 290\) as the true value to three significant figures, rather than a simulation result. The dieharder code uses 290.4622634038.

What it catches and misses. It catches dependence between consecutive numbers in specific bit fields. It looks only at adjacent pairs and only at the chosen 10 bits at a time.

docs.title: 6.9 OQSO
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. OQSO stands for overlapping quadruples sparse occupancy. The keyboard now has just 32 letters, from 5 chosen bits per integer, and the words are four letters long. It still counts missing words, but now four numbers in a row must cooperate.

Example 6.9: OQSO

Again \(32^4 = 2^{20}\) words and \(2^{21}\) typed. A count of 142,000 gives \(z = (142000 - 141909)/295 = 0.308\).

The mathematics.

\[z = \frac{j - 141909}{295}, \qquad p = \Phi(z)\]
  • \(j\) is the number of missing four-letter words, from \(2^{21} + 3\) keystrokes.
  • The mean comes from theory, and \(\sigma = 295\) from extensive simulation.
  • The 5-bit window moves through 28 positions.

What it catches and misses. It catches dependence across four consecutive numbers in small bit fields. Like its siblings, it reports only an overall count, so it does not say which word was odd.

docs.title: 6.10 DNA
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. The keyboard shrinks to four letters, C, G, A and T, from two chosen bits per integer, and the words are ten letters long. So each word stretches across ten numbers in a row. This is the longest memory of the monkey tests.

Example 6.10: DNA

There are \(4^{10} = 2^{20}\) words and \(2^{21}\) are typed. A count of 142,000 gives \(z = (142000 - 141909)/339 = 0.268\).

The mathematics.

\[z = \frac{j - 141909}{339}, \qquad p = \Phi(z)\]
  • \(j\) is the number of missing ten-letter words, from \(2^{21} + 9\) keystrokes.
  • \(\sigma = 339\) comes from simulation.
  • The 2-bit window moves through 31 positions.

What it catches and misses. It catches weak individual bit pairs and dependence over ten successive outputs. It reads only 2 bits of each number, so it says little about the rest.

docs.title: 6.11 Count-the-1s on a stream
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Count the 1 bits in each byte and turn the count into a letter. Middling counts are common, extreme ones are rare, so the five letters have known odds. Then ask whether five-letter words made this way turn up as often as they should. It is a test of how neighbouring bytes relate through their weight alone.

Example 6.11: Count-the-1s on a stream

The bytes 0x31, 0xF0, 0x07, 0xAA, 0xFF have 3, 4, 3, 4, 8 ones, so they spell BCBCE. That word has probability \((56 \cdot 70 \cdot 56 \cdot 70 \cdot 37)/256^5 = 0.000517\), so it should appear about 132 times in 256,000 words. A statistic of \(Q_5 - Q_4 = 2600\) gives \(z = 1.41\).

The mathematics.

\[Q_k = \sum_{\text{words}} \frac{(\mathrm{obs} - \mathrm{exp})^2}{\mathrm{exp}}, \qquad z = \frac{(Q_5 - Q_4) - 2500}{\sqrt{5000}}\]
  • Counts of 0, 1, 2 ones become A; 3 becomes B; 4 becomes C; 5 becomes D; and 6, 7, 8 become E.
  • The letter probabilities are 37, 56, 70, 56 and 37 out of 256.
  • \(Q_5\) and \(Q_4\) cover 5-letter and 4-letter overlapping words. Subtracting handles the overlap.
  • The degrees of freedom are \(5^5 - 5^4 = 2500\). The Diehard text writes this as \(5^4 - 5^3\), which would be 500, so we take that as a slip.

What it catches and misses. It catches bytes whose weights depend on their neighbours, and generators with poor bit balance. Different bytes with equal weight look identical to it.

docs.title: 6.12 Count-the-1s on specific bytes
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This is the same game with one change. Rather than using every byte, we take one specified byte from each integer. That lets us aim the test at one position at a time, like testing each finger of a typist separately.

Example 6.12: Count-the-1s on specific bytes

With a window of bits 9 to 16, the integer 0x12F0A507 contributes byte 0xF0, which has 4 ones and so becomes the letter C. A statistic of 2600 gives \(z = 1.41\) and \(p = 0.921\), the same scale as the stream test.

The mathematics.

\[z = \frac{(Q_5 - Q_4) - 2500}{\sqrt{5000}}, \qquad p = \Phi(z)\]
  • \(Q_5\) and \(Q_4\) are as defined for the stream test.
  • Words come from 256,000 integers, one chosen byte each.
  • The byte window moves through 25 positions, bits 1 to 8 through 25 to 32.

What it catches and misses. It catches defects tied to one byte position, which a whole-stream count might wash out. A defect shared evenly across all bytes is more likely to be picked up by the stream test.

docs.title: 6.13 Parking lot
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Try to park cars at random in a 100 by 100 lot. If a new car would hit one already parked, it goes away and another tries. After 12,000 attempts, a fairly stable number of cars has parked. Clumpy or lattice-like generators leave too many or too few spots.

Example 6.13: Parking lot

If 3500 cars parked, \(z = (3500 - 3523)/21.9 = -1.05\) and \(p = 0.147\).

The mathematics.

\[z = \frac{k - 3523}{21.9}, \qquad p = \Phi(z)\]
  • \(k\) is the number of cars parked after 12,000 attempts.
  • There is no exact theory, so the mean and \(\sigma\) come from simulation.
  • A KS test combines 10 such values.

The Diehard text speaks of circles of radius 1, while dieharder's notes describe square cars. In a quick simulation of ours, a crash rule where both coordinates differ by at most 1 averages about 3520, which fits the constant. Circles of radius 1 average near 1400, which does not.

What it catches and misses. It catches poor uniformity of successive pairs in the plane. It is a fairly gentle test, sensitive mostly to gross two-dimensional structure.

docs.title: 6.14 Minimum distance
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Scatter 8000 points in a big square and find the two closest. That smallest gap follows a known pattern. Points that are too neat give gaps that are too big, and clumped points give gaps too small. Think of the closest pair of strangers in a crowded square.

Example 6.14: Minimum distance

A closest pair with \(d^2 = 0.5\) gives \(1 - e^{-0.5/0.995} = 0.395\), a perfectly ordinary value.

The mathematics.

\[p = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{d^2}{0.995}\right)\]
  • \(d\) is the smallest distance among the \((n^2 - n)/2\) pairs of \(n = 8000\) points in a square of side 10,000.
  • \(d^2\) is approximately exponential with mean 0.995, so \(p\) should be uniform.
  • This is repeated 100 times, with a KS test on the 100 values.

Dieharder's notes say this expression is not accurate enough for very large numbers of trials, and call its own version with corrections a replacement.

What it catches and misses. It catches pairs of outputs that land too close or too far apart in the plane. With only 100 repetitions, it can detect only large errors in the density of points.

docs.title: 6.15 3D spheres
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This is the closest-pair idea in three dimensions. Scatter 4000 points in a cube, grow a sphere around each until it touches its nearest neighbour, and take the smallest sphere. Triples of outputs that fall on planes will show up here.

Example 6.15: 3D spheres

A smallest radius with \(r^3 = 10\) gives \(1 - e^{-10/30} = 0.283\). The mean volume is \((4/3)\pi \cdot 30 = 125.66\), matching the text's \(120\pi/3\).

The mathematics.

\[p = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{r^3}{30}\right)\]
  • \(r\) is the smallest nearest-neighbour distance among 4000 points in a cube of edge 1000.
  • \(r^3\) is approximately exponential with mean 30, a value found by extensive simulation.
  • Twenty such samples go into a KS test.

What it catches and misses. It catches poor three-dimensional uniformity, such as the plane structure of weak linear congruential generators. It uses only 20 values in the KS test, so its power against subtle defects is limited.

docs.title: 6.16 Squeeze
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Start with a huge number and keep multiplying it by a random fraction, rounding up, until you reach 1. Count the steps. Under good randomness, the number of steps follows a known pattern, with a typical squeeze taking a couple of dozen steps. Bad generators reach 1 too fast or too slowly.

Example 6.16: Squeeze

Starting from 100 for simplicity, the fractions 0.5, 0.7, 0.3, 0.9, 0.2, 0.4 give 50, 35, 11, 10, 2, 1, so \(j = 6\).

The mathematics.

\[k_0 = 2^{31}, \qquad k_{t+1} = \lceil k_t U_{t+1} \rceil, \qquad j = \min\{t : k_t = 1\}\] \[\chi^2 = \sum_{\text{cells}} \frac{(\mathrm{obs} - \mathrm{exp})^2}{\mathrm{exp}}, \qquad \text{with 42 degrees of freedom}\]
  • \(U_t\) are uniforms made from the file's integers.
  • This is repeated 100,000 times, with cells for \(j \le 6\), each \(j\) from 7 to 47, and \(j \ge 48\).

What it catches and misses. It catches defects that affect products of successive uniforms and the upper bits. It uses each number only through its size, so it is not sensitive to the low-order bits.

docs.title: 6.17 Overlapping sums
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Add 100 uniforms, then slide along by one and add again. Each sum should be close to bell-shaped, and neighbouring sums share almost everything. In principle, you can untangle them into independent normals and test those. In practice, this one has a known problem.

Example 6.17: Overlapping sums

With a window of 3 and values 0.2, 0.9, 0.4, 0.7, the sums are 1.5 and 2.0, sharing two of their three terms. At the real window of 100, each sum has mean 50 and variance \(100/12 = 8.33\), and neighbouring sums have covariance \(99/12 = 8.25\).

The mathematics.

\[S_i = \sum_{j=0}^{99} U_{i+j}, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(S_i, S_{i'}) = \frac{100 - \lvert i - i' \rvert}{12} \text{ when } \lvert i - i' \rvert < 100\]
  • \(U_i\) are uniforms in \([0, 1)\).
  • A linear transformation is meant to give independent standard normals, which become uniforms for a KS test.
  • Ten KS p-values then go into one final KS test.

What it catches and misses. It is meant to catch slow drift in the mean. Robert Brown's dieharder documentation rates it "Do Not Use" and says it gives a non-flat p-value distribution even for gold-standard generators. His lagged-sums test covers the same ground more reliably, so we would not rely on this one.

docs.title: 6.18 Runs up and down
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. A run up is a stretch of values that keep rising, and a run down is a stretch that keeps falling. In random data, long runs are rare in a precisely known way. It is like counting how many days in a row a share price keeps going up.

Example 6.18: Runs up and down

Marsaglia's own example, 0.123, 0.357, 0.789, 0.425, 0.224, 0.416, 0.95, starts with an up-run of length 3, then a down-run of length 2, then an up-run of at least 2.

The mathematics.

\[Q = (c - \mathrm{E}[c])^{T} \Sigma^{+} (c - \mathrm{E}[c])\]
  • \(c\) holds the counts of runs of each length, for runs up or for runs down, and \(\mathrm{E}[c]\) their expected values.
  • \(\Sigma^{+}\) is the weak inverse of their covariance matrix, and \(Q\) is compared with a chi-square distribution.
  • Each sequence has 10,000 numbers. It is run ten times, then in three more sets of ten.

TestU01's guide gives 6 degrees of freedom for the closely related statistic it uses, with run lengths of 6 or more merged.

What it catches and misses. It catches short-term trends and correlated order between successive values. It uses order only, not magnitude, so a generator with sound ordering but poor values can pass.

docs.title: 6.19 Craps
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Play the dice game craps 200,000 times using the generator. We know exactly how often you should win and how long games should last. A casino would notice odd dice very quickly, and this is the same check. Unusually, it is two tests in one: the win rate and the length of games.

Example 6.19: Craps

The win probability is exactly \(244/495 = 0.492929\), so 200,000 games should give about 98,585.9 wins with \(\sigma = 223.6\). If you see 98,800 wins, \(z = 0.958\) and \(p = 0.831\). The chance of a game ending on the first throw is \(1/3\).

The mathematics.

\[z = \frac{w - 200000p}{\sqrt{200000\,p(1-p)}}, \qquad p = \frac{244}{495}\] \[\pi_1 = \frac{1}{3}, \qquad \pi_{i+1} = \frac{27(27/36)^{i-1} + 40(13/18)^{i-1} + 55(25/36)^{i-1}}{648} \text{ for } i = 1, \ldots, 19\]
  • \(w\) is the number of wins.
  • \(\pi_s\) is the probability that a game ends on throw \(s\), and all games of 21 throws or more share a final cell.
  • A chi-square on those 21 cells, with 20 degrees of freedom, tests game length. We checked these formulas against an exact count.

Each throw of one die is \(1 + \lfloor 6U \rfloor\), using one 32-bit integer.

What it catches and misses. It catches gross dependence between dice throws and weak upper bits. Only the top few bits of each integer decide a die's value, so anything lurking in the lower bits goes unseen.

docs.title: 6.20 About Dieharder
docs.text:
Robert G. Brown of Duke University wrote dieharder, with Dirk Eddelbuettel and David Bauer credited as authors of some versions, as an open, extensible successor to Diehard. It makes four main changes. It draws from a generator directly, so it can use as much data as you like instead of a fixed file. If you do feed it a file and the file runs short, it rewinds, which can distort results, so piping a stream in is better. It uses 100 p-values for its final KS test by default, far more than most of Diehard. It rates its own tests: most are Good, OPERM5 is Suspect and overlapping sums is Do Not Use. And it adds tests: its own RGB tests below, some from NIST's suite (monobit, runs and serial), and others such as Marsaglia and Tsang's GCD test. Where the original tests overlap samples, dieharder prefers non-overlapping versions.

Reading the output is simple in principle. The manual sets the null hypothesis as a perfect generator for any seed, and flags a p-value as weak below 0.5 percent or above 99.5 percent. Those two tails total 1 percent, so that is about one test in 100 on good data. The manual says "at the 1% level total", yet also says one test in two hundred. For failed, the option defaults give one in a million, although one passage of the manual says 0.05 percent, and we could not reconcile those two. Brown is honest that the assessment labels deserve suspicion: a good generator will probably show weak on 0, 1 or 2 tests in a full run, and may fail one test in about 10 such runs. Options exist to resolve ambiguity by adding samples until a weak result clears or fails, or to test a generator to destruction.

docs.title: 6.21 RGB bit distribution (Dieharder)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Take words of \(n\) bits from the stream, without overlap, in small handfuls of 64. For any one word value, the number of times it turns up in a handful should follow a binomial pattern. It is like checking not only that all faces of a die come up equally often, but that their counts in each batch vary by the right amount.

Example 6.21: RGB bit distribution (Dieharder)

For \(n = 2\), each 2-bit value has chance \(1/4\) per draw. So the chance that a value appears exactly 16 times out of 64 is 0.1145. Over 1000 handfuls, you would expect about 114.5 such handfuls.

The mathematics.

\[E_b = t\binom{64}{b} p^b (1-p)^{64-b}, \qquad p = 2^{-n}, \qquad \chi^2 = \sum_{b} \frac{(x_b - E_b)^2}{E_b}\]
  • \(n\) is the tuple size and \(t\) is the number of handfuls (tsamples, default 100,000).
  • \(x_b\) is how many handfuls contain a given value exactly \(b\) times.
  • Bins with small expected counts are pooled.
  • Each run computes a p-value per value and keeps one chosen at random, and a KS test combines 100 of these (psamples).

For \(n\) above 12, Brown says to raise tsamples so that each bin averages about 30 occurrences.

What it catches and misses. It catches bias and clumping in \(n\)-bit words, and by raising \(n\) you can see where a generator starts to fail. Because each run keeps only one p-value, a defect in a few word values may take many runs to show. The source comments admit that a proper combination is still missing.

docs.title: 6.22 RGB generalised minimum distance (Dieharder)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Marsaglia's closest-pair idea is extended here to 2, 3, 4 or 5 dimensions, with a better formula. Scatter points in a unit cube and find the closest pair. Brown's version includes correction terms from M. Fischler, so that the formula stays accurate when you run many more trials.

Example 6.22: RGB generalised minimum distance (Dieharder)

Take \(d = 2\), \(n = 1000\) and \(r = 0.001\). Then \(V = \pi r^2 = 3.1416 \times 10^{-6}\), the exponent is \(-1.5692\), and the correction factor is 1.00397. So \(p = 0.79097\), against 0.79179 with no correction.

The mathematics.

\[p = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{n(n-1)V}{2}\right)\left(1 + \frac{2 + Q_d}{6}\,n^3 V^2\right)\] \[V = \frac{\pi^{d/2} r^d}{(d/2)!} \ (d \text{ even}), \qquad V = \frac{2(2\pi)^{(d-1)/2} r^d}{d!!} \ (d \text{ odd})\]
  • \(n\) is the number of points, \(d\) the dimension, and \(r\) the smallest distance.
  • \(Q_d\) is 0.4135, 0.5312, 0.6202 and 1.3789 for \(d = 2\) to 5.
  • The trial count sets how small a density error can be seen. Brown's comments say Marsaglia's \(n = 8000\) would need about 2500 trials to detect a steady 20 percent error in two dimensions.

What it catches and misses. It catches clumping or excess regularity of points in up to five dimensions, at a scale you can set through \(n\). Without wraparound, edges matter, which is what the correction terms address. It sees only the closest pair, so it does not describe the rest of the distribution.

docs.title: 6.23 RGB permutations (Dieharder)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Take \(n\) numbers at a time and note their order. All \(n!\) orderings should be equally likely. Unlike OPERM5, the groups do not overlap, so the counts are independent and an ordinary chi-square works. Simple often beats clever, and this is the simple version.

Example 6.23: RGB permutations (Dieharder)

For \(n = 3\) there are 6 orderings. Over 600 groups you expect 100 each. Counts of 110, 95, 100, 90, 105, 100 give \(\chi^2 = 2.5\) and, on 5 degrees of freedom, \(p = 0.776\).

The mathematics.

\[\chi^2 = \sum_{\text{orderings}} \frac{(\mathrm{obs} - t/n!)^2}{t/n!}, \qquad \text{with } n! - 1 \text{ degrees of freedom}\]
  • \(n\) is the group size.
  • \(t\) is the number of groups (tsamples, default 100,000).
  • A KS test combines the p-values from 100 runs (psamples).

What it catches and misses. It catches ordering preferences, with no worry over overlap correlations. It uses only relative order and looks only within each group, so a dependence that spans group boundaries may go unseen. It also needs more data than an overlapping test to reach the same sensitivity.

docs.title: 6.24 RGB lagged sums (Dieharder)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Add up a long string of uniforms, skipping a fixed number of values between each one you use. The total should sit near half the count. If the generator has a hidden link at that lag, the total drifts. Brown offers this as the reliable replacement for overlapping sums.

Example 6.24: RGB lagged sums (Dieharder)

With \(t = 1{,}000{,}000\) terms, the mean is 500,000 and \(\sigma = \sqrt{1000000/12} = 288.68\). A total of 500,500 gives \(z = 1.73\) and a two-sided \(p = 0.083\).

The mathematics.

\[z = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{t} U_{i(\ell+1)} - t/2}{\sqrt{t/12}}\]
  • \(U\) are uniforms, \(\ell\) is the lag (the values skipped between terms), and \(t\) is the number of terms (tsamples, default 1,000,000).
  • The sum is approximately normal, and it becomes a p-value through the error function.
  • A KS test combines the p-values from 100 runs (psamples).

What it catches and misses. It catches slow drift and correlation at a chosen lag. Since it adds up values, it responds mainly to the upper bits, and any defect that keeps the mean right will pass. You also have to scan through the lags yourself, as a defect at an untested lag stays hidden.

docs.title: 6.25 Summary
docs.text:
• Diehard reads about 10 to 12 million bytes as 32-bit integers. Most tests return a p-value that should be uniform on \([0,1)\), and many combine repeated runs with a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
  • Hundreds of p-values come out, so a value below 0.025 or above 0.975 is not a failure by itself. A stream that truly fails gives p-values of 0 or 1 to six or more places.
  • The families of tests are: lattice and spacing (birthday spacings, minimum distance, 3D spheres), occupancy of sparse words (bitstream, OPSO, OQSO, DNA), linear dependence (binary ranks), order and size (OPERM5, runs, squeeze, overlapping sums, craps) and geometry (parking lot).
  • Dieharder draws from a generator directly, uses 100 p-values for its final KS test, and labels tests Good, Suspect or Do Not Use. Overlapping sums is rated Do Not Use.
  • Every test reports only an overall result, so a failure says that something is wrong but rarely what.

docs.title: 6.26 Exercises
docs.text:
1. In the birthday spacings test, 8 birthdays fall in a 64-day year. Compute \(\lambda=n^3/(4m)\). What does it represent?

    Answer

    \(\lambda=8^3/(4\times64)=512/256=2\). It is the expected number \(j\) of values that occur more than once among the sorted gaps between birthdays; under randomness that count is approximately Poisson with mean \(\lambda\).

  2. Craps is played 10,000 times with the generator under test. The exact win probability is \(244/495\). Find the expected number of wins and its standard deviation.

    Answer

    Expected wins: \(10{,}000\times244/495=4929.3\). The standard deviation is \(\sqrt{10{,}000\times(244/495)\times(251/495)}=50.0\). A count more than about 150 away (three standard deviations) would be suspicious.

  3. A Diehard run prints a p-value of 0.97 on one test and 0.04 on another, and nothing else is unusual. Should you reject the generator?

    Answer

    No. Marsaglia's advice is that with hundreds of p-values a value below 0.025 or above 0.975 is not a failure by itself, and the normal approximations behind many of them are weakest in the tails. A genuinely failing stream gives p-values of 0 or 1 to six or more places.

  4. List the four main changes that Dieharder made to Diehard.

    Answer

    It draws from a generator directly, so it can use as much data as wanted instead of a fixed file; it uses 100 p-values for its final KS test by default; it rates its own tests (Good, Suspect, Do Not Use); and it adds tests, including its own RGB tests, some from the NIST suite, and others. Where Diehard overlaps samples, it prefers non-overlapping versions.

  5. Why is the OPERM5 or overlapping-sums test treated with caution in Dieharder, and what does that teach about writing a test?

    Answer

    Dieharder rates OPERM5 as Suspect and overlapping sums as Do Not Use, because they give non-flat p-value distributions even for good generators. A test is valid only if it fails good data at the rate it claims, so a test must be calibrated against known-good data before its failures are believed.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Distributions, Corrections and Entropy
docs.text: The tests in this book turn a count into a p-value using one of five shapes: binomial, normal, chi-square, Poisson and exponential. This chapter introduces them with small checkable numbers, adds the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for a list of numbers, and explains why running many tests forces a correction. It then separates Shannon entropy from min-entropy, which is the measure that security depends on, and ends with the most important limit in the book: no test of the output alone can tell a good CSPRNG from a conditioned physical source.

docs.title: 2.1 Five distributions you will see again
docs.text:
Binomial: counting successes. Toss \(n\) coins, each landing heads with probability \(q\), and count the heads. The count follows a binomial distribution. With 10 fair coins, the chance of exactly 7 heads is 0.1172, and the chance of 7 or more is 0.1719.

\[ P(S = k) = \binom{n}{k} q^k (1-q)^{n-k} \]

Normal and erfc: the bell curve. Add up many small independent effects and you get a bell curve, whatever the effects were. We usually standardise a count into a z-score, which says how many standard deviations it sits from its expected value. The function erfc turns a z-score into a two-sided p-value. In the 60 heads example, \(z = (60 - 50)/5 = 2\), and \(\mathrm{erfc}(2/\sqrt{2}) = 0.0455\), close to the exact 0.0569.

\[ z = \frac{S - n/2}{\sqrt{n/4}}, \qquad \mathrm{erfc}(x) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int_x^\infty e^{-t^2}\, dt, \qquad P(|Z| \ge z) = \mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \]

Chi-square: adding up squared misses. Sort outcomes into cells, then measure how far each cell's count misses its expected count. Square the misses, scale them and add them up. For good data the total follows a chi-square distribution, written \(\chi^2(d)\). The number \(d\) is the degrees of freedom, usually the number of cells minus 1, and it is also the expected total. Roll a die 60 times and get counts 8, 12, 9, 11, 6, 14. Each cell expects 10, so \(X^2 = 42/10 = 4.2\) with \(d = 5\), and \(p = 0.521\). Nothing odd there.

\[ X^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{K} \frac{(O_j - E_j)^2}{E_j} \sim \chi^2(K-1) \]

You will also see the chi-square tail written with igamc, the regularised upper incomplete gamma function. Here \(\Gamma\) is the gamma function, which extends the factorial to non-whole numbers. For example, \(d = 255\) and \(X^2 = 270\) give 0.248 either way.

\[ \mathrm{igamc}(a, x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(a)} \int_x^\infty t^{a-1} e^{-t}\, dt, \qquad P\bigl(\chi^2(d) \ge X^2\bigr) = \mathrm{igamc}\!\left(\frac{d}{2},\ \frac{X^2}{2}\right) \]

Poisson: counting rare events. When many independent chances each have a tiny probability, the number of events that occur follows a Poisson distribution with average \(\lambda\). With \(\lambda = 2\), zero events has probability 0.1353 and five or more has probability 0.0527.

\[ P(C = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^k}{k!} \]

Exponential: the size of one spectral value. Add up many unit-length arrows pointing in random directions. The squared length of the result, divided by the number of arrows, follows an exponential distribution with mean 1. Its tail falls fast: values above 3 happen with probability 0.0498, and values above 15 with probability 0.000000306. We use it for one spectral value at a time. For the biggest of many such values, apply the Sidak step in the next section.

\[ P(X > x) = e^{-x}, \quad x \ge 0 \]

One more tool: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Sometimes we have a list of numbers and want to know whether they follow a claimed distribution. Sort them and draw a staircase that climbs by \(1/W\) at each of the \(W\) values. If the claim is right, the staircase hugs the claimed curve. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic \(D\) is the biggest gap between the two, and it has a known distribution that gives a p-value. For the uniform distribution between 0 and 1, the curve is the straight line \(F(x) = x\). The eight values 0.11, 0.23, 0.42, 0.48, 0.59, 0.70, 0.81, 0.95 give \(D = 0.17\) and \(p = 0.95\). The eight bunched values 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.07, 0.09, 0.12, 0.15 give \(D = 0.85\) and \(p = 5.1 \times 10^{-7}\).

\[ D = \max_x \bigl| \hat{F}_W(x) - F(x) \bigr|, \qquad \hat{F}_W(x) = \text{the share of the } W \text{ values at or below } x \] Figure 2.1. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the largest gap between the staircase of the sorted values and the claimed straight line. The eight spread-out values give D = 0.17; the eight bunched values give D = 0.85.

docs.title: 2.2 Why many tests need correction
docs.text:
Run one test at \(\alpha = 0.01\) and a good source fails 1% of the time. Run 18 independent tests and the chance that at least one fails is \(1 - 0.99^{18} = 16.5\%\). Look hard enough and something always looks odd. We saw exactly this: in our calibration, 11 of 120 samples of good data tripped at least one test at the 0.01 line.

So when we look at \(K\) results and care about the smallest one, we have to correct for having looked \(K\) times. There are two standard corrections, and given the smallest of \(K\) p-values, \(p_{\min}\), they are:

\[ p_{\text{Bonferroni}} = \min(1,\ K p_{\min}), \qquad p_{\text{Sidak}} = 1 - (1 - p_{\min})^{K} \]

Bonferroni is valid however the results depend on each other, which is why it is our default. Sidak is exact when the results are independent, and it is slightly less harsh. In practice they are close: for \(K = 20\) and \(p_{\min} = 0.001\), Bonferroni gives 0.02 and Sidak gives 0.0198. We use Sidak in tests U1 and H2, where the coefficients are independent (or asymptotically so) and there are thousands of them.

The same idea sets the bar for the final verdict. With 18 statistical tests, we count a failure towards the verdict only when \(p < 0.01/18 \approx 0.000556\). None of the 120 good samples crossed that line on any test.

docs.title: 2.3 Entropy and min-entropy
docs.text:
Entropy measures surprise. Shannon entropy is the average surprise per symbol, and min-entropy is the surprise of the single most likely symbol:

\[ H = -\sum_v p_v \log_2 p_v, \qquad H_{\min} = -\log_2 \max_v p_v \]

For a uniform byte both equal 8 bits. For anything else, \(H_{\min} \le H\), sometimes by a lot. Imagine a source that outputs the byte 0 half the time and any of the other 255 values otherwise. Its Shannon entropy is 4.997 bits, which sounds healthy. Its min-entropy is 1 bit, because an attacker who simply guesses 0 is right half the time. Security depends on the attacker's best guess, so standards such as NIST SP 800-90B work with min-entropy.

Figure 2.2. A byte source that outputs 0 half the time. Its Shannon entropy of 4.997 bits sounds healthy, but its min-entropy is 1 bit, because an attacker who guesses 0 is right half the time.

docs.title: 2.4 Why no output test can separate a good CSPRNG from a conditioned QRNG
docs.text:
This is the most important limit in this guide. We state it plainly so that nobody expects otherwise.

A CSPRNG is, by definition, a generator whose output no practical test can tell apart from true coin flips. A conditioned QRNG's output is also, if the conditioner works, very close to true coin flips. So both should pass every test. If a test could reliably separate them, that test would be a break of the CSPRNG. The difference is real, but it lies in where the bits came from, and the bits themselves carry no label.

Our data shows this. These 15 samples all reach the same verdict, INDISTINGUISHABLE: os.urandom, SHA-256 counter mode, PCG32, xoshiro256** (those four with two seeds each), AES-OFB, Threefish, SHA-256 conditioned CPU jitter, RDRAND, RDSEED, random.org and the ANU quantum data.

So a clean result is not evidence of a quantum origin. To tell these sources apart you need the design, the raw data before conditioning, or the health data from the device. Our tests can show, with very strong evidence, that data follows a weak generator's simple rule, and they can recognise raw physical behaviour. Everything else gets the honest answer: output alone cannot say.

docs.title: 2.5 Summary
docs.text:
• Five distributions cover almost every test: binomial (counts of successes), normal and erfc (bell curve), chi-square (summed squared misses), Poisson (rare events) and exponential (one spectral value). The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test checks a list of numbers against a claimed distribution.
  • Looking at \(K\) results and keeping the smallest needs a correction: Bonferroni \(\min(1,Kp_{\min})\) is valid whatever the dependence; Sidak \(1-(1-p_{\min})^K\) is exact for independent results.
  • Shannon entropy is the average surprise; min-entropy \(-\log_2\max_v p_v\) is the surprise of the most likely value. Min-entropy is never larger, and it is what an attacker's best guess depends on.
  • A CSPRNG is, by definition, a generator whose output no practical test separates from true coin flips. So no output test can separate a good CSPRNG from a conditioned QRNG; to tell them apart you need the design and the raw data.

docs.title: 2.6 Exercises
docs.text:
1. A die is rolled 60 times and the six faces show 5, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 times. Compute the chi-square statistic, its degrees of freedom and the p-value.

    Answer

    Each face expects 10, so \(X^2=(25+1+0+1+4+9)/10=4.0\). There are 6 cells, so \(d=5\). The upper tail of \(\chi^2(5)\) at 4.0 is \(p\approx0.549\). Nothing is odd.

  2. Twenty tests are run, and the smallest p-value is 0.002. Give the Bonferroni and Sidak corrected values, and say which you would use if the tests were known to be dependent.

    Answer

    Bonferroni: \(\min(1,20\times0.002)=0.04\). Sidak: \(1-(1-0.002)^{20}=0.0392\). For dependent tests use Bonferroni, which stays valid under any dependence. Sidak is exact only for independent results.

  3. Ten independent tests are each run at \(\alpha=0.01\) on a perfect source. What is the probability that at least one fails?

    Answer

    \(1-0.99^{10}=0.0956\), about 9.6%. This is why a single failing test among many is weak evidence.

  4. A byte source outputs 0 with probability 1/4, and each of the other 255 values with equal probability \(0.75/255\). Find its min-entropy and its Shannon entropy.

    Answer

    Min-entropy: \(-\log_2(1/4)=2\) bits. Shannon entropy: \(-\tfrac14\log_2\tfrac14-0.75\log_2(0.75/255)=0.5+0.75\times8.409=6.807\) bits. A datasheet quoting about 6.8 bits per byte would overstate what an attacker faces: guessing 0 succeeds one time in four.

  5. A friend says: "Our generator passed every test in the battery, so it must be a true random source." Explain what is wrong.

    Answer

    A pass only means that no test saw a defect. A CSPRNG is designed so that no practical test can separate its output from true coin flips, and a conditioned physical source is also close to true coin flips if its conditioner works. If a test could reliably separate them, that test would be a break of the CSPRNG. The difference lies in where the bits came from, and the bits carry no label. To tell sources apart you need the design, the raw data before conditioning, or health data from the device.

docs.title: Chapter 8: ENT, TestU01 and PractRand
docs.text: The last three tools in the survey sit at three different points on a scale. ENT is a small command-line program that prints five statistics on any file, with no verdict. TestU01 is a C library whose largest battery is among the most demanding available, and it comes in three levels, SmallCrush, Crush and BigCrush. PractRand does not fix the amount of data in advance: it tests as you feed it and tells you how much data it took for a flaw to appear. Together they show how test power depends on how much data you are willing to spend.

docs.title: 8.1 About ENT
docs.text: John Walker's ENT (the page we read is dated 28 January 2008, and the program is public domain) is a small command-line tool that reports five statistics on any file of bytes, a quick look that also hints at how well a file might compress. It needs no fixed amount of data, though some values, such as pi, converge slowly and benefit from large files. It gives no verdict. It prints numbers, and you read them with judgement.

docs.title: 8.2 Entropy (ENT)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. How many bits of information does each byte carry, if we look at bytes on their own? Full randomness gives 8. Text gives far less. It is like asking how evenly used the letters in a language are, ignoring what order they come in.

Example 8.2: Entropy (ENT)

The bytes 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4 have four equally common values, so the entropy is \(-4 \cdot 0.25 \log_2 0.25 = 2.0\) bits per byte. Walker's example of C source code scores about 4.9, implying roughly 38 percent could be saved by compression.

The mathematics.

\[H = -\sum_{i=0}^{255} p_i \log_2 p_i, \qquad p_i = \frac{c_i}{n}\]
  • \(c_i\) is the count of byte value \(i\), and \(n\) is the total.
  • ENT attaches no p-value to this figure.

What it catches and misses. It catches uneven byte use. It is blind to order, since a file holding all 256 values in a neat loop scores a perfect 8. Walker notes that compressors using longer frames may do better than this figure suggests. Note also that this is Shannon entropy, not min-entropy.

docs.title: 8.3 Chi-square (ENT)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Are all 256 byte values equally common, to within what chance allows? Walker calls it the most commonly used randomness test and a very sensitive one. He reads it as a percentage: how often truly random data would exceed this value. Near the middle is good, and very high or very low is bad.

Example 8.3: Chi-square (ENT)

Walker's Park and Miller generator example gives 212.53, which random data would exceed 97.53 percent of the time. On 255 degrees of freedom, we get the same figure. His JPEG example gives 1542.26, exceeded less than 0.01 percent of the time, so a dense file is not necessarily a random one.

The mathematics.

\[\chi^2 = \sum_{i=0}^{255} \frac{(c_i - n/256)^2}{n/256}, \qquad \text{percentage} = 100 \cdot P\!\left(\chi^2_{255} > \chi^2\right)\]
  • \(c_i\) is the count of byte value \(i\), and \(n\) is the number of bytes.
  • ENT's code sums over 256 cells, which implies 255 degrees of freedom.

Walker's bands are as follows. Above 99 or below 1 percent is almost certainly not random. Between 95 and 99, or between 1 and 5, is suspect. Between 90 and 95, or between 5 and 10, is almost suspect.

What it catches and misses. It is sensitive to any uneven use of byte values. Counts that are too even also stand out, at the other end of Walker's scale: the chi-square falls, so the percentage climbs. A perfect loop of 0, 1, 2 ... 255 has chi-square 0, reads as 100 percent and lands in his almost certainly not random band. Like entropy, though, it knows nothing about order: sort a file with ordinary byte counts into ascending order, and the chi-square does not change at all.

docs.title: 8.4 Arithmetic mean (ENT)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Add up all the bytes and divide by how many there are. Random bytes average 127.5. A persistent shift up or down means the values are skewed. It is the simplest of all the checks.

Example 8.4: Arithmetic mean (ENT)

The bytes 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4 have a mean of 2.5. Walker's JPEG example has 125.93. For a million uniform bytes, the standard deviation of the mean would be only 0.074, so 125.93 would be a long way out for a file that size.

The mathematics.

\[\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} x_j\]
  • \(x_j\) is byte \(j\).
  • For uniform bytes, the mean is 127.5 and the variance of one byte is \((256^2 - 1)/12\). So \(\bar{x}\) has variance \((256^2 - 1)/(12n)\).
  • ENT prints the mean and gives no p-value.

What it catches and misses. It catches overall skew. A very skewed distribution that is balanced around 127.5 scores perfectly, as would half the bytes at 0 and half at 255.

docs.title: 8.5 Monte Carlo value for pi (ENT)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Throw darts at a square board with a circle drawn inside. The share landing in the circle should be \(\pi/4\). Using the file's bytes as dart positions, we get an estimate of \(\pi\). If the bytes are lopsided or correlated, the darts miss their mark. It is memorable, but this is a slowly converging test.

Example 8.5: Monte Carlo value for pi (ENT)

The six bytes 40 10 05 20 80 20 (in hexadecimal) give \(x = 4198405\) and \(y = 2129952\). Then \(x^2 + y^2 \le (256^3 - 1)^2\), so this is a hit. Walker's 500,000-byte radioactive sample gives 3.143580574, an error of 0.06 percent.

The mathematics.

\[\hat{\pi} = 4 \cdot \frac{\text{hits}}{\text{points}}, \qquad \text{a hit if } x^2 + y^2 \le (256^3 - 1)^2\]
  • Each point takes six bytes: three for \(x\) and three for \(y\).
  • ENT prints the estimate and the error percentage, with no p-value.

Under independent uniform bytes, the hit count is close to binomial, with hit chance near \(\pi/4\). By our calculation, an estimate from 500,000 bytes has a standard deviation of about 0.0057.

What it catches and misses. It catches gross dependence between successive 3-byte values. It is not a sharp test: only a few of the top bits decide most points, and the error shrinks slowly with data.

docs.title: 8.6 Serial correlation coefficient (ENT)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. How much does each byte depend on the one before? For random data, the answer should be close to zero. Walker notes that a C program gives around 0.5, and uncompressed bitmaps approach 1. It is like asking whether today's temperature helps predict tomorrow's.

Example 8.6: Serial correlation coefficient (ENT)

For bytes 1, 2, 3, 4 with wraparound, \(n = 4\), \(\sum x_i x_{i+1} = 24\), \(\sum x_i = 10\), \(\sum x_i^2 = 30\). So \(C = (4 \cdot 24 - 100)/(4 \cdot 30 - 100) = -0.2\). His JPEG example scores 0.004249.

The mathematics.

\[C = \frac{n\sum_{i} x_i x_{i+1} - \left(\sum_i x_i\right)^2}{n\sum_i x_i^2 - \left(\sum_i x_i\right)^2}\]
  • \(x_i\) is byte \(i\), and \(n\) is the number of bytes.
  • The last byte is paired with the first, a detail we took from ENT's source code.
  • The page points to Knuth for theory and gives no test. In a quick simulation of ours on uniform bytes, the spread of \(C\) was close to \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so a value several times that from zero is unusual.

What it catches and misses. It catches linear dependence between adjacent bytes. It misses lags other than 1, and relationships that are not linear, so a strong but nonlinear link may give a value near zero.

docs.title: 8.7 About TestU01
docs.text:
Pierre L'Ecuyer and Richard Simard of the University of Montreal built TestU01 as a C library for testing generators of uniform numbers. Their paper appeared in ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, and its largest battery is very demanding. It has three batteries for sequences of numbers in \((0, 1)\), shown below, and three more for bit sequences.

Battery Tests p-values computed Numbers used Time on the paper's 2.4 GHz machine, for MT19937 SmallCrush 10 not stated as a total slightly under 51,320,000 when run on a file 14 seconds Crush 96 144 about \(2^{35}\) 1 hour BigCrush 106 160 about \(2^{38}\) 5.5 hours

The authors suggest starting with SmallCrush, then going on to Crush and BigCrush if everything is fine. Flagging is by reporting, not a fixed level. The batteries print a summary of any p-values outside \([0.001, 0.9990]\), marking values below \(10^{-300}\) as eps and below \(10^{-15}\) as eps1. Very small and very large p-values both count, since a large one can mean excessive uniformity. In their comparison tables, the authors treat a p-value outside \([10^{-10}, 1 - 10^{-10}]\) as a clear failure and values in \((10^{-10}, 10^{-4}]\) or \([1 - 10^{-4}, 1 - 10^{-10})\) as suspect. For a borderline result, you run the test again on fresh numbers until the failure is obvious or the suspicion fades. Since these are large tests on real generators, the small examples below are only toys to show the mechanics. MT19937 is a telling case: the paper reports that it fails only two linear complexity tests, with p-values above \(1 - 10^{-15}\), and that all LFSR and GFSR-type generators fail those two.

docs.title: 8.8 Birthday spacings (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This is Marsaglia's birthday spacings test at larger scale. Throw points into a huge number of cells, sort their cell numbers and look at the gaps. Generators with a lattice structure give far too many equal gaps. It catches linear congruential generators very fast.

Example 8.8: Birthday spacings (SmallCrush)

Cell numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 20, 25 in a space of 32 cells give gaps 3, 5, 7, 4, 5. The value 5 repeats, so \(Y = 1\), while \(\lambda = 6^3/(4 \cdot 32) = 1.6875\). The real SmallCrush settings give \(\lambda = (5 \times 10^6)^3/(4 \cdot 2^{60}) = 27.1\).

The mathematics.

\[Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda) \text{ approximately}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{n^3}{4k}, \qquad k = d^t\]
  • \(n\) is the number of points, and \(k\) the number of cells.
  • \(Y\) is the number of collisions among the gaps.
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 5 \times 10^6\), \(r = 0\), \(d = 2^{30}\) and \(t = 2\).

The p-value comes from the Poisson tail. With repeats, the total of \(Y\) is compared with Poisson of mean \(N\lambda\).

What it catches and misses. It catches lattice structure, and the paper shows linear congruential generators with modulus near \(k\) failing at a sample size that grows only as \(k^{1/3}\). Here it reads just the top 30 bits of each number, so defects in the lowest bits can pass.

docs.title: 8.9 Collision (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Throw \(n\) balls into far more than \(n\) boxes and count how often a ball lands in a box that is already occupied. Too few collisions means the points are too evenly spread, and too many means they are clumped. The authors find this one of the most powerful simple measures.

Example 8.9: Collision (SmallCrush)

Eight balls in 16 boxes landing at 3, 7, 3, 1, 7, 9, 2, 3 occupy 5 boxes, so \(C = 3\), against a rough expectation of \(8^2/(2 \cdot 16) = 2\). In SmallCrush, the expected number is about \((5 \times 10^6)^2/(2 \cdot 2^{32}) = 2910\).

The mathematics.

\[C = n - W_1, \qquad \mu_c \approx \frac{n^2}{2k}\]
  • \(n\) is the number of balls, \(k\) the number of boxes, and \(W_1\) the number of occupied boxes.
  • \(C\) is asymptotically Poisson with mean \(\mu_c\) when \(\mu_c\) stays moderate, and normal when \(n/k\) tends to a positive constant.
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 5 \times 10^6\), \(r = 0\), \(d = 2^{16}\) and \(t = 2\), so \(k = 2^{32}\).

What it catches and misses. It catches clumping and excess regularity, even when the deviation is concentrated in a small part of the space. It sees points two numbers at a time, using only 16 bits from each, so it misses defects outside that field.

docs.title: 8.10 Gap (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Pick a small target zone in \([0, 1)\) and count how many numbers go by between visits. The waits should follow a simple geometric pattern, like waiting for a particular number on a roulette wheel.

Example 8.10: Gap (SmallCrush)

With target width \(p = 1/256\), the chance of a gap of 0 is \(1/256 = 0.0039\), and half of all waits run to at least 177 values, since \((255/256)^{177} = 0.500\).

The mathematics.

\[P(\text{gap} = s) = p(1-p)^s, \qquad \chi^2 = \sum_{s} \frac{(\mathrm{obs}_s - \mathrm{exp}_s)^2}{\mathrm{exp}_s}\]
  • \(p = \beta - \alpha\) is the width of the target interval \([\alpha, \beta)\).
  • \(s\) is the gap length, with classes grouped as needed.
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 2 \times 10^5\), \(r = 22\), \(\alpha = 0\) and \(\beta = 1/256\).

What it catches and misses. It catches a generator that revisits a region too regularly, using bits after dropping the first 22. It watches only one small region, so structure elsewhere goes unnoticed.

docs.title: 8.11 Simple poker (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Deal hands of \(k\) cards from a deck with \(d\) kinds, and note how many distinct kinds each hand holds. Hands holding too few or too many kinds suggest trouble. It tells you whether values spread as they should within short stretches.

Example 8.11: Simple poker (SmallCrush)

With \(d = k = 8\), the hand 1, 4, 4, 2, 7, 1, 4, 0 has 5 distinct values. In SmallCrush, with \(d = k = 64\), the average hand has \(64(1 - (63/64)^{64}) = 40.6\) distinct values.

The mathematics.

\[P(s) = \frac{d(d-1)\cdots(d-s+1)}{d^k}\,S(k, s), \qquad \chi^2 = \sum_s \frac{(\mathrm{obs}_s - nP(s))^2}{nP(s)}\]
  • \(s\) is the number of distinct values in a hand of \(k\), drawn from \(d\) values.
  • \(S(k, s)\) is the Stirling number of the second kind, the number of ways to split \(k\) cards into \(s\) groups.
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 4 \times 10^5\), \(r = 24\) and \(d = k = 64\).

What it catches and misses. It catches local lack of variety in a small field of bits, here six bits after dropping the first 24. It only sees how many values occur, not which.

docs.title: 8.12 Coupon collector (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Collect a set of \(d\) different coupons, drawing one at a time, and note how many draws it takes to get them all. The waiting time has a known pattern. It is exactly like collecting football stickers: the last one or two take much longer than the rest.

Example 8.12: Coupon collector (SmallCrush)

With \(d = 16\), the expected wait is \(16(1 + 1/2 + \cdots + 1/16) = 54.09\) draws. With \(d = 4\), working through the states gives \(P(4) = 0.0938\), \(P(5) = 0.1406\) and \(P(6) = 0.1465\).

The mathematics.

\[P_{i \to i}(\text{next draw}) = \frac{i}{d}, \qquad P_{i \to i+1}(\text{next draw}) = \frac{d-i}{d}, \qquad \chi^2 = \sum_{s} \frac{(\mathrm{obs}_s - \mathrm{exp}_s)^2}{\mathrm{exp}_s}\]
  • \(i\) is the number of distinct coupons seen so far, and \(s\) is the total length.
  • The probabilities for \(s\) follow from this simple chain, with classes merged as usual.
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 5 \times 10^5\), \(r = 26\) and \(d = 16\).

What it catches and misses. It catches a generator whose values do not all appear at the right pace, in a 4-bit field after dropping the first 26. It only looks at this small field.

docs.title: 8.13 MaxOft (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Take \(t\) numbers at a time and keep the largest. The largest of six uniforms has a known distribution, heavily weighted towards 1. Group after group, we check whether the maxima follow that shape. It is like checking that the tallest player on every six-person team has a typical height.

Example 8.13: MaxOft (SmallCrush)

From 0.21, 0.84, 0.33, 0.67, 0.08, 0.52 the maximum is 0.84. Then \(F(0.84) = 0.84^6 = 0.351\). A maximum as low as 0.5 has probability only \(0.5^6 = 0.0156\).

The mathematics.

\[F(x) = x^t, \qquad \text{chi-square on } d \text{ equal-probability cells, plus an Anderson-Darling test}\]
  • \(x\) is a group's maximum, and \(t = 6\) is the group size.
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 2 \times 10^6\), \(r = 0\) and \(d = 10^5\).
  • The cells are chosen so that each expects exactly \(n/d\) values.
  • The Anderson-Darling test is a relative of the KS test that pays more attention to the tails.

What it catches and misses. It catches defects in the top of the range and dependence within short groups. Because only the largest value in each group counts, it is less sensitive to the rest.

docs.title: 8.14 Weight distribution (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Take a block of 256 numbers and count how many land in a chosen interval. That count should have a binomial spread, and we compare many blocks with that shape. The test was proposed by Matsumoto and Kurita.

Example 8.14: Weight distribution (SmallCrush)

With \(k = 256\) and interval width \(p = 1/8\), the mean count is 32 with variance 28. A count of exactly 32 has probability 0.0752, and a count of 45 or more has probability 0.0116.

The mathematics.

\[W = \sum_{j=1}^{k} I[\alpha \le u_j < \beta], \qquad W \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(k, \beta - \alpha)\]
  • \(u_j\) are uniforms, and \(I\) is 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise.
  • A chi-square compares \(n\) values of \(W\) with that law, with classes regrouped so that expected counts are large enough.
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 2 \times 10^5\), \(r = 27\), \(k = 256\), \(\alpha = 0\) and \(\beta = 1/8\).

What it catches and misses. It catches clumping across a stretch of 256 outputs, in low bits after dropping 27. It only considers one interval and a small field of bits.

docs.title: 8.15 Matrix rank (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Our old friend, the rank test, this time with a 60 by 60 grid built from 10 bits per number. It is larger than Diehard's, so it can look further for linear links, though it is still short of the size of very long-period generators.

Example 8.15: Matrix rank (SmallCrush)

For \(2 \times 2\) grids, the probabilities of rank 0, 1 and 2 are 1/16, 9/16 and 6/16. For \(60 \times 60\) grids, the chance of rank 60, 59, 58 and 57 are 0.2888, 0.5776, 0.1284 and 0.0052.

The mathematics.

\[P[R = x] = 2^{x(L+k-x)-Lk} \prod_{i=0}^{x-1} \frac{(1-2^{i-L})(1-2^{i-k})}{1-2^{i-x}}, \qquad P[R = 0] = 2^{-Lk}\]
  • \(R\) is the rank of an \(L \times k\) matrix, with \(1 \le x \le \min(L, k)\).
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 20000\), \(r = 20\), \(s = 10\) and \(L = k = 60\).
  • A chi-square compares observed ranks with these, after merging rare classes.

What it catches and misses. It catches linear dependence over a span of 3600 bits, in a field of 10 bits from each number. A recurrence with a longer state, such as MT19937, passes at this size.

docs.title: 8.16 Hamming independence (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Count the ones in a block, then in the next block. If blocks are independent, a heavy block says nothing about the next. We compare how often each pair of weights occurs with what independence predicts. It is like checking whether a good day on the stock market tells you anything about the next.

Example 8.16: Hamming independence (SmallCrush)

The blocks 1011 and 0110 have weights 3 and 2, forming the pair \((3, 2)\). For the real block size of \(L = 300\), each weight has mean 150 and variance 75.

The mathematics.

\[P(X_i = a, X_{i+1} = b) = \binom{L}{a}\binom{L}{b} 2^{-2L}, \qquad \chi^2 = \sum_{a, b} \frac{(\mathrm{obs}_{ab} - \mathrm{exp}_{ab})^2}{\mathrm{exp}_{ab}}\]
  • \(X_j\) is the Hamming weight of block \(j\), and \(L\) is the block length in bits.
  • Non-overlapping pairs are used, and classes with few expected counts are lumped together.
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 5 \times 10^5\), \(r = 20\), \(s = 10\), \(L = 300\) and \(d = 0\).

What it catches and misses. It catches dependence between the weights of neighbouring blocks. It reads only weights, so patterns that keep weights independent go unseen.

docs.title: 8.17 Random walk (SmallCrush)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Each bit is a step left or right. We look at many walks of 150 steps and ask several questions. How many steps went right? How far did it reach? How much time did it spend on the right? How often did it come home, and how often did it cross over? Each has an exact answer.

Example 8.17: Random walk (SmallCrush)

The steps \(+1, -1, +1, +1, -1, -1, +1, +1\) give positions 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2. So \(H = 5\) steps right, \(M = 2\) for the maximum, \(R = 2\) returns to zero, \(C = 0\) sign changes, and \(J = 8\), since the walk is right of zero at all four odd positions.

The mathematics.

\[p_{k,y} = P[S_k = y] = 2^{-k}\binom{k}{(k+y)/2} \text{ when } k + y \text{ is even}, \qquad 0 \text{ otherwise}\] \[P[H = k] = 2^{-\ell}\binom{\ell}{k}, \qquad P[M = y] = p_{\ell,y} + p_{\ell,y+1}, \qquad P[J = k] = p_{k,0}\,p_{\ell-k,0}\] \[P[R = y] = p_{\ell-y,y}, \qquad P[C = y] = 2p_{\ell-1,2y+1}\]
  • \(S_k\) is the position after \(k\) steps, and \(\ell\) is the walk length.
  • \(H\) counts steps right, \(M\) is the maximum, \(J\) is the time on the right, \(R\) counts returns to 0, and \(C\) counts sign changes.
  • TestU01's guide also lists first-passage times \(P_y\).
  • SmallCrush uses \(N = 1\), \(n = 10^6\), \(r = 0\), \(s = 30\) and \(L_0 = L_1 = 150\).

What it catches and misses. It catches short-range dependence in bits, including linear structure in weak generators. Walks of only 150 steps see nothing further away, so long-memory defects are left to the bigger batteries.

docs.title: 8.18 About PractRand
docs.text: PractRand is an open library and toolset for random number generators, with a command-line tester, RNG_test, that reads from standard input. The pages we read describe version 0.94 and do not name the author. Its approach differs from the other batteries in that it does not fix the amount of data in advance. It tests as you feed it, printing a summary at growing lengths, so you learn how much data was needed before a flaw showed. On the core tests other than BRank, the author reports that real failures usually build gradually, so a failure at \(2^{36}\) bytes would typically be foreshadowed by a warning at \(2^{35}\) bytes. Reading the output is simple: look for FAIL. Each line gives a test name, a raw value, a processed value (a p-value, or pass or fail) and an evaluation in words such as normal, unusual, suspicious, very suspicious or FAIL. The evaluation is a complex function, not a fixed cutoff, and both ends of the range count as bad. The target is about one false positive per 300 million result summaries on good generators. The recommended test set contains the five tests below, plus low-bit variants. Its results table lists MT19937 as failing the standard battery at 256 GB, with lengths rounded up to a power of 2. The author ties that failure to the binary rank test, added to the core set in version 0.91. The documentation gives ideas rather than formulas, so we describe only what it supports. For exact statistics, the source code is the reference.

docs.title: 8.19 BCFN (PractRand)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. BCFN looks for long-range correlations by counting bits. At each level, it adds up the ones across longer and longer overlapping stretches and checks whether those weights are distributed as they should be. The documentation notes it often catches Fibonacci-style generators that use large lags to pass other tests. It is like watching a river's level averaged over days, then weeks, then months, to see a slow pattern.

The mathematics. The documentation describes each level as a frequency test on overlapping sets of Hamming weights, and it does not publish the statistic. The basic fact underneath is that the weight of \(m\) independent fair bits is binomial.

\[W = \sum_{j=1}^{m} b_j, \qquad W \sim \mathrm{Binomial}\!\left(m, \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\]
  • \(b_j\) are the bits of a block, and \(W\) is its Hamming weight.
  • Written BCFN(X,Y), the test's first parameter is the lowest level checked, with 2 recommended. Higher values are faster but can miss shorter-range effects.
  • The second parameter is the base-2 logarithm of its internal table size, typically 10 to 15, depending on the cache.
  • All higher levels are checked as data allows.

What it catches and misses. It catches long-range linear correlations. BCFN tests with similar first parameters are correlated with each other. It is one test family, and it is not designed for the very short-range effects that FPF and DC6 target.

docs.title: 8.20 DC6 (PractRand)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. DC6 is the short-range partner of BCFN. It looks at a few neighbouring integers, takes some information from each, and checks the pattern of weights across them. So it looks for short-range linear correlations, the kind a small mixing step might leave behind.

The mathematics. Like BCFN, it is a frequency test on overlapping sets of Hamming weights, using the same binomial fact, and the documentation does not publish the statistic.

  • Its parameters set the integer size it works on, how many adjacent integers it correlates, and what information it takes from each.
  • The documentation names the form DC6-9x1Bytes-1 and points to the source functions for recommended values.

What it catches and misses. It catches short-range linear dependence. The documentation does not list what it misses. As a bit-counting test, it would not be expected to notice structure that keeps the counts balanced.

docs.title: 8.21 FPF (PractRand)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Despite the name, "floating point frequency", it uses integer maths. Roughly, it takes overlapping windows of the stream, treats each as a number, and looks at how that number would be written in floating-point format. It then runs a frequency test on those formats. That focuses on the rare cases with many zero bits up front.

The mathematics. The documentation describes the approach, with no parameters or formula in the overview we read.

  • The input is overlapping windows of the stream, read as integers.
  • The test is a frequency test on the binary form of their floating-point representations.

What it catches and misses. It catches very short-range correlations, shorter than DC6, especially those involving many 0 bits. It can be slow at some settings, and it is not aimed at long-range structure.

docs.title: 8.22 Gap16 (PractRand)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Gap16 is a variation on the classic gap test, which measures how long a value takes to come back. Clumped or too-regular returns are the warning sign, just as with waiting times between buses. The name suggests 16-bit values, although the documentation does not spell that out.

The mathematics. The documentation describes it as a variation on the classic gap test, with no parameters, and gives no further detail. The classic version's gap probability is shown in the TestU01 section above, but we cannot confirm Gap16's exact variant from the documentation. The output names Gap-16:A and Gap-16:B, and the author notes these two are strongly correlated.

What it catches and misses. It catches irregular returns of values. The documentation gives no more detail, so we leave it there.

docs.title: 8.23 BRank (PractRand)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This is a binary matrix rank test, as seen in Diehard and SP 800-22. What is original is the control logic, which decides when to pull data and what size of matrix to use. Larger matrices can reach longer linear links, at more cost per bit.

The mathematics. It is a fairly standard rank test, compared against the known rank probabilities given earlier for SP 800-22 and Diehard.

\[p_r = 2^{r(2M-r)-M^2} \prod_{i=0}^{r-1} \frac{(1-2^{i-M})^2}{1-2^{i-r}}\]
  • \(p_r\) is the probability of rank \(r\) for a square \(M \times M\) grid.
  • The test's one parameter sets how much time per gigabyte goes on rank calculations, on a log scale.
  • Because results are coarse-grained, precise p-values are not possible for many subtests.

What it catches and misses. It catches linear dependence over large spans, given enough data. The documentation says this is the only PractRand test MT19937 fails, at 256 GB, and calls those failures oddly brittle, since slight variations can let MT19937 pass. Non-linear structure does not show up through rank.

docs.title: 8.24 Summary
docs.text:
• ENT prints entropy, chi-square, arithmetic mean, a Monte Carlo value of \(\pi\) and the serial correlation coefficient. It needs no fixed amount of data and gives no verdict.
  • ENT's entropy and chi-square are blind to order: a file that cycles through 0 to 255 scores a perfect 8 bits and chi-square 0, though it is totally predictable.
  • TestU01 has batteries for numbers in \((0,1)\) (SmallCrush, Crush, BigCrush) and for bit strings; its power comes from enormous amounts of data, close to \(2^{38}\) numbers for BigCrush.
  • PractRand grows its sample until a flaw shows, reports an evaluation (normal, unusual, suspicious, very suspicious, FAIL) and lists MT19937 as failing at 256 GB through its binary rank test.
  • TestU01 and PractRand find flaws in algorithms. They say nothing about how much entropy a physical source produces.

docs.title: 8.25 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Compute the ENT entropy of the byte sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4. What does the answer imply for compression?

    Answer

    Four values occur equally often, each with probability 0.25, so the entropy is \(-4\times0.25\log_20.25=2.0\) bits per byte. Since 8 bits would be needed if bytes were uniform, a compressor could in principle save up to \(75\%\) of the file.

  2. A file contains each byte value 0 to 255 exactly once and then repeats that block many times. What do ENT's entropy and chi-square report, and why is the file not random?

    Answer

    Every value is equally common, so the entropy is a perfect 8.0 bits per byte, and the chi-square is 0, which ENT reads as 100 percent and "almost certainly not random" because the counts are too even. The file is completely predictable: both statistics look only at byte counts and ignore order.

  3. For the byte sequence 1, 2, 3, 4 with wraparound, compute the serial correlation coefficient from \(C=(n\sum x_ix_{i+1}-(\sum x_i)^2)/(n\sum x_i^2-(\sum x_i)^2)\).

    Answer

    With wraparound the products are \(1\cdot2+2\cdot3+3\cdot4+4\cdot1=24\), \(\sum x_i=10\) and \(\sum x_i^2=30\). So \(C=(4\cdot24-100)/(4\cdot30-100)=-4/20=-0.2\).

  4. Why does PractRand report results at growing lengths instead of one verdict?

    Answer

    It does not fix the amount of data in advance. It tests as data is fed, so you learn how much data was needed before a flaw showed. Real failures usually build gradually, so a failure at \(2^{36}\) bytes is typically foreshadowed by a warning at \(2^{35}\) bytes.

  5. Why can TestU01 and PractRand be a poor fit for a quantum random number generator device?

    Answer

    They get their power from very large amounts of data, which a device may not be able to supply quickly, and a defect in a physical noise source may not need that much data to matter. They find flaws in algorithms; they do not estimate the entropy of a physical source.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Estimating Entropy: NIST SP 800-90B
docs.text: SP 800-22 asks whether data looks random. SP 800-90B asks a different and more useful question for cryptography: how many bits of guessing work does each sample of a noise source give an attacker? Its answer is a number, the min-entropy per sample, produced by a family of estimators and made into a continuous safeguard by two health tests that run inside the device. This chapter works through the estimators one at a time, then the restart tests, then the repetition count and adaptive proportion tests.

docs.title: 5.1 The question SP 800-90B asks
docs.text: This one asks a different question. SP 800-22 asks "does this look random?", while SP 800-90B (Turan and colleagues, January 2018) asks "how many bits of guessing work does each sample give an attacker?". It was written for the noise sources inside entropy sources, and it is used in NIST's Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program (CAVP) and Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP). You supply at least 1,000,000 consecutive raw samples, plus a restart matrix of 1000 samples from each of 1000 restarts. You also state your own expected entropy from a design analysis. Data then follows one of two tracks. The IID track is open only if you claim independent, identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples and the tests below find nothing against that. Everything else follows the non-IID track. The output is not a p-value but a number: bits of min-entropy per sample. Taking the smallest estimate is deliberate, because we want the most cautious answer. NIST also warns that these estimators support an analysis of the source and do not replace it.

docs.title: 5.2 Min-entropy framing
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Imagine an attacker with one guess. Their best move is to bet on the most likely value. Min-entropy measures exactly how hard that one bet is, so it is set by the single most likely outcome and nothing else. That is why it is cautious: a distribution can look rich on average and still have one value an attacker will always try first.

Example 5.2: Min-entropy framing

Suppose three values have probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.25. The min-entropy is \(-\log_2 0.5 = 1\) bit, while the Shannon entropy is 1.5 bits. A bit that comes up 1 sixty percent of the time has min-entropy \(-\log_2 0.6 = 0.737\) bits.

The mathematics.

\[H = \min_{1 \le i \le k} \left(-\log_2 p_i\right) = -\log_2 \max_{1 \le i \le k} p_i\] \[H_I = \min\!\left(H_{original},\ n \cdot H_{bitstring},\ H_{submitter}\right)\]
  • \(p_i\) is the probability of value \(x_i\), and \(k\) is the number of possible values, so \(H\) is at most \(\log_2 k\).
  • \(H_{original}\) is estimated on the samples, \(H_{bitstring}\) on the same data read as a bit string, and \(n\) is the number of bits per sample.
  • \(H_{submitter}\) is your own design-based claim. For a binary source, \(H_I\) uses only \(H_{original}\) and \(H_{submitter}\).

What it catches and misses. This framing puts the attacker's best guess at the centre, which suits cryptography. It still only measures what the estimators can spot. A cleverly deterministic source can score high, which is why a design rationale is required.

docs.title: 5.3 Permutation tests (IID track)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Take the data, shuffle it, and measure something. Shuffling destroys any order but keeps the mix of values. If the data really is i.i.d., the original should look like just another shuffle. If its score sits at the extreme end of 10,000 shuffles, then order mattered, and the data is not i.i.d. It is like asking whether a dealt hand looks any different from one dealt after a good shuffle.

Example 5.3: Permutation tests (IID track)

The excursion statistic on \(S = (2, 15, 4, 10, 9)\) has mean 8, giving deviations 6, 1, 3, 1, 0, so \(T = 6\). For \(S = (2, 2, 2, 5, 7, 7, 9, 3, 1, 4, 4)\) the steps are six ups, two downs, then two ups. That gives 3 directional runs, a longest run of 6, and 8 increases.

The mathematics.

\[\text{reject i.i.d. if } C_{i,0} + C_{i,1} \le 5 \quad \text{or} \quad C_{i,0} \ge 9995\]
  • \(T_i\) is statistic \(i\) on the original data, and each of the 10,000 shuffles uses the Fisher-Yates algorithm, a standard shuffle that makes every ordering equally likely.
  • \(C_{i,0}\) counts shuffles with a larger statistic, and \(C_{i,1}\) counts ties.
  • The cutoffs correspond to a type I error (rejecting good data, a false alarm) of 0.001.

The statistics are: excursion, number of directional runs, length of directional runs, number of increases and decreases, number of runs about the median, length of runs about the median, average collision, maximum collision, periodicity and covariance (each at lags 1, 2, 8, 16 and 32), and compressed length under bzip2. Some are applied to binary data after grouping it into 8-bit blocks.
