What it catches and misses. The reference distribution comes from the data itself, so no theory is assumed. It catches trends, repeats and lagged relations in the listed statistics. It cannot reject a source that is i.i.d. but heavily biased, because bias survives shuffling. That is a job for the estimators.

docs.title: 5.4 Chi-square tests (IID track)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Two more checks back up the shuffling. The independence test asks whether a value's neighbour tells you anything about it, by comparing pair counts with what the individual frequencies predict. The goodness-of-fit test asks whether ten slices of the data all share the same distribution, like checking that a factory's output does not change from shift to shift.

Example 5.4: Chi-square tests (IID track)

The standard's non-binary example has \(k = 3\) values, \(L = 100\) and proportions 0.21, 0.41, 0.38. With six bins, the observed counts are 7, 6, 10, 8, 12, 7 against expected 6.2, 8.3, 11.53, 7.79, 7.79, 8.41. So \(T = 3.46\) with 3 degrees of freedom, far below the critical value 16.266, and the test passes.

The mathematics.

\[T = \sum_{\text{bins}} \frac{(o_i - e_i)^2}{e_i}\] Test Data Expected count Degrees of freedom Independence non-binary \(p_i p_j L/2\) for non-overlapping pairs, binned so each bin expects at least 5 \(n_{bin} - k\) Goodness of fit non-binary \(c_i/10\) for each of ten subsets, binned the same way \(9(n_{bin} - 1)\) Independence binary \(p_1^w p_0^{m-w}\lfloor L/m \rfloor\) for each \(m\)-bit tuple with \(w\) ones, \(m\) at most 11 \(2^m - 2\) Goodness of fit binary \((1-p)L/10\) zeros and \(pL/10\) ones in each of ten subsets 9
  • \(o_i\) and \(e_i\) are observed and expected counts, and \(k\) is the alphabet size.
  • \(p_i\) is the proportion of value \(x_i\), and \(c_i\) is its count.
  • Each test fails if \(T\) exceeds the chi-square critical value at 0.001. The document prints that value for 9 degrees of freedom as 27.887, while chi-square tables give 27.877.

What it catches and misses. Independence catches dependence in adjacent samples or nearby bits, and goodness of fit catches drift over the run. Dependence at longer lag is out of reach here, so it relies on the permutation tests.

docs.title: 5.5 Longest repeated substring test (IID track)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. In random data, long repeated stretches are rare, and we can calculate how rare. Find the longest stretch that occurs twice and ask how likely a repeat that long would be if the samples were i.i.d. It is like finding the same long sentence in two parts of a book: past a certain length, chance stops being a good explanation.

Example 5.5: Longest repeated substring test (IID track)

For \(S = (2, 2, 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0)\) we have \(L = 21\), \(p_{col} = 0.3469\) and longest repeat \(W = 5\). That gives \(N = 136\) pairs and \(\Pr(X \ge 1) = 0.496\), comfortably above 0.001, so it passes.

The mathematics.

\[p_{col} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} p_i^2, \qquad N = \binom{L-W+1}{2}, \qquad \Pr(X \ge 1) = 1 - \left(1 - p_{col}^{\,W}\right)^N\]
  • \(p_i\) is the proportion of value \(x_i\), and \(L\) is the sample count.
  • \(W\) is the length of the longest repeated substring.
  • \(X\) is binomial with \(N\) trials and success probability \(p_{col}^{\,W}\).

The test fails if \(\Pr(X \ge 1) < 0.001\).

What it catches and misses. It catches long repeats, such as a source that loops or replays stored data, and it works on binary and non-binary input alike. It uses only the longest repeat, so a source full of medium-length repeats may slip through.

docs.title: 5.6 Most common value estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Find the most frequent value, then allow for sampling luck by taking the top of a 99 percent confidence interval. It is the simplest estimate of all, often shortened to MCV: the attacker's single best guess, treated cautiously. On the IID track, this is the only estimator used.

Example 5.6: Most common value estimate

For \(S = (0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 2, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 2, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1)\), \(L = 20\) and the value 1 appears 8 times, so \(\hat{p} = 0.4\). Then \(p_u = 0.4 + 2.576\sqrt{0.24/19} = 0.6895\) and the estimate is \(-\log_2 0.6895 = 0.5363\) bits. The document prints 0.6822 inside its logarithm, but 0.5363 only follows from 0.6895.

The mathematics.

\[\hat{p} = \max_i \frac{\#\{x_i \text{ in } S\}}{L}, \qquad p_u = \min\!\left(1,\ \hat{p} + 2.576\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{L-1}}\right), \qquad H = -\log_2 p_u\]
  • \(L\) is the number of samples.
  • 2.576 is the normal quantile \(Z_{(1-0.005)}\).

What it catches and misses. It catches bias well. On its own it is blind to dependence: a stream alternating 0, 1, 0, 1 has \(\hat{p}\) near 0.5 and scores nearly a full bit per sample. NIST warns that it typically overestimates entropy when samples are not i.i.d.

docs.title: 5.7 Collision estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Read the stream until you see a value you have already seen, then start again. If one value dominates, repeats come quickly. So the average time to a repeat tells you about the most likely value, much like the birthday puzzle in reverse. This estimator is applied to binary input only.

Example 5.7: Collision estimate

The standard's 40-bit example gives times 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, so \(v = 14\), \(\bar{X} = 2.7143\) and \(\hat{\sigma} = 0.4688\). The lower bound is \(\bar{X}' = 2.3915\). Solving gives \(p = 0.7329\) and an estimate of 0.4483 bits.

The mathematics.

\[\bar{X}' = \bar{X} - 2.576\frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{v}}, \qquad \bar{X}' = pq^{-2}\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{2}(p^{-1} - q^{-1})\right)F(q) - pq^{-1}\,\tfrac{1}{2}(p^{-1} - q^{-1})\]
  • \(t_i\) are the times to a repeat, with mean \(\bar{X}\) and standard deviation \(\hat{\sigma}\) across \(v\) repeats.
  • \(q = 1 - p\) with \(p \ge q\), and \(F(1/z) = \Gamma(3, z)z^{-3}e^z\), using the incomplete gamma function.
  • \(p\) is found by binary search between \(1/2\) and 1, and the estimate is \(-\log_2 p\), or 1 if there is no solution.

For bits, the right-hand side works out to \(2 + 2pq\), which we checked against the standard's example.

What it catches and misses. It catches considerable bias towards one value. In bits, a repeat comes after two or three steps, so the measure is coarse. It sees only nearby repeats and cannot read longer-term structure.

docs.title: 5.8 Markov estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Suppose each bit depends only on the one before it. We measure the four transition chances from the data, then ask which 128-bit sequence is most likely and how likely it is. Dividing by 128 gives entropy per bit. Think of predicting tomorrow's weather from today's alone.

Example 5.8: Markov estimate

The standard's 40-bit example gives \(P_0 = 0.475\), \(P_1 = 0.525\), \(P_{0,0} = 0.389\), \(P_{0,1} = 0.611\), \(P_{1,0} = 0.571\) and \(P_{1,1} = 0.429\). The likeliest path is 1010...10, with probability about \(4.6288 \times 10^{-30}\) on those rounded inputs. So the estimate is \(\min(-\log_2(4.6288 \times 10^{-30})/128, 1) = 0.761\) bits.

The mathematics.

\[\hat{p}_{max} = \max\left\{P_0 P_{0,0}^{127},\ P_0 P_{0,1}^{64} P_{1,0}^{63},\ P_0 P_{0,1} P_{1,1}^{126},\ P_1 P_{1,0} P_{0,0}^{126},\ P_1 P_{1,0}^{64} P_{0,1}^{63},\ P_1 P_{1,1}^{127}\right\}\] \[H = \min\!\left(-\frac{\log_2 \hat{p}_{max}}{128},\ 1\right)\]
  • \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) are the proportions of zeros and ones.
  • \(P_{a,b}\) is the observed chance that bit \(a\) is followed by bit \(b\).

This is applied to binary input only. NIST notes that the per-sample extrapolation from a 128-long chain is not strictly correct but is close in practice.

What it catches and misses. It catches first-order dependence such as a stickiness or a tendency to alternate. It assumes a one-step memory, so it does not model dependence two or more steps back.

docs.title: 5.9 Compression estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This uses Maurer's idea from SP 800-22 in a new way. Warm up a dictionary, then measure how far back each block last appeared. Then find the most skewed distribution that would produce an average that small, and read off its entropy. In effect, we ask how compressible the data is, then assume the worst source consistent with that.

Example 5.9: Compression estimate

The standard's illustration uses \(d = 4\), \(L = 48\) and \(b = 6\), with test blocks at distances \(D = (5, 6, 7, 7)\). So \(\bar{X} = 2.6304\), \(\hat{\sigma} = 0.9074\) and \(\bar{X}' = 1.4617\). Solving gives \(p = 0.5715\) and \(H = -\log_2(0.5715)/6 = 0.1345\) bits.

The mathematics.

\[\bar{X} = \frac{1}{v}\sum_{i=1}^{v} \log_2 D_i, \qquad \hat{\sigma} = c\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i (\log_2 D_i)^2}{v-1} - \bar{X}^2}, \qquad \bar{X}' = \bar{X} - 2.576\frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{v}}\] \[\bar{X}' = G(p) + (2^b - 1)G(q), \qquad G(z) = \frac{1}{v}\sum_{t=d+1}^{\lfloor L/b \rfloor}\sum_{u=1}^{t} \log_2(u)\,F(z,t,u)\]
  • \(b = 6\) is the block size, \(d = 1000\) the dictionary size, and \(c = 0.5907\) the correction factor.
  • \(q = (1-p)/(2^b - 1)\), and \(F(z,t,u) = z^2(1-z)^{u-1}\) if \(u < t\) and \(z(1-z)^{t-1}\) if \(u = t\).
  • \(p\) is searched between \(2^{-b}\) and 1, and \(H = -\log_2(p)/b\), or 1 if no solution exists.

What it catches and misses. It assumes no independence, so dependence does show through. It catches repeats at the 6-bit level. It reasons about a near-uniform worst case, and it is applied only to binary input.

docs.title: 5.10 t-tuple estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Rather than looking at single values, we also look at pairs, triples and longer groups. If some group is much too common, its frequency implies a high per-sample probability. We take the worst such implied probability. It is like noticing a loaded die through its favourite pairs of rolls, not just its single numbers.

Example 5.10: t-tuple estimate

Using a cutoff of 3 for illustration and the \(L = 21\) samples

\[S = (2, 2, 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0),\]

we get \(Q[1] = 9\), \(Q[2] = 4\), \(Q[3] = 3\). The values \(P_{max}[i]\) are 0.4286, 0.4472, 0.5405. So \(p_u = 0.8276\) and the estimate is 0.273 bits.

The mathematics.

\[P[i] = \frac{Q[i]}{L-i+1}, \qquad P_{max}[i] = P[i]^{1/i}, \qquad \hat{p}_{max} = \max_{1 \le i \le t} P_{max}[i]\] \[p_u = \min\!\left(1,\ \hat{p}_{max} + 2.576\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{max}(1-\hat{p}_{max})}{L-1}}\right), \qquad H = -\log_2 p_u\]
  • \(t\) is the largest length whose most common tuple occurs at least 35 times.
  • \(Q[i]\) is the count of the most common \(i\)-tuple, with overlaps allowed.

What it catches and misses. It catches repeated short patterns that single-value counts miss. It is limited to tuples common enough to count at least 35 times, which leaves longer patterns for the next estimator.

docs.title: 5.11 Longest repeated substring (LRS) estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This one picks up where the t-tuple estimate stops. For tuple lengths too rare to count well, we look at how often two positions match, a collision measure. It estimates collision entropy, which is an upper bound on min-entropy, so NIST uses it to complement the other estimates.

Example 5.11: Longest repeated substring (LRS) estimate

With the same \(S\) and the same illustrative cutoff of 3, \(u = 4\) and \(v = 5\). Then \(P_4 = 0.0131\) and \(P_5 = 0.0074\), so \(P_{max,4} = 0.3381\) and \(P_{max,5} = 0.3744\). So \(p_u = 0.6531\) and the estimate is 0.6146 bits.

The mathematics.

\[P_W = \frac{\sum_i \binom{C_i}{2}}{\binom{L-W+1}{2}}, \qquad P_{max,W} = P_W^{1/W}, \qquad \hat{p} = \max_{u \le W \le v} P_{max,W}\] \[p_u = \min\!\left(1,\ \hat{p} + 2.576\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{L-1}}\right), \qquad H = -\log_2 p_u\]
  • \(u\) is the smallest length whose most common tuple occurs fewer than 35 times.
  • \(v\) is the longest length that repeats at all. If \(v < u\) the estimate cannot be computed.
  • \(C_i\) is the number of occurrences of the \(i\)th distinct \(W\)-tuple.

What it catches and misses. It handles tuple sizes too long for the t-tuple estimate, and so catches long repeats and replay. Because it measures collision rather than min-entropy, it can sit above the true min-entropy, and this is one reason the minimum across all estimates is taken.

docs.title: 5.12 MultiMCW prediction estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Here we stop counting and start guessing. Four simple predictors each guess the most common value in a recent window, and a scoreboard picks whichever has been right most often. If the guesses beat chance, the data is predictable. This suits sources whose favourite value drifts over time.

Example 5.12: MultiMCW prediction estimate

The standard's illustration uses \(S = (1, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0)\) with windows 3, 5, 7, 9. This gives correct \(= (0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1)\), so \(P_{global} = 0.3333\), \(P'_{global} = 0.7627\) and \(P_{local} = 0.036\). The estimate is \(-\log_2 0.7627 = 0.3908\) bits.

The mathematics. All four prediction estimators share this ending.

\[P_{global} = \frac{C}{N}, \qquad P'_{global} = \min\!\left(1,\ P_{global} + 2.576\sqrt{\frac{P_{global}(1-P_{global})}{N-1}}\right)\] \[0.99 = \frac{1 - P_{local}\,x}{(r + 1 - rx)\,q} \cdot \frac{1}{x^{N+1}}, \qquad x_j = 1 + q P_{local}^{\,r} x_{j-1}^{\,r+1}\] \[H = -\log_2 \max\!\left(P'_{global},\ P_{local},\ \frac{1}{k}\right)\]
  • \(C\) is the number of correct predictions out of \(N\). If \(C = 0\), \(P'_{global} = 1 - 0.01^{1/N}\).
  • \(r\) is one more than the longest run of correct predictions, \(q = 1 - P_{local}\), \(x = x_{10}\) and \(x_0 = 1\).
  • \(k\) is the alphabet size. Here the windows are \(w = 63, 255, 1023, 4095\) and \(N = L - 63\).

What it catches and misses. It catches a most common value that shifts over time, and the local term catches bursts of predictability. A predictor can only prove structure it knows how to exploit, so a failure to predict is not proof of entropy.

docs.title: 5.13 Lag prediction estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. There are 128 subpredictors, and each simply guesses "the next value equals the one \(d\) steps back". If the data has a rhythm of period \(d\), that subpredictor starts winning. It is like predicting that this week's quiz question will match the one from exactly a fortnight ago.

Example 5.13: Lag prediction estimate

The standard's illustration uses \(S = (2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2)\) with \(D = 3\). This gives correct \(= (0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0)\), so \(P_{global} = 0.2222\), \(P'_{global} = 0.6008\) and \(P_{local} = 0.1167\). The estimate is 0.735 bits.

The mathematics. The prediction at step \(i\) comes from the current winner \(d\):

\[\mathrm{lag}_d = s_{i-d}, \qquad 1 \le d \le D, \qquad D = 128, \qquad N = L - 1\]
  • \(s_i\) is sample \(i\), and the winner is the subpredictor with the top score. When a subpredictor is correct and its score reaches or passes the winner's, it becomes the winner.
  • \(C\), \(r\), \(P'_{global}\), \(P_{local}\) and \(H\) follow the MultiMCW formulas above.

What it catches and misses. It catches periodic sources with a period of up to 128 samples, such as interference from a clock. It sees only exact repeats at a fixed lag, so a period beyond 128 or a pattern that drifts in phase is missed.

docs.title: 5.14 MultiMMC prediction estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. A Markov model with counting asks: after this recent context, which value usually came next? We run 16 of them, using contexts of length 1 to 16, and a scoreboard picks the best. Think of predictive text on a phone, trying short and long contexts at once.

Example 5.14: MultiMMC prediction estimate

The standard's illustration uses \(S = (2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 1, 3, 1)\) with \(D = 3\). This gives correct \(= (0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0)\), so \(P_{global} = 0.4286\), \(P'_{global} = 0.9490\) and \(P_{local} = 0.1307\). The estimate is 0.0755 bits.

The mathematics.

\[\mathrm{subpredict}_d = \arg\max_{y}\ M_d\big[(s_{i-d}, \ldots, s_{i-1}),\ y\big], \qquad 1 \le d \le 16, \qquad N = L - 2\]
  • \(M_d[x, y]\) counts how often context \(x\) of length \(d\) was followed by \(y\), with ties going to the greatest \(y\).
  • Each model holds at most maxEntries \(= 100{,}000\) entries.
  • \(C\), \(r\), \(P'_{global}\), \(P_{local}\) and \(H\) follow the MultiMCW formulas above.

What it catches and misses. It catches dependence on up to 16 previous samples, which suits non-binary sources with real memory. The entry limit means very rich context spaces fill up, and it cannot see dependence beyond 16 samples.

docs.title: 5.15 LZ78Y prediction estimate
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This predictor builds a dictionary of the strings it has seen, as a compressor does, with each string recording what tends to follow it. To predict, it looks for the current context in the dictionary. If it has seen this story before, it bets on the same ending.

Example 5.15: LZ78Y prediction estimate

The standard's illustration uses \(S = (2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2)\) with \(B = 4\), so \(N = 8\). This gives correct \(= (0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0)\), so \(P_{global} = 0.5\), \(P'_{global} = 0.9868\) and \(P_{local} = 0.1229\). The estimate is 0.0191 bits.

The mathematics.

\[\text{prediction} = \arg\max_{y}\ D[\mathrm{prev}][y] \text{ over the context lengths } j = B, \ldots, 1, \qquad B = 16, \qquad N = L - B - 1\]
  • \(D[\mathrm{prev}][y]\) counts how often string prev was followed by \(y\).
  • Each new sample updates every substring of the last \(B\) samples, and the dictionary stops growing at 65,536 entries.
  • Starting from the longest context, a shorter one replaces the current choice only if its count is higher. Ties between values go to the higher value.
  • \(C\), \(r\), \(P'_{global}\), \(P_{local}\) and \(H\) follow the MultiMCW formulas above.

What it catches and misses. It catches repeated strings of up to 16 samples, whether or not they sit at a fixed lag. Once the dictionary fills, strings not already stored are never added, so structure that first appears late in a long stream can be missed.

docs.title: 5.16 Restart tests
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. A source might give a good estimate from one long run, yet start up the same way every time. An attacker who can reboot your device would love that. So we restart the source 1000 times, take 1000 samples each time, and check both across and along the results. It is like checking that a shuffled deck is not in the same order after every break.

Example 5.16: Restart tests

Suppose \(H_I = 8\), so \(p = 2^{-8}\). If the highest count in any row or column is 15, then \(\Pr(X \ge 15) = 1.44 \times 10^{-5}\), above the limit of \(5 \times 10^{-6}\), so the sanity check passes. A highest count of 16 gives \(3.41 \times 10^{-6}\) and fails.

The mathematics.

\[\Pr(X \ge X_{max}) = \sum_{j=X_{max}}^{1000} \binom{1000}{j} p^j (1-p)^{1000-j} < \alpha \implies \text{fail}, \qquad p = 2^{-H_I}, \quad \alpha = 0.000005\] \[H_r, H_c \text{ estimated on row and column data}, \qquad \min(H_r, H_c) < \frac{H_I}{2} \implies \text{fail}, \qquad H = \min(H_r, H_c, H_I)\]
  • \(X_{max}\) is the highest count of any value in any row or column of the \(1000 \times 1000\) matrix.
  • \(H_I\) is the initial estimate from earlier.
  • \(\alpha = 0.000005\) gives 0.01 overall across 2000 experiments.

What it catches and misses. It catches correlated start-up behaviour, and it is unique in testing the source across restarts. It needs real restarts, so it cannot be run from a stored file, and it only tests the restart process you define, under normal conditions.

docs.title: 5.17 Repetition count test (RCT)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This is a smoke alarm, running all the time inside the device. If the same sample repeats too many times in a row, the source has probably stuck. It is cheap and quick, and NIST describes it as an update of the older stuck test from FIPS modules.

Example 5.17: Repetition count test (RCT)

With \(\alpha = 2^{-20}\) and \(H = 2\) bits per sample, \(C = 1 + \lceil 20/2 \rceil = 11\), the standard's example. A source assessed at 8 bits with \(C = 6\) gives a false alarm about once in \(10^{12}\) samples, as the standard notes.

The mathematics.

\[C = 1 + \left\lceil \frac{-\log_2 \alpha}{H} \right\rceil\]
  • \(H\) is the assessed min-entropy per sample, and \(\alpha\) is the accepted false-alarm probability.
  • The chance of \(C\) identical samples in a row is at most \(2^{-H(C-1)}\).
  • An error is raised when a sample repeats \(C\) or more times. NIST recommends \(\alpha\) between \(2^{-20}\) and \(2^{-40}\).

How a laboratory sets \(H\). NIST tests against the developer's claimed \(H\), so the lab accepts one as the declared min-entropy. Without a claim it uses the sample's most common value estimate, because the fuller assessment collapses on a single stuck patch and would hide the fault under test. If \(H\) is so low that a cutoff cannot be reached, a measured value fails the test and a declared value skips it. The same applies to the APT below.

What it catches and misses. It catches total failure, where the source gets stuck. NIST is frank that it is not very powerful. If that 8-bit source drops to 4 bits per sample, each sample matching the last with chance \(1/16\), it would still take about a million samples to notice.

docs.title: 5.18 Adaptive proportion test (APT)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This alarm watches for a subtler failure, where one value becomes too common without necessarily repeating in a row. Take a sample, then count how often it comes up in the next window. If the count hits a cutoff, the source has probably lost entropy. It is like spotting that one face of a die has started turning up too often.

Example 5.18: Adaptive proportion test (APT)

The standard's table for \(\alpha = 2^{-20}\) follows. We recomputed every entry and they all match.

Binary, \(W = 1024\): \(H\) Cutoff \(C\) Non-binary, \(W = 512\): \(H\) Cutoff \(C\) 0.2 941 0.5 410 0.4 840 1 311 0.6 748 2 177 0.8 664 4 62 1 589 8 13

The mathematics.

\[\Pr(B \ge C) \le \alpha, \qquad B \sim \mathrm{Binomial}\!\left(W, 2^{-H}\right), \qquad C = 1 + \mathrm{CRITBINOM}\!\left(W, 2^{-H}, 1 - \alpha\right)\]
  • \(W\) is the window size: 1024 for binary sources and 512 otherwise.
  • \(B\) counts how often the window's first sample occurs in the window, including itself.
  • CRITBINOM is the spreadsheet function giving the smallest count whose cumulative binomial probability reaches \(1 - \alpha\).

For binary sources, a developer may also check that \(W - B\) stays below \(C\).

What it catches and misses. It catches a large loss of entropy from a physical fault or a change in environment. It follows only the first value of each window, so it needs some windows to see the fault. Failures that keep all value frequencies normal, such as a predictable cycle, pass straight through.

docs.title: 5.19 Summary
docs.text:
• SP 800-90B estimates min-entropy per sample of a raw noise source, from at least \(10^6\) consecutive samples and a \(1000\times1000\) restart matrix. The result is the minimum over the estimators, which is deliberately cautious.
  • The IID track applies only if the samples are claimed i.i.d. and the permutation, chi-square and longest-repeated-substring tests find nothing; everything else follows the non-IID track with the most-common-value, collision, Markov, compression, t-tuple, LRS and four predictor estimators.
  • The predictor estimators (MultiMCW, Lag, MultiMMC and LZ78Y) turn guessing into entropy: if a predictor beats chance, the data is predictable. A failure to predict is not proof of entropy.
  • Restart tests check that a source does not start up the same way each time. RCT and APT are the continuous health tests: RCT catches a stuck source, APT catches one value becoming too common.
  • The estimators support an analysis of the source; they do not replace it. A cleverly deterministic source can score high, which is why a design rationale is required.

docs.title: 5.20 Exercises
docs.text:
1. Three values have probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.25. Find the Shannon entropy and the min-entropy. Which does SP 800-90B use, and why?

    Answer

    Shannon: \(-0.5\log_20.5-2\times0.25\log_20.25=0.5+1=1.5\) bits. Min-entropy: \(-\log_20.5=1\) bit. SP 800-90B uses min-entropy, because security depends on the attacker's best single guess, which is the most likely value.

  2. Apply the most common value estimate to a sample of \(L=100\) values in which the most common value appears 30 times.

    Answer

    \(\hat p=0.30\). Then \(p_u=0.30+2.576\sqrt{0.30\times0.70/99}=0.30+2.576\times0.0461=0.4186\) and the estimate is \(-\log_2 0.4186=1.256\) bits per sample.

  3. Find the repetition count cutoff \(C=1+\lceil20/H\rceil\) for \(H=2\), \(H=4\) and \(H=8\) bits per sample at \(\alpha=2^{-20}\). What happens to the cutoff as \(H\) rises, and why?

    Answer

    \(H=2\): \(C=11\). \(H=4\): \(C=6\). \(H=8\): \(C=4\). As the source is assessed to have more entropy, a long run of identical samples becomes less plausible, so the cutoff falls: a run of 4 identical bytes from an 8-bit source is already very unlikely.

  4. Why does the most-common-value estimate alone overestimate the entropy of a stream that simply alternates 0, 1, 0, 1, ...?

    Answer

    The two values are equally common, so \(\hat p\) is close to 0.5 and the estimate is close to a full bit per sample. But the stream is completely predictable. The MCV estimate sees only frequencies and is blind to dependence, which is why the other estimators exist and why the final answer is the minimum over all of them.

  5. Why are restart tests needed, and why can they not be run from a stored file?

    Answer

    A source might give a good estimate from one long run yet start up the same way every time, which an attacker who can reboot the device would exploit. The restart tests restart the source 1000 times, take 1000 samples each time, and check the rows and columns of the resulting matrix. They need genuine restarts, so a stored file of one long run cannot supply them.

docs.title: Chapter 7: FIPS 140-2 and BSI AIS 31
docs.text: Two standards come from the world of certification rather than research. The FIPS 140-2 power-up tests are four quick checks on 20,000 bits, designed to run inside a device at start-up; they were struck out of the standard in 2002 but remain widely known. BSI's AIS 20 and AIS 31 are the evaluation method for random number generators in the German Common Criteria scheme, and they take a different view altogether: statistical tests are not enough for a physical generator, which needs a stochastic model and on-board tests. This chapter covers both.

docs.title: 7.1 About the FIPS 140-2 power-up tests
docs.text: FIPS 140-2 (May 2001) is the US standard for cryptographic modules. Its section 4.9.1 originally listed four quick statistical checks on one stream of 20,000 bits from each generator, meant to run inside a device at power-up or on demand. There are no p-values here: each test has fixed limits, and a block either passes or fails. They do not have a long life in the standard. Change Notice 1 (10 October 2001) corrected the runs intervals, and Change Notice 2 (3 December 2002) struck all four tests out of section 4.9.1, along with the related requirement in section 4.7.1, so the statistical tests are no longer FIPS 140-2 requirements. We include them because they remain widely known and because BSI's T1 to T4 descend from the same family in FIPS 140-1, with wider limits.

docs.title: 7.2 Monobit (FIPS 140-2)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Count the ones in 20,000 bits. A fair source gives close to 10,000. The limits are wide enough that a healthy device will almost never trip them. It is a sanity check, like asking whether a coin has two heads.

Example 7.2: Monobit (FIPS 140-2)

A block with 10,100 ones passes, as \(9725 < 10100 < 10275\). A block with 10,275 ones fails, since the limits are strict. The limit is about 3.89 standard deviations out, as \(\sigma = \sqrt{5000} = 70.71\).

The mathematics.

\[X = \sum_{i=1}^{20000} b_i, \qquad \text{pass if } 9725 < X < 10275\]
  • \(b_i\) is bit \(i\), and \(X\) is the count of ones.
  • Under a fair source, \(X\) is Binomial(20000, 1/2). We compute a false-failure rate of about \(1.03 \times 10^{-4}\) per block.

The standard gives only the limits, with no p-value.

What it catches and misses. It catches a dead or badly biased source at start-up. A pattern as simple as 0101... passes. So it is an alarm for disasters, not a test of quality.

docs.title: 7.3 Poker (FIPS 140-2)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Cut the block into 5000 pieces of 4 bits and count each of the 16 possible values. They should appear about equally often, but not too exactly: real randomness has some wobble. So the test fails a block that is too lumpy, and also one that is too even.

Example 7.3: Poker (FIPS 140-2)

If the counts are eight values at 300 and eight at 325, \(X = 8.0\), which passes. If they are all 312 or 313, \(X = 0.0128\), below 2.16, so the block fails as too even. If one value fills all 5000 slots, \(X = 75000\).

The mathematics.

\[X = \frac{16}{5000} \sum_{i=0}^{15} f(i)^2 - 5000, \qquad \text{pass if } 2.16 < X < 46.17\]
  • \(f(i)\) is the count of 4-bit value \(i\).
  • \(X\) is approximately chi-square with 15 degrees of freedom. On that basis, the limits leave about \(5 \times 10^{-5}\) in each tail, by our calculation.

What it catches and misses. It catches bias in short patterns and sources that are suspiciously regular. It looks only at aligned 4-bit pieces, so a defect that lies across piece boundaries may be missed.

docs.title: 7.4 Runs (FIPS 140-2)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Count the runs of each length, separately for ones and zeros. About half of all runs should be length 1, a quarter length 2, and so on. There are 12 counts and each must land in its own interval, so it checks the whole shape, not just the total.

Example 7.4: Runs (FIPS 140-2)

The expected number of runs of length 1 of one value is \((20000 - 1 + 3)/2^3 = 2500.25\), comfortably in the middle of 2315 to 2685. A block with 2700 runs of length 1 fails.

The mathematics.

Run length Required interval, corrected by Change Notice 1 Interval first published 1 2315 to 2685 2343 to 2657 2 1114 to 1386 1135 to 1365 3 527 to 723 542 to 708 4 240 to 384 251 to 373 5 103 to 209 111 to 201 6 or more 103 to 209 111 to 201 \[r(n, i) = \frac{n - i + 3}{2^{i+2}}\]
  • All 12 counts, for ones and for zeros, must lie in the interval for their length. Runs longer than 6 count as length 6.
  • \(r(n, i)\) is the expected number of runs of length \(i\) of one value in \(n\) bits, a formula quoted in BSI's document.

What it catches and misses. It catches sticky or over-alternating sources. Since it counts runs without regard to position, it is blind to where they fall in the block.

docs.title: 7.5 Long run (FIPS 140-2)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. If 26 or more identical bits appear in a row anywhere in the block, the test fails. In a good source that is rare, so a long run strongly suggests something has stuck, even briefly. It is the simplest of the four.

Example 7.5: Long run (FIPS 140-2)

A run of 25 passes, and a run of 26 fails. For either bit value, the expected number of such runs in 20,000 bits is about \(20000 \cdot 2^{-26} = 0.0003\), so about three good blocks in 10,000 would fail by chance.

The mathematics.

\[\text{pass if } \max_{\text{runs}} (\text{run length}) < 26\]
  • Runs of zeros and of ones both count.
  • The 0.0003 above is our own estimate, not a number from the standard.

What it catches and misses. It catches a source that sticks briefly, which an average would hide. It tells you nothing about anything shorter than 26 bits, and it would not catch a source that fails slowly.

docs.title: 7.6 About BSI AIS 31
docs.text:
BSI, Germany's federal cybersecurity office, uses AIS 20 and AIS 31 as the evaluation method for random number generators in its Common Criteria certification scheme. Common Criteria is the international framework for evaluating the security of IT products. The tests here come from the technical document by Killmann and Schindler, version 2.0 (18 September 2011). Its core idea differs from everything above: statistical tests are not enough for a physical generator. You also need a stochastic model of the noise source and on-board tests. It defines classes such as PTG.1, PTG.2 and PTG.3 for physical generators, DRG.1 to DRG.4 for deterministic ones, and NTG.1 for non-physical true generators. Tests have fixed limits and a retest rule, and T0 to T8 are grouped into procedures A and B below.

An important update: version 3.0 (Peter and Schindler, September 2024) replaces this arrangement. It removes class PTG.1 and allows min-entropy claims. Its black-box suite for PTG.2 has four tests on 2,040,000 bits: monobit (pass from 9655 to 10345), poker (\(1.03 < t < 57.4\)), and the MultiMMC and LZ78Y predictors from SP 800-90B, on \(10^6\) bits each, failing below 0.95. Version 3.0 calls this suite a sanity check and says passing alone does not warrant a meaningful statement about quality. Read T0 to T8 as the 2011 scheme.

docs.title: 7.7 T0: disjointness test
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Take 65,536 words of 48 bits. There are so many possible 48-bit words that two matching words should almost never happen. If any two are the same, the test fails. It is the birthday problem with a very long year.

Example 7.7: T0: disjointness test

The number of pairs is \(2^{16}(2^{16} - 1)/2\), and each pair matches with chance \(2^{-48}\). So the chance of a match on ideal data is about \(7.63 \times 10^{-6}\), which is the document's \(2^{-17}\).

The mathematics.

\[\text{pass if and only if } w_1, \ldots, w_{2^{16}} \text{ are all different}, \qquad w_i \in \{0, 1\}^{48}\]
  • \(w_i\) are the 48-bit words, taken from consecutive outputs.
  • The rejection probability for an ideal generator is \(2^{-17}\).

What it catches and misses. It catches short cycles and repeated output, and very small effective state. It reads only 65,536 words, though, so a generator whose period is just above that passes as long as no word repeats within the cycle, however weak its statistics are.

docs.title: 7.8 T1: monobit test
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Count ones in 20,000 bits, just like the FIPS test, but with wider limits. BSI wants the chance of a false alarm in a single test to be about one in a million, because this test is repeated 257 times.

Example 7.8: T1: monobit test

A block with 10,300 ones fails FIPS 140-2 but passes T1, since \(9654 < 10300 < 10346\). At the top of the band, the share of ones is 0.5173, for which the document gives a min-entropy of at least 0.9509 and a Shannon entropy of at least 0.9991.

The mathematics.

\[T_1 = \sum_{j=1}^{20000} b_j, \qquad \text{pass if and only if } 9654 < T_1 < 10346\]
  • \(b_j\) is bit \(j\).
  • We compute the false-failure rate on ideal data as about \(1.03 \times 10^{-6}\) per block.

What it catches and misses. It catches gross bias. Its limits are too wide for mild bias, which is why the 257 repetitions and the stricter T6 exist. It is blind to order.

docs.title: 7.9 T2: poker test
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Same as the FIPS poker test: count the 16 possible 4-bit values across 5000 pieces. Too lumpy fails, and so does too even. Again, the limits are wider so that good data rarely trips the alarm.

Example 7.9: T2: poker test

Counts of eight values at 300 and eight at 325 give \(T_2 = 8.0\), inside the band. Perfectly even counts of 312 and 313 give 0.0128, below 1.03, and fail.

The mathematics.

\[T_2 = \frac{16}{5000} \sum_{i=0}^{15} f[i]^2 - 5000, \qquad \text{pass if } 1.03 < T_2 < 57.4\]
  • \(f[i]\) counts the 4-bit value \(i\), built as \(c_j = 8b_{4j-3} + 4b_{4j-2} + 2b_{4j-1} + b_{4j}\).
  • For an ideal generator, \(T_2\) is chi-square with 15 degrees of freedom. The document gives a rejection probability of \(1.014 \times 10^{-6}\), which our calculation reproduces.

What it catches and misses. It catches short-pattern bias and excess regularity. It is limited to aligned 4-bit pieces.

docs.title: 7.10 T3: runs test
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Same idea as the FIPS runs test: 12 counts of runs of each length and value, each inside its own interval. It checks the whole shape of the run-length distribution, with limits set for a one-in-a-million false alarm rate.

Example 7.10: T3: runs test

The expected count for length 1 is about 2500, so a block with 2740 runs of length 1 fails, as it is over the limit of 2733. A block with 2700 fails FIPS 140-2, whose corrected limit is 2685, but passes here.

The mathematics.

Run length Lower bound Upper bound 1 2267 2733 2 1079 1421 3 502 748 4 223 402 5 90 223 6 or more 90 223
  • \(T_3(\ell, p)\) is the number of runs of length \(\ell\) of value \(p\). Runs longer than 5 are summed together into the last row.
  • All 12 counts must lie within their bounds. The rejection probability is about \(10^{-6}\).

What it catches and misses. It catches over-alternating or sticky behaviour. It does not see where runs fall, nor relations between one run and the next.

docs.title: 7.11 T4: long run test
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. If any run of 34 or more identical bits appears, the block fails. It is the same simple alarm as in FIPS, with a longer limit to match this standard's lower false-alarm rate.

Example 7.11: T4: long run test

A run of 33 passes, and a run of 34 fails. By the same estimate as before, the expected number on good data is \(20000 \cdot 2^{-34} = 1.16 \times 10^{-6}\).

The mathematics.

\[\text{pass if and only if } T_3(\ell, p) = 0 \text{ for all } \ell \ge 34 \text{ and } p \in \{0, 1\}\]
  • \(T_3(\ell, p)\) is the count of runs of length \(\ell\) and value \(p\).
  • The document gives a rejection probability of about \(10^{-6}\).

What it catches and misses. It catches a source that sticks for at least 34 bits. Shorter stuck periods can pass, and repeated runs of 33 would not be flagged here.

docs.title: 7.12 T5: autocorrelation test
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Compare a sequence with a shifted copy of itself. If the bits are independent, they should agree about half the time, whatever the shift. If agreement at some shift is way off, the source has a memory or rhythm. This is the only test in T1 to T5 that looks directly at dependence at a distance.

Example 7.12: T5: autocorrelation test

Over 5000 comparisons, we expect 2500 with \(\sigma = \sqrt{1250} = 35.36\). The limits 2326 and 2674 sit 174 away, about 4.92 standard deviations. So a count of 2700 at some shift fails.

The mathematics.

\[T_5(\tau) = \sum_{j=1}^{5000} \left(b_j \oplus b_{j+\tau}\right), \qquad \text{pass if and only if } 2326 < T_5(\tau) < 2674\]
  • \(\tau\) is the shift, from 1 to 5000, and \(\oplus\) is exclusive or.
  • \(b_1\) to \(b_{10000}\) are the 10,000 input bits.
  • In procedure A, the worst shift on the first half of a block is chosen, and then tested on the second half, so that picking the worst shift does not bias the result.
  • The rejection probability is about \(10^{-6}\) per test.

What it catches and misses. It catches periodic structure and memory, up to a lag of 5000 bits. It sees only linear pairwise agreement, so a higher-order dependence that leaves each pair balanced would slip through.

docs.title: 7.13 T6: uniform distribution test
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Count how often each \(k\)-bit word appears as a share of the total, and check that every share stays within a small band around the fair value. It is a direct, strict check of frequency. In procedure B, this is the first test applied to raw bits.

Example 7.13: T6: uniform distribution test

With \(k = 1\), \(n = 100{,}000\) and \(a = 0.025\), the share of ones must lie between 0.475 and 0.525. A share of 0.53 fails. On unbiased data, the band is about 15.8 standard deviations wide on each side, so a failure means a real bias.

The mathematics.

\[T_6(x) = \frac{\lvert \{j : w_j = x\} \rvert}{n}, \qquad \text{pass if } T_6(x) \in \left[2^{-k} - a,\ 2^{-k} + a\right] \text{ for all } x \in \{0, 1\}^k\]
  • \(w_j\) are the \(k\)-bit words, and \(n\) is how many there are.
  • \(a\) is the allowed tolerance.

What it catches and misses. It catches meaningful bias in raw bits, which is what matters for a physical source. This band is wide by design, as AIS 31 expects a slightly biased raw source. Small biases that are harmless to entropy pass, and it says nothing about dependence.

docs.title: 7.14 T7: comparative test (homogeneity)
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Do two sets of data come from the same distribution? Here that question is asked about transitions. For example: does the next bit behave the same after context "00" as after "10"? If so, the bit two steps back has no further effect. This lets the source have a small one-step memory while ruling out longer ones.

Example 7.14: T7: comparative test (homogeneity)

Suppose the next bit gives 50,200 and 49,800 in one context, and 49,700 and 50,300 in the other, with 100,000 each. Then \(T_7 = 5.00\), which is below the limit of 15.137 at \(\alpha = 0.0001\) on 1 degree of freedom, so it passes.

The mathematics.

\[p_t = \frac{f_1[t] + \cdots + f_h[t]}{hn}, \qquad T_7(h, s) = \sum_{i=1}^{h} \sum_{t=0}^{s-1} \frac{(f_i[t] - np_t)^2}{np_t}\]
  • \(h\) is the number of samples compared, \(s\) the number of outcomes, and \(n\) the number of trials per sample.
  • \(f_i[t]\) counts outcome \(t\) in sample \(i\), and \(p_t\) is the pooled share.
  • The test fails if \(T_7\) exceeds the chi-square bound with \((h-1)(s-1)\) degrees of freedom at level \(\alpha\).

What it catches and misses. It catches dependence on more than one earlier bit, up to the contexts tested. It only compares contexts with each other, so if both are biased in the same way, it would not notice.

docs.title: 7.15 T8: entropy estimation
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This one, due to Coron, refines Maurer's universal test. For each 8-bit word, look at how far back it last appeared, and turn that distance into an entropy score. Under the right assumptions, the average is an estimate of entropy per word. BSI requires that it comes out close to the full 8 bits.

Example 7.15: T8: entropy estimation

The function \(g\) gives \(g(1) = 0\), \(g(2) = 1.4427\), \(g(3) = 2.1640\) and \(g(5) = 3.0056\). If four test words had distances 3, 1, 5, 6, then \(f_C = (2.1640 + 0 + 3.0056 + 3.2942)/4 = 2.1160\). That is far too short and far too low for the real test, which uses \(K = 256{,}000\) words.

The mathematics.

\[f_C = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{n=Q+1}^{Q+K} g(A_n), \qquad g(i) = \frac{1}{\ln 2} \sum_{k=1}^{i-1} \frac{1}{k}\]
  • \(A_n\) is the distance back to the last occurrence of word \(w_n\), or \(n\) if there is none.
  • \(L\) is the word length, and \(Q\) and \(K\) are the warm-up and test counts.
  • Procedure B uses \(L = 8\), \(Q = 2560\) and \(K = 256{,}000\), and passes if \(f_C > 7.976\).
  • That limit is \(8 \times 0.997\), tying in with the 0.997 bits of Shannon entropy that class PTG.2 requires per bit.
  • For independent bits, the expected value is \(L\) times the entropy per bit.

What it catches and misses. It gives an entropy estimate, but only if the source is stationary with a finite memory and the transition effects are negligible. It is a Shannon-style estimate, not min-entropy, so it can sit above the attacker's best guess.

docs.title: 7.16 Procedure A
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Procedure A checks that outputs look statistically unremarkable. It runs T0 once, then T1 to T5 on each of 257 blocks. It is for all kinds of generators, applied to internal random numbers, and it checks the traces of each bit position as well as the whole words.

Example 7.16: Procedure A

The total input is \(2^{16} \times 48 = 3{,}145{,}728\) bits for T0, plus \(20000 \times 257 = 5{,}140{,}000\) bits for the rest. If one of those tests fails, you run the whole procedure once more on new data. If two fail, the procedure fails outright.

The mathematics.

\[\text{number of basic tests} = 1 + 257 \times 5 = 1286\]
  • The document prints 1285 beside this sum, which we take as a slip.
  • Passing all basic tests passes the procedure, which happens with probability 0.9987 for an ideal generator.
  • If more than one fails, the procedure fails.
  • If exactly one fails, you repeat once on fresh data, and any failure in the repeat fails the procedure.

What it catches and misses. It catches statistical defects in the output and in individual bit positions. Output from a well-seeded software generator passes, so it says nothing about true entropy.

docs.title: 7.17 Procedure B
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Procedure B is mainly for raw bits from a physical source, and its target is entropy per bit. A small bias and slight one-step dependence are allowed, but dependence further back is not. Think of it as checking that a coin may be slightly unfair, and slightly sticky, but has no longer memory.

Example 7.17: Procedure B

The five steps need at least 100,000, then 400,000, 1,200,000 and 3,200,000 bits, then 2,068,480 bits for T8, a total of 6,968,480 bits if every class fills evenly. A biased source needs more, because the input is not fixed in advance.

The mathematics.

Step Test Rule 1 T6 with \((k, n, a) = (1, 100000, 0.025)\) as T6 2 one-step transitions from 100,000 pairs per first bit \(\lvert u_{emp(0)}(1) + u_{emp(1)}(0) - 1 vert < 0.02\) 3 T7 on 2-step transitions, for each middle bit \(\alpha = 0.0001\), 2 comparisons 4 T7 on 3-step transitions, for each pair of middle bits \(\alpha = 0.0001\), 4 comparisons 5 T8 with \(L = 8\), \(Q = 2560\), \(K = 256000\) \(f_C > 7.976\)
  • \( u_{emp(r)}(i)\) is the observed chance of bit \(i\) following bit \(r\).
  • That gives \(1 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 9\) basic tests. All passing passes the procedure, with probability 0.9998 for an ideal generator.
  • The retest rule is the same as for procedure A.

What it catches and misses. It catches low entropy and longer-term dependence in raw data. It cannot on its own prove entropy, because the T8 estimate relies on assumptions that the stochastic model has to justify.

docs.title: 7.18 Stochastic model requirement
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. This is not a test but a requirement, and it is the heart of AIS 31 for classes PTG.2 and PTG.3. You must explain mathematically how the noise source makes randomness, and from that derive a lower bound on entropy. Tests of data alone can never establish that bound, as a well-made deterministic generator passes them too.

Example 7.18: Stochastic model requirement

Coin tossing is the simplest teaching case, and version 3.0 opens its examples with it. If each bit is independent with bias \(\varepsilon\), so that \(P(1) = 0.5 + \varepsilon\), then the entropy per bit is a known function of \(\varepsilon\). At \(\varepsilon = 0.0173\), the Shannon entropy per bit is 0.99914. The model turns one measurable parameter into an entropy bound. Models of real noise circuits are much harder.

The mathematics.

\[H_1 \approx n\left(1 - \frac{2\varepsilon^2}{\ln 2}\right) \text{ for small bias}, \qquad H_{min}(n, \varepsilon) = -n\log_2(0.5 + \lvert \varepsilon \rvert)\]
  • \(n\) is the number of independent bits, and \(\varepsilon\) is the bias as above.
  • \(H_1\) is Shannon entropy and \(H_{min}\) is min-entropy. These are the forms in the document's monobit discussion, and they match its figures for T1.
  • In general, the model gives a family of distributions with parameters that can be estimated from samples.
  • Class PTG.2 requires average Shannon entropy above 0.997 per internal random bit.

What it catches and misses. It addresses what black-box testing cannot: why the numbers should be unpredictable at all. A model is only as good as its assumptions, so the standard requires checking it against data, and it depends on the true physical design being known.

docs.title: 7.19 Online and total-failure tests
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. A generator can break while in the field, so AIS 31 requires alarms in the device itself. A total-failure test detects a complete breakdown of the noise source, and output must stop immediately. An online test looks for intolerable statistical defects as the device runs. These are the same kind of idea as SP 800-90B's health tests.

Example 7.19: Online and total-failure tests

Suppose an amplifier in a noise circuit dies, so the digitiser gives all zeros. A tot test built on run length would catch that quickly, and the device must then stop producing output. Each design chooses its own tests to fit its failure modes, and section 5.5 of the document shows worked examples.

The mathematics. The document does not fix one formula, because the tests depend on the design. Its requirements are as follows.

  • The tot test must detect a total failure of the source quickly, and it must prevent further output. Some latency is allowed if, for example, entropy is stored in the internal state.
  • The online test may run on raw numbers (for PTG.2 and PTG.3) or on internal numbers (allowed in PTG.1).
  • PTG.1 needs a tot test and an online test, and PTG.2 adds a stochastic model and raw-data tests.

What it catches and misses. These tests catch breakdowns during operation, which a one-off lab evaluation never could. They catch only the failures their designers foresaw, and an online test after heavy post-processing may see nothing wrong even when the source has died, which is why tests on raw numbers are preferred.

docs.title: 7.20 Summary
docs.text:
• The FIPS 140-2 tests (monobit, poker, runs, long run) have fixed pass limits on one 20,000-bit block, not p-values. They were removed by Change Notice 2 (3 December 2002), but BSI's T1 to T4 descend from the same family, with wider limits.
  • The limits are chosen so that a good source fails very rarely: about \(1.03\times10^{-4}\) per block for the monobit test and about \(10^{-6}\) for the poker and long-run tests.
  • AIS 31 (version 2.0, 2011) groups tests T0 to T8 into procedure A (for deterministic generators, about 8.3 million bits) and procedure B (for physical generators, including the entropy estimate T8).
  • AIS 31's core idea is the stochastic model: the vendor must justify, from the physics of the device, why the entropy claim holds, and online and total-failure tests must catch breakdowns in operation.
  • Version 3.0 (2024) removes class PTG.1, allows min-entropy claims, and calls its black-box suite a sanity check.

docs.title: 7.21 Exercises
docs.text:
1. A 20,000-bit block has 10,280 ones. Does it pass the FIPS 140-2 monobit test (limits \(9725<X<10275\))? What about the AIS 31 T1 test (limits \(9654<X<10346\))?

    Answer

    It fails FIPS 140-2, because 10,280 is not below 10,275. It passes T1, because \(9654<10{,}280<10{,}346\). This shows that the AIS 31 limits are wider than those of FIPS 140-2.

  2. How many standard deviations from the mean is the upper FIPS 140-2 monobit limit?

    Answer

    The number of ones in 20,000 fair bits has mean 10,000 and standard deviation \(\sqrt{5000}=70.71\). The limit 10,275 is \(275/70.71=3.89\) standard deviations from the mean.

  3. Why were the FIPS 140-2 statistical tests struck out of the standard, and why does the book still describe them?

    Answer

    Change Notice 2 (3 December 2002) struck all four tests out of section 4.9.1, along with the related requirement in section 4.7.1, so they are no longer FIPS 140-2 requirements. They remain widely known, and BSI's T1 to T4 descend from the same family.

  4. Explain why AIS 31 insists on a stochastic model, and give the simplest example of one.

    Answer

    Statistical tests on output cannot say why the numbers should be unpredictable. The stochastic model explains from the physics of the noise source why the entropy claim holds, turning measurable parameters into an entropy bound. The simplest example is coin tossing: if each bit is independent with \(P(1)=0.5+\varepsilon\), the entropy per bit is a known function of \(\varepsilon\); at \(\varepsilon=0.0173\) the Shannon entropy is 0.99914 bits.

  5. A noise-circuit amplifier dies and the digitiser outputs only zeros. Which kind of AIS 31 test should catch this, and why must it run on raw numbers?

    Answer

    A total-failure test (one of the online tests) built on run length should catch it quickly, and the device must then stop producing output. It should run on raw numbers because after heavy post-processing the output may look fine even when the source has died.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
The terms below are used throughout the book. The chapter in which each is introduced is given in brackets.

Alpha (\(\alpha\)) The significance line chosen in advance. A test fails when its p-value is below \(\alpha\). This book uses \(\alpha=0.01\) (Chapter 1). APT (adaptive proportion test) An SP 800-90B health test that counts how often a window's first sample recurs in that window (Chapter 5). Bonferroni correction Reporting \(\min(1,Kp_{\min})\) for the smallest of \(K\) p-values. Valid under any dependence (Chapter 2). Chi-square (\(\chi^2\)) The distribution of summed squared misses, used for tests of counts in cells (Chapter 2). Conditioner A function, often a hash, that smooths the output of a physical source. Bits before conditioning are called raw (Chapter 1). CSPRNG A cryptographically secure pseudo-random generator: a formula designed so that nobody can predict its output with practical work (Chapter 1). Entropy, Shannon The average surprise per symbol, \(H=-\sum p_v\log_2p_v\) (Chapter 2). Entropy, min-entropy The surprise of the most likely symbol, \(H_{\min}=-\log_2\max p_v\). It governs an attacker's best guess (Chapter 2). i.i.d. Independent and identically distributed: the coin-flip model (Chapter 1). igamc The regularised upper incomplete gamma function, used to write the chi-square tail (Chapter 2). Kolmogorov-Smirnov test A test of whether a list of numbers follows a claimed distribution, using the largest gap between the empirical and claimed distribution functions (Chapter 2). Linear complexity The length of the shortest linear feedback shift register that produces a bit string (Chapter 4). Null hypothesis The boring claim that nothing is going on; here, that the data are i.i.d. fair coin flips (Chapter 1). p-value The probability, under the null hypothesis, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed (Chapter 1). PRNG A pseudo-random number generator: a formula with a short seed (Chapter 1). QRNG A quantum random number generator: a physical source based on a quantum process (Chapter 1). RCT (repetition count test) An SP 800-90B health test that raises an alarm when a sample repeats too many times in a row (Chapter 5). Sidak correction Reporting \(1-(1-p_{\min})^K\). Exact for independent results (Chapter 2). Stochastic model In AIS 31, the vendor's physical justification for why a noise source's entropy claim holds (Chapter 7). docs.title: Chapter 3: NIST SP 800-22 (I): Balance, Runs and Spectra
docs.text: NIST SP 800-22 is the best-known set of statistical tests for random and pseudo-random bit generators. It has fifteen tests, each of which turns a bit string into a p-value. This chapter covers the first six: the three counting tests (frequency, block frequency and runs), the longest-run test, the binary matrix rank test and the discrete Fourier transform test. They look at balance, local drift, oscillation, clustering, linear dependence between rows and hidden periodicity. The chapter after this one completes the suite.

docs.title: 3.1 The NIST SP 800-22 battery
docs.text:
Before we trust a random number generator, we want to know it has no obvious flaw. That is what the batteries in Chapters 3 to 8 are for: each one is a collection of experiments that good random data should survive, each tuned to catch a different kind of flaw. Keep one sentence in mind throughout. Passing means "no defect found", never "quantum". A well-built pseudorandom generator passes most of these batteries, so a pass cannot tell you where the numbers came from. We lean on Chapters 1 and 2 for p-values, the chi-square and normal distributions, and the functions erfc and igamc, and we will not explain those again.

This suite comes from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (Rukhin and colleagues, revised by Bassham, April 2010). It was written to test random and pseudorandom bit generators for cryptographic use, and it has 15 tests. Most need sequences of about \(10^6\) bits: the document says its reference distributions assume lengths of order \(10^3\) to \(10^7\) bits. You run many sequences, with the sample size on the order of \(1/\alpha\), so at least 1000 sequences at \(\alpha = 0.001\). Each test gives a p-value per sequence, compared with a significance level \(\alpha\) that NIST recommends keeping between 0.001 and 0.01. The results are then read at a second level across all sequences, which has its own section at the end. The document itself warns that no finite set of tests can be called complete. The worked examples below use the document's own strings, and they are deliberately too short for the real tests.

docs.title: 3.2 Frequency (monobit) test
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. Toss a fair coin many times and you expect about half heads. This test counts ones and zeros and asks whether the gap between them is bigger than chance allows. NIST recommends running it first, because almost nothing else matters if it fails.

Example 3.2: Frequency (monobit) test

Take the string 1011010101. Turning ones into \(+1\) and zeros into \(-1\) and adding gives \(S_{10} = 2\), so \(s_{obs} = 2/\sqrt{10} = 0.632456\) and the p-value is 0.527089. The standard's 100-bit example gives \(S_{100} = -16\), \(s_{obs} = 1.6\) and p-value 0.109599.

The mathematics.

\[S_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (2\varepsilon_i - 1), \qquad s_{obs} = \frac{\lvert S_n \rvert}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad p = \mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{s_{obs}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\]
  • \(\varepsilon_i\) is bit \(i\), and \(n\) is the number of bits (at least 100 is recommended).
  • \(S_n\) is the running total of the \(\pm 1\) values.
  • For large \(n\), \(s_{obs}\) follows a half normal distribution (a normal value with its sign dropped), which gives the erfc form.

What it catches and misses. It catches plain bias, such as a stuck or lopsided source. It knows nothing about order: 0101 0101 repeated forever has \(S_n = 0\) and scores a perfect p-value of 1.

docs.title: 3.3 Frequency test within a block
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. A coin could be fair overall yet run hot for a while and then cold. So we cut the sequence into blocks and check the share of ones in each, the way a teacher might check each class rather than just the school average.

Example 3.3: Frequency test within a block

With 0110011010 and block size \(M = 3\) we get blocks 011, 001, 101 and drop the final bit. The shares of ones are \(2/3\), \(1/3\), \(2/3\), so \(\chi^2 = 4 \cdot 3 \cdot (1/36 + 1/36 + 1/36) = 1\) and \(p = \mathrm{igamc}(3/2, 1/2) = 0.801252\).

The mathematics.

\[\pi_i = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{j=1}^{M} \varepsilon_{(i-1)M+j}, \qquad \chi^2 = 4M \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(\pi_i - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2, \qquad p = \mathrm{igamc}\!\left(\frac{N}{2}, \frac{\chi^2}{2}\right)\]
  • \(M\) is the block length and \(N = \lfloor n/M \rfloor\) is the number of blocks.
  • \(\pi_i\) is the share of ones in block \(i\).
  • \(\chi^2\) follows a chi-square distribution with \(N\) degrees of freedom.

The document asks for \(M \ge 20\), \(M > 0.01n\) and \(N < 100\).

What it catches and misses. It catches local drift that cancels out overall, such as a long stretch of ones followed by a long stretch of zeros, which monobit would pass. It ignores the order inside each block.

docs.title: 3.4 Runs test
docs.text:
The idea in plain words. A run is an unbroken stretch of the same bit. A sequence can have the right number of ones yet flip too often (0101...) or too rarely (long slabs). Think of a walker's zigzag: this test counts the turns.

Example 3.4: Runs test

The string 1001101011 has \(\pi = 3/5\) and splits into 1, 00, 11, 0, 1, 0, 11, so \(V_{10} = 7\). The formula gives \(p = 0.147232\). The 100-bit example has \(\pi = 0.42\), \(V = 52\) and \(p = 0.500798\).

The mathematics.

\[V_n = 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} r(k), \qquad p = \mathrm{erfc}\!\left(\frac{\lvert V_n - 2n\pi(1-\pi) \rvert}{2\sqrt{2n}\,\pi(1-\pi)}\right)\]
  • \(r(k) = 0\) if \(\varepsilon_k = \varepsilon_{k+1}\), and \(1\) otherwise.
  • \(\pi\) is the proportion of ones.
  • As a prerequisite, if \(\lvert \pi - 1/2 \rvert \ge 2/\sqrt{n}\) the test is not applicable and the p-value is set to 0.

What it catches and misses. It catches oscillation that is too fast or too slow. The standard's example is 100 ones, 73 zeros, 127 ones: only 3 runs where about 150 are expected. It looks only at the total number of runs, not at how they are arranged or how long each one is.

Try both tests on sequences of your own. Type bits, pick an example, or generate a sequence with a bias or a tendency to repeat the last bit, and read off the statistics and p-values. The last button repeats the experiment 200 times and draws the histogram of p-values.
